title: IYT Bareboat Skipper
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the IYT Bareboat Skipper theory syllabus. Not official IYT exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

topics.title: Nautical terms & parts of the boat

questions.q: You are at the helm, sailing with the wind over your right shoulder and the boom out to the left. Which tack are you on?

figure.note: Wind over the starboard side, boom to port

options: Starboard tack
Lee tack
Windward tack
Port tack
questions.why: The tack is named after the side the wind comes over.

questions.q: The skipper shouts "fender on the port quarter!". Where do you hang it?
options: Left side, near the bow
Left side, near the stern
Right side, near the bow
Right side, near the stern
questions.why: Port = left; quarter = the side near the stern.

questions.q: From this point of sail you want to turn to sail downwind. Which way do you turn the boat?
options: Heave to
Tack
Bear away — turn the bow away from the wind
Luff up — turn the bow towards the wind
questions.why: Bearing away takes you from close-hauled towards a run.

questions.q: The boat is on this heading relative to the wind. What point of sail is it?
options: Close-hauled
Broad reach
Run
Beam reach
questions.why: Wind on the beam, about 90° off the bow.

questions.q: The boat is pointing into the shaded sector. What happens?

figure.note: Red sector: about 45° either side of the wind

options: The sails flap and the boat stops — it is the no-go zone
The boat sails fastest
The boat gybes
The boat heels the most
questions.why: A yacht cannot sail closer than about 40–45° to the wind.

questions.q: The anchorage shows 2.4 m on the sounder at low water. The boat's draft is 1.9 m. Can you stay?
options: No — draft must be at least twice the depth
Yes — 0.5 m under the keel, but allow for swell
Only if you lift the keel
No — the mast is too tall
questions.why: Draft is the keel depth below the waterline; compare it with depth at low water.

questions.q: The genoa is flapping on a beam reach. Which line do you pull in?
options: The topping lift
The genoa halyard
The genoa sheet
The mainsheet
questions.why: Sheets trim sails; halyards only hoist them.

questions.q: Downwind the mainsail twists and the top spills wind. Which control pulls the boom down?
options: The backstay
The outhaul
The Cunningham
The kicker (boom vang)
questions.why: Off the wind the mainsheet no longer holds the boom down; the vang does.

questions.q: You are about to turn the stern through the wind on a run. What do you do first?
options: Centre the mainsheet and warn the crew: "Gybe-ho"
Drop the headsail
Release the kicker
Ease the mainsheet fully
questions.why: A controlled gybe keeps the boom from slamming across.

questions.q: Berthing in a marina with a strong crosswind, which yacht is harder to keep off the pontoon?
options: Freeboard makes no difference
The one with high freeboard — more hull for the wind to push
The one with a longer keel
The one with low freeboard
questions.why: Freeboard is the hull above the water: more freeboard, more windage.

questions.q: You need to put a loop in the end of a mooring line to drop over a bollard. Which knot?

figure.note: Loop in the end of a line

options: Clove hitch
Reef knot
Bowline
Figure of eight
questions.why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip and unties after loading.

questions.q: The jib sheet has run out through the block and is flogging. What stops this happening again?
options: A reef knot in the end of the sheet
A clove hitch round the block
A bowline tied to the clew
A figure of eight in the end of the sheet
questions.why: The stopper will not pass through the block.

questions.q: Hanging fenders on the guardrail before berthing, you want to adjust their height quickly. Which knot?
options: Clove hitch
Bowline
Sheet bend
Round turn and two half hitches
questions.why: Quick to tie and slide; not for anything that must not work loose.

questions.q: You must join the thin dinghy painter to a thick mooring line. Which knot?
options: Reef knot
Sheet bend
Bowline
Clove hitch
questions.why: A sheet bend holds ropes of different sizes; a reef knot can capsize.

questions.q: The dinghy is tugging hard on its painter and you must tie it to a ring on the quay. Which knot can you tie under load?
options: Figure of eight
Reef knot
Round turn and two half hitches
Sheet bend
questions.why: The round turn takes the load while you tie the hitches.

questions.q: This line is being made fast to a cleat. What completes it correctly?
options: Five round turns and no hitch
A bowline round the cleat
Two half hitches on the horn
A full turn round the base, figure-of-eight turns, one locking hitch
questions.why: The turn takes the load; the locking hitch holds without jamming.

questions.q: A riding turn has jammed the genoa sheet on the winch under full load. How do you free it?
options: Tie a rolling hitch on the sheet with a spare line, take the load on another winch, then clear the turns
Pull the tail harder to drag the riding turn through
Release the halyard
Cut the sheet
questions.why: The rolling hitch grips the loaded sheet and lets you transfer the load.

questions.q: You are choosing rope for a new anchor rode. Which material?
options: Polyester — low stretch
Nylon — it stretches and absorbs shock loads
Dyneema — strongest
Polypropylene — it floats
questions.why: Elastic nylon protects the boat and fittings in gusts and waves.

questions.q: The dinghy painter keeps sinking and nearly fouled the propeller. Which rope should it be?
options: Wire
Polyester
Polypropylene — it floats
Nylon
questions.why: A floating painter stays clear of the prop.

questions.q: You are loading the genoa sheet onto a winch in a fresh breeze. How many turns before you start winding?
options: As many as fit
Five, anticlockwise
One, anticlockwise
Two or three, clockwise, fingers clear of the drum
questions.why: Yacht winches turn clockwise; three turns give grip without a riding turn.

questions.q: You are crossing to the next island at night in 20 knots. Who wears a lifejacket?

figure.title: Night passage
lines: Crew of 5, two have never sailed

options: Everyone on deck, clipped on when going forward
Only non-swimmers
Nobody — the sea is moderate
Only the helm
questions.why: Night, fresh wind and deck work are the standard triggers.

questions.q: A pan of oil has caught fire on the galley stove. What do you do?

figure.title: Galley fire
lines: Pan of oil burning on the stove

options: Open all hatches
Turn off the gas, smother it with the fire blanket
Throw water on it
Carry the pan on deck
questions.why: Water turns to steam and spreads burning fat.

questions.q: Before lighting the stove you notice a faint gas smell in the cabin. What first?
options: Light the stove quickly to burn it off
Switch on the cabin fan
No flames or switches — ventilate, pump the bilge by hand, check the system
Start the engine to ventilate
questions.why: LPG sinks into the bilge; any spark can ignite it.

questions.q: You are driving the dinghy alone to the beach. Where is the kill cord?
options: Left on the yacht
In your pocket
Tied to the dinghy handle
Attached to your leg or lifejacket
questions.why: If you fall out, the cord pulls and the engine stops.

questions.q: A crew member goes over the side on a broad reach. What is the very first thing you shout and do?
options: "Man overboard!" — throw the danbuoy and horseshoe, point at the casualty
Send a Mayday
Start the engine
Drop the sails
questions.why: Flotation first and a spotter who never looks away.

questions.q: The yacht has hit a rock and is taking water, but the pumps are keeping up for now. The liferaft?
options: Launch and board it immediately
Prepare it on deck on its painter, but stay aboard while the yacht floats
Inflate it in the cockpit
Leave it stowed until the deck is awash
questions.why: "Step up into the liferaft" — the yacht is the better survival platform.

questions.q: The charter check-out is done and the crew are aboard. Before leaving the marina you…
options: Set the sails
Hand out the cabins
Give the safety briefing: lifejackets, gas, heads, fire, MOB, VHF, flares
Check their passports
questions.why: Everyone must know where the gear is and how to call for help.

questions.q: You have recovered a crew member after 15 minutes in 16 °C water. They shiver, mumble and cannot grip. What do you do?
options: Make them walk around the deck
Give brandy to warm them
Put them in a hot shower immediately
Handle gently and horizontally, strip wet clothes, insulate, warm slowly
questions.why: Hypothermia: gradual rewarming, no alcohol, no rough handling.

questions.q: During check-in you find the spare gas bottle stowed under the aft bunk. Where should it be?
options: In the gas locker that drains overboard
In the engine bay
Under the bunk is fine
In the cockpit locker with the fuel
questions.why: Leaking gas must drain over the side, not into the bilge.

questions.q: Reefing in a rising wind, the foredeck crew goes forward. What is clipped where?
options: Nothing — it only takes a minute
Harness tether to the jackstay before leaving the cockpit
Tether to the halyard
Tether to the guardrail
questions.why: Jackstays run the length of the deck; guardrails are not strong points.

questions.q: Both yachts are sailing. Who gives way?
options: The windward boat
She gives way
You — you are on port tack, she is on starboard
Neither
questions.why: Rule 12: port tack keeps clear of starboard tack.

questions.q: Both yachts are on starboard tack. Who gives way?
options: She gives way
The faster boat
The one to port
You — you are the windward boat
questions.why: Rule 12: same tack, windward keeps clear of leeward.

questions.q: You are motor-sailing with the engine in gear. A yacht under sail alone is crossing from your starboard. Who gives way?

figure.note: Your engine is running and in gear

options: You — under power you are a power-driven vessel
The one on port tack
She does — you have sails up
Nobody, both are sailing
questions.why: Rule 3: sail plus engine = power-driven; show the cone by day.

questions.q: Motoring, you see a motorboat crossing on this bearing, which has not changed for five minutes. What do you do?
options: Alter course to port
Give way — alter course to starboard, early and clearly, and pass astern of her
Hold course, she is to starboard so she gives way
Speed up to cross ahead
questions.why: Rule 15: she is on your starboard side, so you keep clear; avoid crossing ahead.

questions.q: Two motor yachts are meeting head-on in a channel. What do you do?
options: Stop and wait
Hold course — the bigger one moves
Alter course to starboard; pass port side to port side
Alter to port
questions.why: Rule 14: both turn to starboard.

questions.q: Under sail you are catching up a slow motorboat from astern. Who gives way?

figure.note: You are faster, approaching from well abaft her beam

options: The motorboat — sail has priority
Neither
The one to starboard
You — the overtaking vessel always keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 13 overrides sail-over-power.

questions.q: Under sail you meet a vessel with these shapes, towing nets. Who gives way?

figure.note: Two cones apexes together: vessel engaged in fishing

options: You — sail keeps clear of a vessel engaged in fishing
The fishing vessel
Whoever is on port tack
Neither, pass at a distance
questions.why: Rule 18: sail gives way to fishing, NUC and RAM.

questions.q: In sight of a ship, you hear one short blast from her. What is she telling you?
options: I am altering to port
I am altering my course to starboard
I am going astern
I do not understand your intentions
questions.why: One short: starboard; two: port; three: astern; five: doubt.

questions.q: You are sailing up a narrow channel with a ferry coming behind you. Where do you keep?
options: In the middle, you have right of way under sail
On the port side
As far to the starboard side of the channel as is safe, and do not impede the ferry
Tack across the channel freely
questions.why: Rule 9: keep right and do not hamper vessels confined to the channel.

questions.q: Motoring at night you see these lights on a steady bearing, closing. What vessel is it and what do you do?
options: A sailing vessel — hold course
A vessel at anchor — pass either side
A vessel overtaking you — hold course
A power-driven vessel crossing from your starboard — give way, turn to starboard
questions.why: Red sidelight with a masthead light above: a power vessel showing you her port side.

questions.q: You need the distance between two headlands on the chart. Where do you measure it?
options: On the latitude scale at the side, level with the position
On the longitude scale along the bottom
With the compass rose
Anywhere on the border
questions.why: One minute of latitude = one nautical mile; longitude minutes shrink with latitude.

questions.q: The chart gives this variation; your compass has no deviation. Your plotted true course is 090°. What do you steer?
questions.why: True to magnetic: add west ("west is best").

questions.q: The compass reads 215°C. Deviation on this heading is 3°E, variation 2°W. What is the true course?
questions.why: Compass → true: add east, subtract west: 215 + 3 − 2 = 216.

questions.q: The hand-bearing compass agrees with the steering compass on some headings but differs by 5° on others. What is this error?
options: Leeway
Tidal set
Variation
Deviation — the boat's own magnetic field
questions.why: Deviation changes with heading; variation does not.

questions.q: You left the marina at 09:30 and the log reads 12.0 M at 12:00. What has your average speed been?
options: 4.8 knots
6.0 knots
5.2 knots
4.0 knots
questions.why: 12 miles in 2.5 hours.

questions.q: Your draft is 1.9 m. Can you cross the shoal on the track at the time shown?

figure.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

options: No — 1.5 m is less than the draft
Yes — 1.5 m charted + 1.2 m tide = 2.7 m, about 0.8 m clearance
Only at low water
Only if the tide is falling
questions.why: Depth now = charted depth + height of tide.

questions.q: Which of the depths on this chart will dry at low water?

figure.note: Depths in metres · underlined = drying height

options: None of them
The 1.5
The underlined 0.8 — a drying height above chart datum
The 4
questions.why: Underlined figures are heights above datum that uncover.

questions.q: Entering harbour, the two beacons must be kept in line. What are they called and what do they give you?
options: A cardinal pair — safe water between them
A traffic lane
A range marker for distance
A transit (leading line) — a precise position line without a compass
questions.why: Two charted objects in line = one accurate position line.

questions.q: You take bearings of the lighthouse, the tower and the headland and plot them. They form a small triangle. Where are you?
options: Inside the cocked hat — take the corner nearest danger as your position
At the lighthouse bearing
You cannot tell without GPS
Halfway to the tower
questions.why: A three-bearing fix; the triangle shows the error.

questions.q: High water is 3.6 m, low water 1.2 m. What is the range, and what does the rule of twelfths say about the third hour of the rise?
options: Range 1.2 m; 3/12 in the third hour
Range 2.4 m; 3/12 of it (0.6 m) rises in the third hour
Range 4.8 m; 1/12 in the third hour
Range 2.4 m; half of it in the third hour
questions.why: Range = HW − LW; twelfths: 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1.

questions.q: Entering a Mediterranean harbour from seaward you see this buoy. Which side do you leave it on?
options: To starboard
Pass astern of it
To port
Either side
questions.why: Region A: red can to port when returning.

questions.q: This mark is ahead. Where is the safe water?
options: West of the mark
South of the mark
Either side
North of the mark
questions.why: North cardinal: black over yellow, both cones up.

questions.q: At night you see a white light flashing six times then one long flash. What is it and where do you pass?

figure.note: Night · six quick flashes, then one long

options: A south cardinal — pass south of it
A north cardinal — pass north
An isolated danger — any side
A west cardinal — pass west
questions.why: Clock face: 6 o'clock plus a long flash = south.

questions.q: You see this mark. Which way round do you go?
options: Through the middle
Keep clear, but you may pass on any side
Only to the north
Only to the east
questions.why: Isolated danger: black with red bands, two balls; danger right under it.

questions.q: This buoy is at the harbour approach. What does it tell you?
options: Danger right here
An anchorage limit
Safe water all round — a landfall or mid-channel mark
Keep to the west
questions.why: Red and white vertical stripes, red ball: safe water.

questions.q: A yellow buoy with this topmark sits off the beach. What is it?
options: A lateral mark
A wreck mark
A cardinal mark
A special mark — check the chart (swimming area, pipeline, spoil ground)
questions.why: Yellow with an X: not a navigation mark in itself.

questions.q: At night you see these lights ahead and no others. What is it?
options: A sailing vessel under sail (red over green masthead lights optional)
A trawler
A vessel aground
A pilot vessel
questions.why: Red over green at the masthead plus sidelights is a sailing vessel.

questions.q: You see a single steady white light low down, its bearing slowly changing. What is most likely?

figure.note: Night · steady white light, bearing drawing slowly left

options: A lighthouse
The sternlight of a vessel moving away — or an anchored vessel; watch the bearing
A fishing vessel
A vessel coming straight at you
questions.why: One white light: stern view or at anchor; only the bearing tells you which.

questions.q: At night you see these lights. What vessel, and who gives way?
options: A pilot vessel — hold course
A vessel not under command
A trawler — green over white; you keep clear under sail or power
A vessel towing
questions.why: Green over white = trawling; fishing has priority over sail.

questions.q: You are switching from sail to engine at night. Which lights do you turn on and off?

figure.note: Yacht under sail — about to start the engine

options: Only the all-round white
Tricolour and anchor light
Leave the tricolour on and add the steaming light
Off: tricolour. On: steaming light plus deck-level sidelights and sternlight
questions.why: Tricolour is for sail only; never with the steaming light.

questions.q: The forecast chart shows isobars packed tightly over your area tomorrow. What do you expect?
options: Strong wind — stay in port or reef early
Light variable winds
A sea breeze only
Calm and fog
questions.why: Close isobars = steep pressure gradient = strong wind.

questions.q: The low is to the north-west of you. From which direction will the wind blow?

figure.note: Low centre to the NW of the yacht

options: Straight towards the low
From the south-west, veering as the low passes
From the east, steady
From the north-east
questions.why: Northern hemisphere: wind anticlockwise round a low; Buys Ballot — back to wind, low on the left.

questions.q: The forecast says "F6, occasionally 7". What wind speed is that?
options: 4–6 knots
11–16 knots
About 22–33 knots
41–47 knots
questions.why: F6 is 22–27 kn, F7 28–33 kn — the limit for comfortable cruising.

questions.q: In three hours the barometer has fallen from 1012 to 1006 hPa. What does it mean for your afternoon passage?

figure.title: Barometer
lines: Sky: high cloud thickening from the west

options: Fog is likely
Fine settled weather
No change
A depression is approaching — expect strengthening wind; reconsider
questions.why: A fall of 6 hPa in 3 h is a strong warning.

questions.q: A hot sunny morning, calm. By 14:00 a steady 15-knot onshore wind has set in. What is it?
options: A sea breeze — it will die at sunset
The Meltemi
A land breeze
A front passing
questions.why: Warm land draws air in from the sea on sunny afternoons.

questions.q: Aegean, July. The forecast shows this pattern for a week. What wind?

figure.note: High to the NW, low over Anatolia to the E

options: Sea fog
The Meltemi — strong dry northerly, F5–7, strongest in the afternoon
A warm southerly
Thunderstorms
questions.why: High over the Balkans, low over Turkey: the Meltemi.

questions.q: Thin high cloud is thickening from the west, a halo rings the sun, the glass is falling. What is coming?
options: A sea breeze
Settled high pressure
A warm front — rain and strengthening wind within hours
A squall line in minutes
questions.why: Cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus is the warm-front sequence.

questions.q: You have no internet. Where do you get a reliable marine forecast?
options: Yesterday's newspaper
A crew member's guess
The marina bar
Navtex, the coastal VHF broadcast or the harbour office
questions.why: Use current official sources and note the time of issue.

questions.q: Wind F5 blowing against a 2-knot current in the strait you are about to enter. What sea do you expect?

figure.note: Wind from the north · current setting north at 2 kn

options: Short, steep breaking seas — worse than the wind suggests
A long smooth swell
No change
Flatter water
questions.why: Wind against tide shortens and steepens the waves.

questions.q: The forecast says visibility "poor". What does that mean for your passage?
options: Under 100 m
1000 m to 2 miles — post a lookout, slow down, sound fog signals if it closes
Normal summer haze
More than 5 miles
questions.why: Fog <1000 m; poor 1000 m–2 M; moderate 2–5 M; good >5 M.

questions.q: You anchor in 5 m at high water with all chain, settled weather. How much chain do you let out?
options: 5 m
At least 24 m (4 × depth to the roller), more if wind is expected
questions.why: Chain scope 4:1 minimum, measured from the bow roller; 6:1 or more in strong wind.

questions.q: Wind is forecast to go round to the south overnight. Which spot do you anchor in?

figure.note: Forecast: wind backing south overnight, F5

options: Spot C — in the channel
Spot B — open to the south
Any, the bay is calm now
Spot A — sheltered by the land to the south
questions.why: Choose shelter from the forecast wind, not the present one.

questions.q: The chart shows these seabeds. Where will the anchor hold best?
options: Sand (S)
Shingle (Sn)
Weed (Wd)
Rock (R)
questions.why: Sand and mud let the anchor dig in; weed and rock do not.

questions.q: The anchor is down and the chain paid out. What next?
options: Go below for dinner
Reverse gently to dig it in, then check transits ashore or the anchor alarm
Motor ahead over the anchor
Tie the chain to the pulpit
questions.why: Set the anchor and prove it is holding before relaxing.

questions.q: You are anchored in a busy bay by day. What do you hoist?
options: Nothing by day
A yellow flag
A black ball forward
A black cone
questions.why: Rule 30: ball by day, all-round white light at night.

questions.q: The anchor is fouled under a rock and will not come up. What would have made this easy?
options: A second anchor
A longer chain
A heavier anchor
A trip line and buoy on the anchor crown
questions.why: Pull the crown and the anchor comes out backwards.

questions.q: Berthing stern-to with your own anchor in a Greek harbour. When do you drop the anchor?
options: About 3–4 boat lengths out, reversing towards the quay, paying out as you go
After the stern lines are on
Before turning, at the harbour entrance
When the stern touches the quay
questions.why: Drop early, keep tension, stern lines ashore, then snug the chain.

questions.q: The marinero hands you a slimy line from the quay as you reverse in. What is it and where does it go?
options: A spring — tie it to the midship cleat
A lazy line — walk it forward and make the heavy end fast on the bow cleat
The stern line — cleat it aft
A fender line
questions.why: The lazy line replaces your anchor; it holds the bow.

questions.q: Alongside a pontoon the boat surges back and forth with the wash. Which line stops it?
options: A second stern line
A breast line
A spring — run diagonally from bow aft or from stern forward
The bow line
questions.why: Breasts and bow/stern lines hold the boat in; springs stop fore-and-aft movement.

questions.q: The wind is pinning you against the pontoon. How do you leave?
options: Push off by hand and hope
Full ahead with full rudder
Wait for the wind to change
Spring the stern out: bow spring led aft, fender the bow, helm towards the pontoon, gently ahead, then astern clear
questions.why: Ahead against a bow spring pivots the boat on the bow and swings the stern out into the wind.

questions.q: Before starting the engine for the day, what do you check?
options: Oil, coolant, belt, raw-water seacock open, bilge, gear in neutral
That the sails are furled
Fuel level only
Battery voltage only
questions.why: A daily engine check takes two minutes and prevents most breakdowns.

questions.q: The engine has just started. What is wrong here?

lines: Exhaust: dry, no water pulsing out

options: The battery is flat
No cooling water at the exhaust — stop, check the seacock and strainer
The oil pressure is too high
Nothing, it needs to warm up
questions.why: Running dry overheats the engine and shreds the impeller.

questions.q: Half an hour into the passage you see this. What do you do?
options: Open the coolant cap and add cold water now
Rev it to clear the blockage
Stop the engine, sail or anchor, let it cool and find the cause
Keep going to the marina
questions.why: An overheating engine can seize; never open a hot pressurised cap.

questions.q: Morning after a night at anchor with fridge and lights on. Can you start the engine?

lines: Fridge and anchor light ran all night

options: No — all batteries are flat
Only by hand crank
Only after an hour of solar
Yes — the engine battery was isolated; the house bank is low
questions.why: Separate banks keep starting power away from house loads.

questions.q: The engine loses power, surges and stops after you refuelled at a dusty quay. Most likely?
options: Dirty or watery fuel — drain the separator, change the filter
A flat battery
A fouled propeller
A broken belt
questions.why: Fuel contamination is the commonest cause of stopping.

questions.q: A loud bang, the engine stops; the dinghy painter is no longer in the water. What now?
options: Restart in reverse to unwind it
Do not restart; try to free the rope from the prop from the dinghy, engine off and key out
Keep trying to start
Send a Mayday
questions.why: A line round the prop; a spinning prop and a swimmer never mix.

questions.q: Water is coming in at the heads inlet hose. What do you do first?
options: Open all seacocks
Switch off the batteries
Close that seacock
Pump the heads faster
questions.why: Every through-hull has a seacock; know where they are.

questions.q: Briefing the crew on the marine toilet, what are the rules?
options: Use bleach daily
Pump once only
Flush with the inlet closed
Nothing but what you have eaten, a little paper, pump plenty, close the seacocks at sea
questions.why: Blocked heads are the number-one charter complaint.

questions.q: Reversing out of the berth the stern swings to port by itself. What is happening and how do you use it?

figure.note: Engine astern, rudder centred: stern walks to port

options: Prop walk from a right-handed propeller — berth port-side-to and use a burst astern to pull the stern in
The bow thruster is stuck
A crosswind
Rudder failure
questions.why: A right-handed prop kicks the stern to port in astern.

questions.q: At the fuel berth with two deck fillers side by side. What do you do?
options: Fill to the brim
Check the cap says DIESEL, engine and electrics off, no smoking, fill slowly
Fill the nearer one
Keep the engine running to save time
questions.why: Diesel in the water tank ruins the trip; a spill is a fine.

questions.q: You want to call the marina for a berth. Which channel do you call on, and where do you move to?
options: Channel 70
Channel 6 only
Call on 16 (or the marina's working channel if known), then switch to the working channel
Call and talk on 16
questions.why: Channel 16 is for calling and distress; routine talk moves off it.

questions.q: Which call is right for this situation?

figure.title: Fire below
lines: Engine-bay fire spreading to the saloon

options: PAN-PAN
A routine call to the coastguard
SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY — grave and imminent danger to the vessel and crew
questions.why: Fire spreading below with people aboard is grave and imminent danger.

questions.q: After "MAYDAY ×3, this is Aurora ×3", what comes next?
options: MAYDAY Aurora, position, nature of distress, help required, persons aboard, OVER
Switch to channel 70
Weather and destination
The charter company's phone number
questions.why: Position early so rescue starts even if you are cut off.

questions.q: Your DSC radio has a red button under a flap. What happens when you hold it for five seconds?
options: The EPIRB activates
A digital distress alert with your MMSI and position goes out on channel 70; the radio switches to 16 for the voice Mayday
A flare fires
It calls the marina
questions.why: DSC first, then voice on 16.

questions.q: Which signal for this situation?

figure.title: Night, 10 miles offshore
lines: Radio dead, lights of a ship on the horizon

options: Orange smoke
A white hand flare
A red parachute flare
A green flare
questions.why: Parachute flares are seen from far away at night; hand flares when help is close.

questions.q: Smoke is coming from the engine compartment hatch. What do you do?
options: Pour sea water in
Abandon ship at once
Open the hatch wide to see
Stop the engine, do not open the hatch, discharge an extinguisher through the fire port
questions.why: Opening the hatch feeds the fire with air.

questions.q: Water is rising fast in the bilge. First action?
options: Find and stop the inflow — seacocks, hoses, stern gland — while pumping
Head for deep water
Send a Mayday and wait
Launch the liferaft
questions.why: Pumps only buy time: find the inflow and stop it. Taste the water — fresh = tank, salt = hull or fitting; bungs ready.

questions.q: Which call for this?

figure.title: Engine failure
lines: No wind, drifting at 0.5 kn towards rocks 3 miles off
Anchor ready, 60 m depth — too deep

options: SÉCURITÉ
PAN-PAN — urgent, not yet life-threatening
No call needed
MAYDAY
questions.why: Engine failure drifting slowly with time in hand: urgency, not distress.

questions.q: You are coming back to the man overboard under power. How do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Final approach under power, wind from ahead

options: Fast, then a burst astern beside them
Downwind, engine ahead to hold position
Slowly, heading into the wind; neutral as they come alongside near the bow
Stern-first, so they can reach the ladder
questions.why: Into the wind you stop easily; a turning prop next to a swimmer is lethal.

questions.q: The yacht has an EPIRB in the cockpit locker. When do you use it?
options: When the VHF is busy
To test the batteries each morning
To call the marina
In a real emergency when the vessel or crew are in grave danger — it alerts rescue services by satellite
questions.why: Cospas-Sarsat alerts rescue worldwide; false alerts cost real rescues.

questions.q: You are sailing from Paros to Naxos on this heading. What point of sail are you on?
options: Broad reach
Close reach
Dead run
Beam reach
questions.why: Wind on the quarter, about 135° off the bow, is a broad reach.

questions.q: The genoa and main are sheeted in hard and you cannot steer any closer to the wind. What point of sail is this?
options: Beam reach
Close-hauled
Close reach
In irons
questions.why: Close-hauled is the closest course to the wind that keeps the sails full, about 45°.

questions.q: You were close-hauled and have borne away a little to this heading. What point of sail are you on now?
options: Broad reach
Still close-hauled
Close reach
Beam reach
questions.why: Between close-hauled (45°) and a beam reach (90°) is a close reach.

questions.q: You settle on this heading for the long leg down to Kos. Where do you set the mainsail, and what is the main risk?
options: Sheeted in hard; the sails stalling
Half out; the boat tacking by itself
Centred; the boat going into irons
Eased right out; an accidental gybe
questions.why: On a run the main is eased fully, and a wind shift or wave can swing the boom across.

questions.q: You have just borne away from close-hauled onto this heading. What do you do with the sheets?
options: Ease both until the sails just stop luffing
Pull both in harder to keep the speed
Ease the main and pull in the genoa
Leave them — the sails trim themselves
questions.why: As you bear away, ease the sheets: trim each sail to the edge of luffing.

questions.q: You were close-hauled on 045°. Now the sails start to lift and flap. What has happened and what do you do?
options: You are headed: ease the sheets and hold course
You are headed: bear away to keep the sails full
Nothing has changed: hold your heading
You are lifted: luff up and point higher
questions.why: A veer of 20° puts 045° inside the no-go zone; bear away or tack.

questions.q: The skipper calls "luff up 20 degrees". What heading do you steer?
options: 090° with the sheets eased
questions.why: Luffing up turns the bow towards the wind: 090° − 20° = 070°.

questions.q: You bear away 45° from this heading. What is your new heading and point of sail?

figure.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

options: 225°, beam reach
270°, broad reach
000°, in irons
270°, beam reach
questions.why: Bearing away turns from the wind: 315° − 45° = 270°, wind now on the beam.

questions.q: Your boat tacks through 90°. After tacking from this heading, what course will you be steering?

figure.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

questions.why: Close-hauled 45° each side of a northerly wind: 315° tacks to 045°.

questions.q: You need to know which tack you are on. On this heading, what is it?
options: Starboard tack
Port tack
Neither — you are on a reach
Leeward tack
questions.why: The tack is named after the side the wind comes over; tacks apply on every point of sail.

questions.q: You are on a dead run with the main boom out to starboard. Which tack are you on?

figure.note: Dead run, main boom to starboard

options: Starboard tack
Whichever side the genoa is on
Port tack
No tack — the wind is dead astern
questions.why: On a run the tack is the side opposite the main boom.

questions.q: The skipper asks where the other yacht is. How do you call it?
options: Abeam to port
On the starboard quarter
On the starboard bow
Abeam to starboard
questions.why: Abeam is 90° from the bow; starboard is the right-hand side facing forward.

questions.q: A ferry is coming up from this direction to overtake you. How do you call its position to the crew?
options: On the starboard quarter
On the starboard bow
Abeam to starboard
On the port quarter
questions.why: The quarter is about 45° abaft the beam, between the beam and the stern.

questions.q: Your lookout spots a fishing boat here. How should she call it out?
options: Abeam to port
On the port bow
On the port quarter
On the starboard bow
questions.why: The bow is about 45° either side of dead ahead; port is the left side.

questions.q: A small motorboat is close to your heading line, a little to the right. How do you report it?
options: Broad on the starboard bow
Fine on the port bow
Fine on the starboard bow
Abeam to starboard
questions.why: "Fine" means close to the bow line; "broad" means nearer the beam.

questions.q: A RIB is following in your wake. Where is it?
options: On the port quarter
Abaft the beam to starboard
Dead ahead
Dead astern
questions.why: Directly behind the stern is dead astern.

questions.q: You and another yacht are sailing side by side. Which boat is the windward boat?
options: The other yacht
Whichever boat is ahead
Whichever boat is on starboard tack
Your yacht
questions.why: The windward boat is the one nearer the wind, upwind of the other.

questions.q: You are on the foredeck facing aft, towards the cockpit. Which side of the boat is port?
options: It depends on the tack
On your right
In front of you
On your left
questions.why: Port is the left side when facing forward, so it is on your right when you face aft.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to lay the passerelle "fore-and-aft" on the side deck. How do you place it?
options: Across the boat, side to side
Upright against the mast
Lengthways, along the boat
Hanging over the transom
questions.why: Fore-and-aft means lengthways, bow to stern; athwartships means across.

questions.q: A crew member feels seasick and wants to be sick over the side. Which side do you send them to?
options: Whichever side is higher
Starboard, the windward side
Over the transom, behind the helm
Port, the leeward side
questions.why: Always to leeward, downwind, so it blows away from the boat.

questions.q: A gust heels the boat hard. The skipper calls "everyone to windward!". Where does the crew sit?
options: Port side, the high side
Down below, on the saloon sole
In the middle of the cockpit
Starboard side, the low side
questions.why: Windward is the side the wind comes from; crew weight there reduces heel.

questions.q: Reversing into the berth, the skipper calls "helm amidships!". What do you do?
options: Hand the wheel to the crew in the middle
Centre the wheel so the rudder is straight
Put the engine into neutral
Steer for the middle of the gap
questions.why: Amidships on the helm means the rudder is centred, in line with the keel.

questions.q: You are sailing along this coast towards the next harbour. What is it called, and how far off do you keep?
options: A lee shore; close in for shelter
A weather shore; keep well off
A lee shore; keep well off
A weather shore; close in for flat water
questions.why: A lee shore has the wind blowing onto it; a failure there drives you onto the rocks.

questions.q: You are trimming the genoa on this winch. The skipper calls "ease the genoa". What do you do?
options: Take the sheet off the winch
Roll the genoa away a little
Wind the sheet in a little
Let the sheet out a little, under control
questions.why: To ease is to let a line out gradually; to trim or sheet in is to pull it in.

questions.q: Before a tack, the skipper asks you to put two turns of the lazy sheet on a winch. Which line do you load?
options: The unused one on the windward side
The mainsheet on the traveller
The loaded one on the leeward side
The furling line for the genoa
questions.why: The lazy sheet is the one not working; it becomes the working sheet after the tack.

questions.q: You call "lee-ho" and turn the boat. When does the crew release the old genoa sheet?
options: As soon as you call "lee-ho"
As the bow comes through the wind
Once settled on the new tack
Before you start to turn
questions.why: Too early and the genoa flogs; too late and it is backed and stops the turn.

questions.q: Your destination is upwind, to the north-west. Which manoeuvre puts you on the other close-hauled course?
options: Gybe: turn the stern through the wind
Bear away onto a run
Tack: turn the bow through the wind
Heave to and wait
questions.why: Changing from one close-hauled course to the other means tacking.

questions.q: You are outside the harbour and about to hoist the mainsail under engine. How do you point the boat?
options: Beam-on to the wind
Downwind, so the sail fills
Straight for the next headland
Head to wind, motoring slowly
questions.why: Head to wind the sail does not fill or snag while it goes up.

questions.q: At check-in you find a bent post holding up the guardwires next to the cockpit. Which part is damaged?
options: A stanchion
The pushpit
A spreader
A shroud
questions.why: Stanchions are the posts that carry the guardwires along the deck.

questions.q: The bow navigation lights on your yacht are fixed to the steel rail around the bow. What is that rail?
options: The bow roller
The pulpit
The toerail
The pushpit
questions.why: The pulpit is the rail at the bow; the pushpit is the rail at the stern.

questions.q: The dinghy outboard is clamped to a bracket on the steel rail around the stern. What is that rail?
options: The transom
The coaming
The pushpit
The pulpit
questions.why: The pushpit (stern rail) surrounds the cockpit at the stern.

questions.q: A big following sea is starting to break into the cockpit. Which opening do you close so it cannot flood the cabin?
options: The anchor locker lid
The cockpit drains
The heads seacock
The companionway, with the washboards
questions.why: Washboards close the companionway; the cockpit drains must stay open to empty it.

questions.q: Your charter yacht has a deep fin keel with a bulb. Compared with a long-keeled boat, how does she handle?
options: Turns tightly but tracks less steadily
Heels less and needs no ballast
Tracks steadily but turns slowly
Can dry out upright on a beach
questions.why: A short fin pivots easily; a long keel holds a straight course.

questions.q: A friend's boat sits upright on the mud at low tide in her UK harbour. What keel does she most likely have?
options: A fin keel with a bulb
Twin (bilge) keels
A deep fin keel
A long full keel
questions.why: Twin keels let a boat take the ground upright; fin and long keels fall over.

questions.q: Your yacht has twin rudders and a wide stern. Heeled over upwind, what do they give you?
options: The boat can turn in its own length
Strong prop wash over both rudders
The leeward rudder stays deep and keeps grip
Better steering when going astern
questions.why: A single central rudder lifts out as a wide boat heels; the lee rudder of a pair stays in.

questions.q: Your charter yacht has twin rudders and one central propeller. Manoeuvring slowly in the marina, what do you notice?
options: Steering astern is easier than ahead
Prop wash kicks the stern very hard
She pivots on the spot like a cat
Little steering until she has way on
questions.why: The rudders are off-centre, out of the prop wash, so they only work with water flowing past.

questions.q: Water drips into the cabin where a shroud passes through the deck. Which fitting is leaking?

figure.title: Below decks, after rain
lines: Drip from the deckhead beside the saloon
Directly under where a shroud meets the deck

options: The chainplate
The gooseneck
The stanchion base
The spreader root
questions.why: Shrouds are anchored to chainplates that pass through the deck to the hull.

questions.q: You roll the genoa away with the furling line. Which wire does the sail wrap around?
options: The topping lift
The forestay
A cap shroud
The backstay
questions.why: A roller-furling genoa rolls round a foil over the forestay.

questions.q: At check-in you find damage on this wire. What is it and what do you do?

figure.title: Check-in: rig
lines: Wire from the mast to the side deck
Three strands broken at the lower end
Boat due to leave in an hour

options: The forestay: keep the genoa furled
A shroud: tape it and sail gently
A shroud: report it and do not sail
A halyard: turn it end for end
questions.why: Shrouds hold the mast up sideways; a damaged one can bring the rig down.

questions.q: At check-in you see a split pin missing from the threaded fitting at the foot of a shroud. What is the fitting and what do you do?
options: A chainplate: tighten it by hand
A clutch: tape over the gap
A gooseneck: leave it, it needs no pin
A bottlescrew: fit and tape a new pin
questions.why: Bottlescrews (turnbuckles) adjust the rigging; without a pin they can unscrew.

questions.q: The mainsail has chafe marks halfway up, where it rubbed on the struts sticking out sideways from the mast. What rubbed it?
options: The spreaders
The cap shrouds
The kicker
The gooseneck
questions.why: Spreaders hold the shrouds out from the mast; downwind the main presses on them.

questions.q: The pin joining the boom to the mast has worked loose. Which fitting is it?
options: The kicker
The gooseneck
The spreader
The clew
questions.why: The gooseneck is the hinge between the boom and the mast.

questions.q: On your fractional-rigged yacht the wind is building. What does pulling on the backstay adjuster do?
options: Lifts the boom and opens the leech
Moves the genoa sheet car forward
Bends the mast and flattens the main
Makes the main fuller and more powerful
questions.why: Backstay tension bends a fractional mast, flattening the main and tightening the forestay.

questions.q: Close-hauled on starboard tack, a windward shroud parts with a bang. What do you do at once?
options: Ease all sheets and hold the course
Luff up head to wind and stop
Bear away onto a run
Tack, to put the broken side to leeward
questions.why: Tacking takes the load onto the intact leeward shroud before the mast falls.

questions.q: Beating up to Hydra, the forestay fitting breaks at the bow. Which way do you turn?

figure.title: Forestay failure
lines: Forestay pulled out at the stemhead

options: Bear away onto a run
Luff up head to wind
Hold course and ease the main
Tack straight away
questions.why: Running puts the wind load on the backstay and takes it off the forestay.

questions.q: You are bending on the genoa at check-in. To which corner do you attach the sheets?
options: The tack
The clew
The head
The luff
questions.why: The clew is the lower aft corner, where the sheets go.

questions.q: Putting in a slab reef, you hook the reef cringle at the front of the sail onto the hook by the gooseneck. Which cringle is it?
options: The clew cringle
The leech cringle
The tack cringle
The head cringle
questions.why: The new tack goes on the reefing hook; the reef line pulls the new clew to the boom.

questions.q: The back edge of the genoa vibrates with a buzzing noise. Which edge is it and what fixes it?
options: The foot: ease the genoa sheet
The luff: tighten the genoa halyard
The leech: ease the sheet right out
The leech: tighten the leech line a little
questions.why: The leech is the trailing edge; the leech line stops it fluttering.

questions.q: A batten falls out of its pocket as you hoist the main. What will the sail lack without it?
options: Support for the curved leech
Tension along the luff
A mark for the reef points
Shape along the foot
questions.why: Battens hold out the roach, the curve of the leech beyond a straight line.

questions.q: Your charter yacht has an in-mast furling main and the wind is rising. How do you reduce it?
options: Tighten the outhaul and ease the furling line
Ease the outhaul and wind in the furling line
Lower the halyard and tie in the reef points
Roll the sail round the boom
questions.why: The main rolls into the mast; keep a little outhaul tension so it rolls tightly.

questions.q: Your new charter boat has a self-tacking jib. What does the crew do with the jib sheet when you tack?
options: Release it and winch in the other sheet
Ease it fully before the tack
Nothing — it crosses on its own track
Move the car to the new side by hand
questions.why: A self-tacking jib has one sheet on a track across the foredeck.

questions.q: You drop the main and it falls neatly into the bag on the boom. Next morning, hoisting, the battens catch on lines either side. What helps?
options: Pull the kicker on before hoisting
Hoist on a reach so the sail fills
Tighten the lazy jacks hard first
Point head to wind and watch the battens
questions.why: The lazy jacks guide the sail down; head to wind the battens clear them.

questions.q: On a dead run in light wind the genoa keeps collapsing behind the main. What can you do?
options: Goose-wing it on the opposite side
Sheet the genoa in hard amidships
Tighten the genoa halyard
Ease the main outhaul fully
questions.why: Set the genoa on the side away from the main, ideally held out by a pole.

questions.q: Upwind in 18 knots, the lower part of the main is too full and the boat heels. Which line do you pull?
options: The topping lift
The outhaul
The lazy jack
The furling line
questions.why: Outhaul tension flattens the foot of the main and depowers it.

questions.q: As the wind rises the deepest part of the main moves back towards the leech. Which control pulls it forward again?
options: The outhaul
The traveller
The cunningham
The topping lift
questions.why: More luff tension (cunningham or halyard) moves the draft forward.

questions.q: You are about to drop the main for the night. The boom is not held up by a rigid vang. What do you do first?
options: Tighten the cunningham
Tighten the kicker hard
Ease the outhaul right off
Take up the topping lift
questions.why: The topping lift holds the boom up so it does not fall into the cockpit or bimini.

questions.q: Close-hauled, the boom rides high and the main leech stays loose even with the mainsheet hard in. What is the likely cause?
options: The topping lift is still tight
The outhaul is too loose
The traveller is to leeward
The cunningham is too tight
questions.why: A tight topping lift holds the boom up; ease it once the sail is hoisted.

questions.q: Close-hauled in a gusty F5, the boat heels hard in each gust. Which quick move depowers the main?
options: Tighten the topping lift
Let the traveller down to leeward
Ease the outhaul to make it fuller
Pull the traveller up to windward
questions.why: Dropping the traveller opens the main's angle to the wind without changing its shape.

questions.q: The halyard is in a clutch, loaded by the hoisted main. You need to ease it. What do you do before opening the clutch?
options: Open the clutch and hold the tail
Uncleat the mainsheet first
Put it on a winch and take the load
Pull the halyard tail tight by hand
questions.why: Opening a loaded clutch lets the line run; the winch must hold it first.

questions.q: The wind has risen to 25 knots and you must roll the genoa away. How do you handle the sheet?
options: Ease the halyard, then furl
Let it run free, then furl
Keep it cleated while you furl
Ease it slowly, keeping some tension
questions.why: A little sheet tension stops the sail flogging and rolls it tightly.

questions.q: During slab reefing, which line pulls the new clew down to the boom?
options: The reefing line
The outhaul
The topping lift
The cunningham
questions.why: Each reef has its own clew line (pennant) led along the boom.

questions.q: Close-hauled in a rising Meltemi, you decide to reef the main. What do you ease before lowering the halyard?
options: The topping lift and the backstay
The mainsheet and the kicker
The outhaul and the cunningham
The genoa sheet and the traveller
questions.why: Easing the main spills wind; easing the kicker lets the boom rise as the sail comes down.

questions.q: You are leaving the harbour at Mykonos with this forecast. When do you reef?
options: When the rail first goes under
When the gusts reach F6
Before you leave the shelter of the harbour
Only if the genoa will not furl
questions.why: Reef early: it is easiest in sheltered water before the wind arrives.

questions.q: The wind has dropped and you want to shake out the reef. What is the right order?
options: Ease the reef line, hoist, then untie the ties
Tighten the kicker, then hoist hard
Hoist, then untie the ties and reef line
Untie the ties, ease the reef line, then hoist
questions.why: Hoisting against tied reef points tears the sail.

questions.q: Close-hauled, you check the genoa telltales. Which way do you move the sheet car?
options: Forward
Inboard towards the mast
Aft
Leave it; ease the halyard
questions.why: If the top luffs first the leech is too open; moving the car forward closes it.

questions.q: Steering close-hauled, you watch the genoa telltales. Which way do you steer?
options: Hold this heading
Bear away a little
Tack at once
Luff up a little
questions.why: Windward telltales lifting mean you are pinching; bear away until they stream.

questions.q: On a beam reach, you watch the genoa telltales. What do you do with the sheet?
options: Leave it; bear away
Leave it; ease the halyard
Ease it until both stream
Pull it in harder
questions.why: A fluttering leeward telltale means the sail is stalled: over-sheeted.

questions.q: On a beam reach the sails are pinned in tight, the boat heels and slows. What is happening?

figure.title: Beam reach
lines: Main and genoa sheeted in hard

options: The boat is about to gybe
The boat is in irons
The sails are luffing: under-sheeted
The sails are stalled: over-sheeted
questions.why: Sheeted too tight for the course, the airflow breaks away and drive drops.

questions.q: The top leech telltale on the main keeps disappearing behind the sail. What do you do?
options: Ease the mainsheet or kicker a little
Pull the mainsheet in harder
Tighten the topping lift
Ease the outhaul right off
questions.why: A hidden top telltale means the leech is too closed and stalled; twist it open.

questions.q: A light F2 breeze on a flat sea, beam reaching to Antiparos. How do you set the main?
options: Boom hard down with the kicker
Fuller: ease the outhaul a little
Reefed, to keep the boat upright
Flat: outhaul and cunningham hard on
questions.why: Light wind wants a fuller sail; flatten it as the wind rises.

questions.q: Reaching in a gusty F6, you want the top of the main to spill the gusts by itself. What do you adjust?
options: Pull the traveller up to windward
Tighten the kicker to stop any twist
Ease the kicker a little to let it twist
Ease the outhaul to make it fuller
questions.why: More twist lets the top of the main open and spill wind in the gusts.

questions.q: Beating in this breeze, the boat keeps rounding up and you are fighting the wheel. What do you reduce first?
options: Roll away the genoa
Move the genoa cars aft
Pull the traveller to windward
Reef the main
questions.why: Weather helm comes from too much drive aft; reducing the main moves it forward.

questions.q: You roll away a third of the genoa as the wind builds. Now the top of the sail luffs early. What do you do with the sheet car?

figure.title: Reefed genoa
lines: Car where it was for full sail

options: Move it forward
Move it aft
Leave it; ease the sheet
Leave it; tighten the halyard
questions.why: Furling moves the clew up and forward, so the lead must follow it forward.

questions.q: Broad reaching in a Meltemi with full main, the boat suddenly rounds up and heels hard, the wheel loose in your hands. What was it?

figure.title: Broad reach, F6
lines: Rudder losing grip in the gusts

options: A broach: sheet the main in hard
A broach: ease the main, then reef
In irons: back the genoa
A gybe: centre the boom quickly
questions.why: Too much sail off the wind overpowers the rudder; dump the main, then reduce sail.

questions.q: After a slow tack the boat has stopped like this and will not turn either way. What is it and what do you do?
options: In irons: sheet the main in hard
Hove-to: wait for the wind to shift
In irons: back the genoa to push the bow off
Luffing: steer further into the wind
questions.why: Head to wind with no way on; backing the headsail turns the bow.

questions.q: You want to stop under sail off Poros to sort out a tangled line. How do you heave to?
options: Gybe and sheet the main in hard
Tack, release the genoa, sheet the main hard
Drop both sails and leave the helm free
Tack, leave the genoa sheet, lash the helm to turn up
questions.why: The backed genoa and the rudder turning up balance each other; the boat lies quietly.

questions.q: You have hove-to to sort out a jammed reef line. Is this a good place to stay?

figure.title: Hove-to
lines: Rocky island 0.5 M to the south

options: No: you drift downwind towards the rocks
Yes: the backed genoa drives you upwind
Yes: a hove-to boat makes no leeway
No: the boat will tack by itself
questions.why: Hove-to, the boat drifts slowly to leeward; you need sea room downwind.

questions.q: Running in a swell, the boom keeps threatening to swing across. What prevents an accidental gybe?
options: Tighten the topping lift hard
Rig a preventer and steer a little higher
Ease the kicker right off
Pull the traveller up to windward
questions.why: A preventer holds the boom forward, and a broad reach keeps the wind clear of the leech.

questions.q: You need to change to the other broad reach. With this crew, how do you do it?
options: Drop the genoa and gybe the main alone
Gybe with the mainsheet fully eased
Luff up, tack round, bear away again
Gybe quickly between two gusts
questions.why: In strong wind a tack round avoids a violent gybe; it costs only a little ground.

questions.q: You plan to motor under this bridge. Can you pass?

figure.title: Bridge ahead
lines: VHF aerial on the masthead: 0.8 m

options: Yes, with 0.3 m to spare
Yes, 15.5 + 0.8 = 16.3 m clears it
Yes, with 1.5 m to spare
No: your air draft is 17.5 m
questions.why: Air draft is the height of the highest point above the water: 15.5 + 1.2 + 0.8 = 17.5 m.

questions.q: Your yacht's figures are below. Roughly what is her maximum speed through the water, short of surfing?
options: About 8 knots
About 12 knots
About 10 knots
About 6 knots
questions.why: Hull speed ≈ 1.34 × √LWL in feet: 1.34 × √36 ≈ 8 knots.

questions.q: This season you move up to a bigger, heavier yacht. Coming into a berth, what changes most?
options: She stops sooner because she is heavier
She carries her way longer: slow down earlier
She turns in a much tighter circle
She draws less water at the bow
questions.why: More displacement means more momentum: she takes longer to stop and to start.

questions.q: The bay is 2.0 m deep near the beach. Which of the two charter boats can anchor there?
options: Only the monohull
Neither boat
Only the catamaran
Both boats
questions.why: Draft is the depth of the hull below the waterline; the cat's 1.25 m leaves 0.75 m.

questions.q: The quay attendant offers you this gap. What is the problem?
options: None: cats squeeze in with fenders
The LOA: too long for stern-to
The draft: too deep at the quay
The beam: the cat will not fit
questions.why: Beam is the widest point of the boat; a 42 ft cat is about 7.7 m wide.

questions.q: On your catamaran the skipper sends you forward across the netting between the two bows. What is the netting called?
options: The trampoline
The pulpit
The bridgedeck
The foredeck locker
questions.why: The trampoline spans the forward beam between the hulls.

questions.q: Beating into a short Meltemi chop, the catamaran shudders with loud bangs under the saloon. What is happening and what do you do?
options: Rudder stall: centre the wheel
Bridgedeck slamming: bear away and slow down
Keels touching: tack at once
Bridgedeck slamming: point higher
questions.why: Waves hit the underside of the bridgedeck; a freer, slower course eases it.

questions.q: You swap a monohull for a cruising catamaran on the same upwind leg. What do you expect?
options: She points higher, so fewer tacks
She heels more than the monohull
She points lower, so you need more tacks
She tacks faster and more easily
questions.why: A cruising cat without daggerboards sails wider of the wind and makes more leeway.

questions.q: On a cruising catamaran, how do you decide when to reef?
options: By the angle of heel
When the helm gets heavy
When the windward hull starts to lift
By the wind speed, using the reefing table
questions.why: A cat barely heels, so it gives no warning; reef by the wind speed.

questions.q: A crew member asks why the catamaran has no heavy keel. Which is true about the stability of the two types?
options: A monohull rights itself; a capsized cat does not
A cat rights itself; a monohull does not
A cat heels further than a monohull first
Both right themselves after a capsize
questions.why: The ballast keel brings a monohull back up; an inverted cat is stable upside down.

questions.q: Tacking your charter catamaran in light wind, it keeps stopping head to wind. What helps it round?
options: Ease the main fully, then tack
Build speed, keep the jib backed briefly
Slow down and release the jib early
Tack from a broad reach
questions.why: A cat carries little way; speed and a backed jib push the bows through.

questions.q: You are bending the new genoa sheets onto the clew of the sail before leaving Lefkas. Which knot do you tie?
options: Rolling hitch
Clove hitch
Bowline
Reef knot
questions.why: A bowline makes a fixed loop through the clew that will not slip and unties after use.

questions.q: You have pulled down the first reef and are tying the reef points round the loose bundle of sail. Which knot?
options: Clove hitch
Figure of eight
Sheet bend
Reef knot
questions.why: Binding round a bundle is the reef knot's proper job: it lies flat and unties easily.

questions.q: You are on the foredeck as this line starts to run. Where do you put your feet?

figure.title: Leaving the quay
lines: Stern line paying out across the deck
A loop of slack lies round your feet
Engine in gear, boat moving off

options: Outside the loop, clear of the line
Inside the loop, to hold it down on deck
On the line, to stop it running out
Anywhere, as the line is still slack
questions.why: A bight snaps tight the instant the line takes up: never stand in one.

questions.q: You are holding the dinghy painter while the crew climbs down, and the dinghy is pulling in the current. How do you hold the line?
options: Wrapped once round your hand for a better grip
In your hands, not wrapped round them
Looped round your wrist for grip
Tied round your waist to free your hands
questions.why: A wrapped line can trap your hand and drag you if the load surges.

questions.q: Your crew will handle sheets and mooring lines this afternoon. What should they wear on their hands?

figure.title: Meltemi afternoon
lines: Stern-to in a crowded harbour tonight

options: One glove on the hand that tails
Thick woollen gloves for padding
Sailing gloves against rope burn
Nothing: bare hands grip better
questions.why: Sailing gloves protect palms from rope burn while keeping a good grip.

questions.q: What do you do with the mooring lines before you stow them?

figure.title: Charter handover, Saturday
lines: Lines go back into the cockpit locker

options: Scrub them clean with bleach
Stow them wet, salt and all, to keep them soft
Dry them in the sun without rinsing
Rinse in fresh water, then dry them
questions.why: Salt crystals cut the fibres and stiffen rope; rope stowed wet goes mouldy.

questions.q: The cut end of a new polyester sheet has started to unravel. What do you do?
options: Whip the end and seal it with heat
Tie an overhand knot in the end to stop it
Wet the end to swell the fibres
Wrap insulating tape round it
questions.why: Whipping binds the end and heat fuses the synthetic fibres so it cannot fray.

questions.q: You have finished winching in the genoa sheet. What do you do with the winch handle?
options: Leave it in the winch for the next tack
Take it out and stow it
Hang it over the guardrail
Lay it on the cockpit seat
questions.why: A handle left in fouls the sheets, gets kicked overboard or injures someone.

questions.q: Six clutches sit side by side on the coachroof. Before you open one to drop the main, you…
options: open the one nearest the companionway
open each in turn until it moves
check its label and follow the line
take the turns off the winch first
questions.why: Opening the wrong clutch can drop a loaded line such as the kicker or a reef line.

questions.q: You are reversing onto the quay in Poros and a long slack loop of the stern line hangs over the transom into the water. What is the risk?
options: It will stretch and lose strength
It acts as a brake on the stern
It will float away from the boat
It can wrap round the propeller
questions.why: Keep lines on deck and out of the water whenever the engine is in gear.

questions.q: Your crew has led the bow line straight over the toerail to the cleat. What should they do?
options: Lead it through the fairlead first
Tie it round the pulpit instead
Add a second line over the toerail
Leave it, the toerail is smooth
questions.why: A fairlead gives a smooth lead; a toerail edge chafes the line.

questions.q: You want a quiet night and less wear on the lines. What do you do?
options: Ease the halyards so they hang slack
Tie them off away from the mast
Take the shackles off and let them swing free
Leave them; the noise does no harm
questions.why: Tied off away from the mast, halyards stop slapping and chafing.

questions.q: You are hauling in the mainsheet where it runs into the block on the traveller. Where do you keep your hands?
options: Either side of the sheave
On the block itself, guiding the line in
Well back from the block
Right up at the block for the best grip
questions.why: A sudden load can drag fingers into the block.

questions.q: What do you tell the charter base about this sheet?

figure.title: Pre-charter check
lines: Genoa sheet: cover worn through at clew

options: Turn it so the wear is underneath
Tape over the worn part and sail
It is fine while the core is still intact
It needs replacing before you sail
questions.why: Once the cover is through, the core chafes fast and the sheet can part.

questions.q: You are about to throw the stern line to a helper on the pontoon. What do you do with the other end first?
options: Make it fast to the cleat on board
Throw it as well, so they have both
Leave it loose on the deck
Tie it round your wrist
questions.why: If the inboard end is made fast, the whole line cannot go overboard.

questions.q: A tired swimmer beside the boat needs a loop under the arms to help them up the stern ladder. Which knot?
options: Slip knot
Bowline
Clove hitch
Running bowline
questions.why: A bowline's loop is fixed: it will not tighten round the chest.

questions.q: You are tying the sail ties round the flaked mainsail and want each one to come off with one pull when you next hoist. Which knot?
options: Double sheet bend
Clove hitch
Slipped reef knot
Reef knot pulled tight
questions.why: The slipped loop releases the knot with a single tug.

questions.q: You are buying a spare mooring line for an Ionian charter, where you will often lie stern-to in a swell. Which material?
options: Polyester
Dyneema
Polypropylene
Nylon
questions.why: Nylon stretches and absorbs the surge before it reaches the cleats.

questions.q: You are bending a nylon warp straight onto the ring of the kedge anchor. Which knot?
options: Anchor bend
Reef knot
Double sheet bend
Clove hitch
questions.why: The anchor (fisherman's) bend nips tight on the ring and will not shake loose.

questions.q: Overnight, the clove hitch on the bollard has worked loose as the boat surged. What should you have tied?
options: Slipped reef knot
Round turn and two half hitches
Sheet bend
Reef knot
questions.why: The round turn takes the surge and the half hitches stay locked; a clove hitch can roll loose.

questions.q: The single sheet bend joining these two lines keeps working loose. What do you tie instead?
options: Reef knot
Clove hitch
Double sheet bend
Slipped reef knot
questions.why: The extra turn of a double sheet bend grips slippery or very unequal lines.

questions.q: You want a stopper knot in the end of the mainsheet that you can still undo after it has been jerked hard against the block. Which knot?
options: Double overhand knot
Overhand knot
Reef knot
Figure of eight
questions.why: A figure of eight is bulky enough to stop and does not jam like an overhand.

questions.q: Tying the reef points, your crew passes left over right, then left over right again. What has she tied?
options: A granny, which can slip or jam
A reef knot, ready to use
A clove hitch, for a rail
A sheet bend, for unequal ropes
questions.why: Right over left then left over right makes a reef knot; the same way twice makes a granny.

questions.q: Your crew has made the stern line fast with three locking hitches piled on top of the cleat. What is wrong?
options: It needs another turn round the base
It can jam and be slow to release
Nothing, more hitches hold better
It should have been a bowline
questions.why: One locking hitch is enough; more of them jam just when you need to let go.

questions.q: You are making the stern line fast on a pontoon cleat. Where does the line go first?
options: Into figure-of-eight turns with no turn first
Straight into a locking hitch on the near horn
Far horn first, then a turn round the base
Round the near horn, then over the top
questions.why: Leading to the far horn first lets the base turn take the load without the line trapping itself.

questions.q: The stern line is loaded and you need to ease it by a metre. How do you do it?
options: Pull the locking hitch tighter first
Lift the whole lot off the horns at once
Take it off the cleat and hold it by hand
Keep one turn on and let it slip round
questions.why: The turn round the base holds the load while you ease under control.

questions.q: Your crew is on the pontoon holding the bow line, and the wind is blowing the boat off. She cannot hold it. What does she do?
options: Take a turn round the cleat
Dig in and pull with both hands
Wrap the line round her wrist
Run along the pontoon with it
questions.why: A turn round a cleat gives the grip no person has; a yacht cannot be held by hand.

questions.q: You are tacking in light air and pulling the new genoa sheet in fast by hand. How many turns are on the winch?
options: Four from the start, so it cannot slip
Two, adding more as the load comes on
One, then the rest with the handle
None until the sail is fully in
questions.why: Few turns let the slack come in fast without riding turns; add turns as the load builds.

questions.q: The helm calls "Lee-oh" and you must let the old genoa sheet go. How?
options: Take the handle out and spin the drum back
Unwind the turns one at a time
Pull the tail free, lift the turns off
Leave it on the winch to pull itself free
questions.why: Flicking the turns up off the drum releases the sheet at once so the sail can cross.

questions.q: You are loading the sheet onto a self-tailing winch. What is the order?
options: Turns anticlockwise, then into the jaws
Straight into the jaws with no turns on the drum
One turn, then hold the tail by hand
Clockwise turns, then over the arm into the jaws
questions.why: The drum turns do the gripping; the jaws only hold the tail.

questions.q: You are tailing while a crew member grinds the genoa in. What is your job?
options: Pull the tail steadily so the turns grip
Grind as well with your other hand
Push the turns up the drum as they come in
Hold the tail loosely and let the winch work
questions.why: Tension on the tail is what makes the turns grip the drum.

questions.q: You need to ease the loaded genoa sheet a few centimetres on a plain winch. How?
options: Take all the turns off and let it run
Keep the turns on and ease them round
Uncleat it and let go of the tail
Wind the handle backwards a little
questions.why: With the turns kept on, the drum's friction lets you ease under control.

questions.q: The main halyard is loaded and you want to ease it. What do you do first?

figure.title: Main halyard
lines: Winch beside the clutch is free

options: Open the clutch and let it run to the mark
Open the clutch, then put it on the winch
Load the winch, then open the clutch
Open the clutch and hold the tail by hand
questions.why: With the load on the winch the clutch opens gently and the line cannot run away.

questions.q: You have hoisted the main on the coachroof winch. What do you do before you take the turns off the winch?
options: Open the clutch to check it runs
Ease the halyard a little first
Cleat the tail on the winch top
Make sure the halyard clutch is closed
questions.why: The closed clutch holds the halyard so the winch is free for the next line.

questions.q: What do you replace it with?
options: Low-stretch polyester or Dyneema braid
Polypropylene braid, which is light
New nylon three-strand of the same size
A thicker nylon braid for strength
questions.why: Halyards need low stretch to hold luff tension; nylon stretches.

questions.q: The charter boat's genoa sheets have been replaced with nylon. What will you notice?
options: Nothing: nylon is ideal for sheets
The sail eases itself in every gust
They float and trail in the water
They are too stiff to go round a winch
questions.why: Nylon stretches; sheets need low-stretch polyester.

questions.q: Why has this line aged so fast?

figure.title: Dinghy painter
lines: Snaps when you bend it hard

options: Salt water slowly dissolves polypropylene
It has soaked up too much water
Polypropylene breaks down in sunlight
It was always coiled the wrong way
questions.why: Polypropylene has poor UV resistance; check it and replace it often.

questions.q: You want to splice an eye into a new mooring line yourself, on board, with only a knife and tape. Which construction is easiest?
options: Braid with a Dyneema core
Double-braid polyester
Braid-on-braid nylon
Three-strand
questions.why: Three-strand is spliced by tucking strands by hand; braid needs fids and skill.

questions.q: What has caused this?

figure.title: Halyard inspection
lines: Hard, shiny patch on the cover
Where it surged round the winch

options: Friction heat has melted the fibres
The sun has bleached the cover
Salt has crystallised in the cover
Oil from the winch has soaked in
questions.why: A line surging fast round a drum heats up enough to glaze synthetic fibres.

questions.q: This line is bar taut in a gust. Where do you stand?

figure.note: Nylon stern line under heavy load

options: Next to the bollard, to check it
To one side, out of line with it
Astride it, ready to hold it down
Right behind it, to watch it
questions.why: A stretched nylon line that parts whips back along its own path.

questions.q: Where the stern line crosses the quay edge it rubs every time the boat moves. What do you do?

figure.title: Stern-to, stone quay
lines: Stern line running over the edge

options: Tie a knot at the rubbing point
Tighten it until it stops moving
Fit a chafe sleeve at the edge
Wet it now and then to cool it
questions.why: A hose or chafe guard takes the wear instead of the rope.

questions.q: You need to cut a 10 m length off a new coil of braided polyester. How?
options: Burn through it with a lighter alone
Cut it, then tie an overhand knot in each end
Cut it with a knife and whip the ends next week
Tape it, cut through the tape, heat-seal
questions.why: Tape stops the braid unravelling as you cut; heat then fuses the ends.

questions.q: You are coiling a three-strand mooring line. Which way do you lay the loops?
options: Clockwise, with the lay
Round your elbow, either way
Either way, lay does not matter
Anticlockwise, against the lay
questions.why: Most three-strand is right-hand laid; coil it clockwise to avoid kinks.

questions.q: A braided sheet keeps forming twists when you coil it in round loops. What works better?
options: Wet it first so it lies flat on deck
Lay it in figure-of-eight loops
Coil it tighter and faster
Coil it anticlockwise instead
questions.why: Braid has no lay; figure-of-eight loops put no twist into it.

questions.q: After hoisting, you have coiled the halyard tail from this cleat. How do you hang it?
options: Leave the coil lying loose on the deck by the mast
Tie the coil to the guardrail with its own end
Pull a loop through the coil, twist it, hang it
Wrap the tail round the whole coil and drop it
questions.why: The hung coil stays tidy and lifts off ready to run.

questions.q: You are coiling a mooring line that is still made fast on the cleat. Where do you start?
options: In the middle, working both ways
Anywhere, as long as the loops are equal
At the free end, working back to the cleat
At the cleat, working out to the free end
questions.why: Twists then run out of the free end instead of building up in the coil.

questions.q: What do you check before opening the halyard clutch?

figure.title: Dropping the main
lines: Halyard tail in a heap in the cockpit
Boat head to wind under engine

options: The tail is flaked and free to run
The tail is tied to the boom
The tail is made fast on a cleat
The tail is coiled and hung up
questions.why: A kinked or knotted tail jams at the clutch and leaves the sail half down.

questions.q: After a season, the genoa sheets are starting to wear where they run through the fairleads. What do you do?
options: Tape over the worn part
Swap each sheet end for end
Swap the port and starboard sheets
Throw them both away
questions.why: End-for-ending moves the wear to a fresh part of the rope.

questions.q: You are making up a permanent mooring line with a loop in one end. Why splice the eye rather than tie a bowline?
options: A splice is quicker to undo
A splice lets you change the loop size
It keeps more of the rope's strength
A bowline cannot go over a bollard
questions.why: A knot weakens a rope far more than a well-made splice.

questions.q: You are shackling a rope warp to a length of chain. What goes inside the eye splice?
options: A knot, to stop it pulling through
Tape, to help it slide on the shackle
Nothing, the splice is strong enough
A thimble, to protect the eye
questions.why: The metal thimble spreads the load and protects the eye from chafe.

questions.q: You are throwing the bow line to a helper on the pontoon. Where do you aim?
options: Above and just beyond them
Straight at their chest
Short, into the water by them
At their feet on the pontoon
questions.why: A line aimed past the person drops across them; one aimed at them falls short.

questions.q: Your thrown stern line falls short into the water between the boat and the quay. What now?
options: Throw the rest of the line out after it
Pull it in fast, clear of the prop
Motor astern so the helper can reach it
Leave it there and throw the other line
questions.why: A line in the water near the stern can foul the prop; recover it first.

questions.q: The marinero has done this with your stern line. Where is it adjusted and made fast?

figure.note: Line taken round the bollard, end handed back

options: With a bowline round the bollard
On the bollard, by the marinero
On the boat's cleat, by your crew
Held by hand until the engine stops
questions.why: Made fast on board, the line can be adjusted or slipped without going ashore.

questions.q: The quay is too far to throw the heavy stern line. What do you do?
options: Throw the heavy line again, much harder
Throw the coil without holding the end
Tie both stern lines together and throw them
Throw a light line first to pull it across
questions.why: A light heaving line carries further; the heavy line follows it.

questions.q: How do you rig the stern line so you can let go from on board?
options: Both ends aboard, middle round the bollard
Round turn and two half hitches ashore
A bowline round the bollard, end on board
A clove hitch on the bollard, end on board
questions.why: A slip line is released from aboard by letting one end go and pulling in the other.

questions.q: You are letting go a slip line from the stern. What must be true before you put the engine in gear?
options: The line is bar tight on the cleat
The whole line is back aboard
One end is let go and trailing
The free end is thrown onto the quay
questions.why: A slip line trailing astern can wrap the prop the moment it turns.

questions.q: You are lashing the upturned dinghy on the foredeck and want the lashing bar tight. Which hitch?
options: Round turn and two half hitches
Reef knot
Trucker's hitch
Clove hitch
questions.why: The loop in a trucker's hitch works like a pulley, giving purchase to tension the line.

questions.q: You must cast off this line while the boat is still pulling on it. How?
