figure.note: Round turn and two half hitches, under load

options: Wait until the load comes off it first
Cut it, as the hitches will be jammed
Pull the whole knot off the ring at once
Undo the hitches while the turn holds the load
questions.why: The round turn takes the strain while the half hitches are undone.

questions.q: You are stowing a spare line in the cockpit locker. How do you keep it from tangling?
options: Coil it, bind it, tuck the end through
Knot both ends together and drop it in
Leave it flaked loose on the locker floor
Stuff it in loose so it can breathe
questions.why: A bound coil stays together and is ready to use.

questions.q: How do you get the stern line in?

figure.title: Stern-to, crosswind
lines: Windward stern line on the quay bollard
Too heavy to pull in by hand

options: Motor ahead to slacken the line
Lead it to a winch and grind it in
Tie it to the next boat's cleat
Two people pull and hold it by hand
questions.why: A winch gives the purchase that hands cannot; keep a fair lead to the drum.

questions.q: A loaded mooring line starts running out fast through your hands. What do you do?
options: Grip harder with both hands until it stops
Stand on it to stop it running
Let it go and regain it with a turn on a cleat
Wrap it round your wrist for more grip
questions.why: Gripping a running line burns hands; a turn on a cleat stops it safely.

questions.q: Why does this shorten the life of the lines?

figure.title: Charter base quay
lines: Mooring lines left on the sandy quay

options: Being walked on stretches them
Sand makes the lines float
It only marks the cover, no harm done
Grit cuts the fibres from inside
questions.why: Sand and grit grind the fibres from inside; keep lines off the ground.

questions.q: You are grinding the genoa in and this is happening. What do you do?

figure.note: Sheet creeping round the drum, 22 kn

options: Add another turn on the drum
Let the tail go slack
Take a turn off the drum
Grind faster to keep up with it
questions.why: More turns give more friction; under heavy load the drum needs three or four.

questions.q: You are about to throw a coiled stern line. How do you hold the coil?
options: The whole coil in your throwing hand
Split: half to throw, half to pay out
Tied together with its own end
Wound round your forearm
questions.why: The thrown loops carry the line while the rest runs free from the other hand.

questions.q: The genoa sheet is getting too heavy to grind on the two-speed winch. What do you do?
options: Take a turn off the drum
Put more turns on and grind harder
Turn the handle the other way
Let the tail go and grind faster
questions.why: Reversing the handle on a two-speed winch selects the lower, more powerful gear.

questions.q: You need to release the mainsheet from its cam cleat. How?
options: Push it down deeper into the cams
Let go and wait for it to slip free
Pull it sideways against the cams
Pull in slightly, then lift it out
questions.why: A small pull takes the load off the cams so the line lifts out.

questions.q: You are joining a thin line to a thick one with a sheet bend. Which line forms the U-shaped bight?
options: The thicker line
Either, it makes no difference
Both, laid side by side
The thinner line
questions.why: The thick line makes the bight and the thin line wraps round it.

questions.q: After a week of use, the three-strand stern line is full of kinks. How do you get them out?
options: Leave it coiled in the sun to soften
Lay it out and work twists out of the end
Coil it tighter to press the kinks out
Soak it in fresh water overnight to relax it
questions.why: Twist must run out of an end; coiling or soaking just traps it.

questions.q: Your crew has long loose hair and a scarf and is about to grind the halyard winch. What do you say?
options: Keep the scarf on against the sun
Stand further back from the drum while grinding
Tie the hair back, tuck the scarf away
Wear gloves and carry on
questions.why: Hair and loose clothing can be wound into a turning drum.

questions.q: A heavy stern line is under strain round a big bollard ashore. You must hold it, ease it under control, then cast it off with the load still on. Which hitch?
options: Bowline
Double sheet bend
Clove hitch
Lighterman's hitch
questions.why: The lighterman's (tugboat) hitch holds a heavy load on a post and still releases under strain.

questions.q: Your bow line is tied to the quay ring with a bowline, and the wind presses the boat off so it is bar tight. You want to leave. What is the problem?

figure.note: Bowline, wind pressing the boat off

options: A loaded bowline cannot be untied
The bowline will slip through the ring
The bowline capsizes when touched
Nothing: a bowline frees under load
questions.why: A bowline holds well but the load must come off before it can be untied.

questions.q: A crew member has loaded the genoa sheet like this. What happens when the sail fills?
options: The winch locks and cannot be eased
The sheet runs out round the drum
Nothing, the direction does not matter
It holds, but grinding is much harder
questions.why: Yacht winches only hold one way; the turns must go on clockwise.

questions.q: How much load should you plan to put on it?

figure.title: New mooring line
lines: Will be knotted and run over a quay edge

options: About half, 1,900 kg
Up to the full 3,800 kg
About a fifth of that, at most
About 3,000 kg, a 20% margin
questions.why: Safe working load allows for knots, wear and shock, so it is far below breaking strength.

questions.q: A crew member ties a bowline in uncovered Dyneema to lift the outboard onto the pushpit. Why are you wary?
options: It stretches too much under load
It sinks if dropped over the side
It is too weak for an outboard
Knots can slip in it; splice it
questions.why: Dyneema is slippery and many knots creep in it, so it is spliced for loads.

questions.q: Your crew offers this line for the windward stern line. What is the problem?

figure.title: Stern-to, Kos harbour
lines: Swell rolling in from the gap

options: No stretch, so surges snatch the cleats
It cannot be tied to a bollard
It is too weak to be used as a mooring line
It sinks and chafes on the seabed
questions.why: Mooring lines need stretch; Dyneema passes shock loads straight to the fittings.

questions.q: Why did it part?

figure.title: Town quay, Vis
lines: Swell arrived: boat surging, lines snatching
One stern line parted at 3 am

options: The wind rose by a few knots
Snatch loads far above the steady pull
Wet rope always loses half its strength
The line was too stretchy
questions.why: Shock loads can be many times the steady load; stretch and snubbers absorb them.

questions.q: The chain hook on your snubber has gone over the side. You want to tie the nylon snubber line onto the anchor chain so it takes the pull along the chain. Which knot?
options: Clove hitch
Double sheet bend
Rolling hitch
Bowline
questions.why: A rolling hitch grips when pulled along the chain; a clove hitch slides.

questions.q: You need to put your own loop on this bollard. How?

figure.note: Another boat's loop is already on it

options: Tie your loop to theirs with a bowline
Lift theirs off and put yours on first
Drop your loop over the top of theirs
Up through their loop, then over the top
questions.why: Dipping the eye lets either boat lift its loop off without disturbing the other.

questions.q: You rig a slip line through a quay ring. Your crew wants to tie a bowline in the end that will run through the ring. Why not?

figure.note: Slip line: both ends on board

options: The knot can jam in the ring
The bowline will shake itself undone
It is harder to make fast on board
A bowline weakens the line too much
questions.why: A slip line must run free; any knot or eye can snag the ring.

questions.q: You arrive for two nights on the town quay and plan an early start. When do you rig the stern lines as slip lines?
options: Never: only when single-handed
Just before leaving, not on arrival
Only if the marinero asks you to
On arrival, to save time later
questions.why: Both parts of a slip line move and chafe; rig it just before you go.

questions.q: You keep getting riding turns on this winch. How should the sheet lead onto the drum?
options: From well above, sloping down onto it
From any angle, it makes no difference
From slightly below the drum
Level with the top of the drum
questions.why: A lead from slightly below makes each new turn go on under the others.

questions.q: Your new halyard, one size thinner than the old one, creeps through the closed clutch under load. Why?
options: Clutches only grip nylon line
The clutch needs oiling
The halyard is led the wrong way
The clutch suits the old diameter
questions.why: Clutch jaws grip a set range of diameters; thinner or slicker rope slips.

questions.q: Leaving the dinghy astern overnight, a crew member ties the painter with a slipped hitch so it is quick to free. Why is this a poor choice?

figure.title: Overnight at anchor
lines: Dinghy towed astern on its painter
Wind expected to rise after midnight
Painter on the stern rail, slipped hitch

options: A tug or a snag can release it
Slipped hitches jam solid when wet
A slipped hitch cannot go on a cleat
It weakens the painter by half
questions.why: Slipped knots are for quick release while attended, not unattended loads.

questions.q: You have agreed to tow a disabled yacht into Göcek. Which of your lines do you use for the tow?
options: The polypropylene line, as it floats
The long nylon line, for its stretch
The Dyneema spare, as it is strongest
A polyester sheet, as it is stiff
questions.why: A long, stretchy tow absorbs the snatching between the two boats.

questions.q: You are kitting out your own yacht. Which set of rope choices is right?
options: Polyester warp, nylon sheets, polypropylene painter
Nylon warp, polypropylene sheets, polyester painter
Nylon warp, polyester sheets, polypropylene painter
Polypropylene warp, polyester sheets, nylon painter
questions.why: Stretch for the warp, low stretch for sheets, floating rope for the painter.

questions.q: You have your finger on the winch button. What now?

figure.title: Hoisting the main
lines: Sail stops 2 m below the masthead

options: Keep the button pressed until it frees
Add another turn and keep going
Switch to the faster speed
Stop it and find the snag
questions.why: An electric winch can break gear or crush hands; look before you pull.

questions.q: You need to ease the loaded sheet on a self-tailing winch. What do you do first?
options: Take the tail out of the jaws
Push the turns down with the handle
Ease it while it stays in the jaws
Take all the turns off the drum
questions.why: Out of the jaws, you control the tail and the drum turns do the easing.

questions.q: The spring and the stern line share one cleat, with the stern line on top. Why is this a problem when you leave?

labels: spring under, stern line on top

options: The cleat cannot take the load of two lines
The spring is trapped under the stern line
The stern line will slip off the spring
Two lines must be tied together first
questions.why: The line underneath is trapped until the one on top is taken off.

questions.q: This line takes a hard snatch in a gust and parts. Where is it most likely to break?

figure.note: Bowline on the bollard, cleated on board

options: At the cleat on board
Halfway along, where the load is
At the bowline, its weakest point
Anywhere, all points are equal
questions.why: The tight bends in a knot weaken a rope far more than a smooth turn or a splice.

questions.q: Your crew wants to take a loaded sheet off a winch by unwinding it from the drum one turn at a time. Why do you stop them?
options: Unwinding damages the winch ratchet
The drum will spin backwards
It puts a twist into the sheet each time
The line can run away as turns come off
questions.why: Under load, ease with all turns on, or flick them off together with hands clear.

questions.q: You are issuing lifejackets for a coastal passage between the Cyclades. Which rating do you give each adult as a minimum?
options: Any rating, if it fits
questions.why: 150 N suits coastal and offshore sailing; 50 N is a buoyancy aid, 100 N is for sheltered water.

questions.q: The charter boat has both automatic and manual gas lifejackets. You give the automatics to the crew who will be on deck at night. Why?
options: They can be worn without a crotch strap
They inflate even if the wearer is knocked out
They never need a service or a re-arm kit
They give more buoyancy than the manual ones
questions.why: Automatic inflation works on immersion — a stunned wearer cannot pull the toggle.

questions.q: A crew member is ready to go on deck wearing her lifejacket like this. What do you change?

figure.title: Lifejacket check
lines: Waist buckle done up, but loose
Crotch strap tucked inside the jacket

options: Nothing — a fastened waist buckle is enough
Move it under the foul-weather jacket instead
Tighten the waist belt, fasten the crotch strap
Partly inflate it so it is ready to float
questions.why: Without a snug belt and crotch strap an inflated jacket rides up over the face.

questions.q: You have fallen in during a rough night passage and waves keep breaking over your face. What do you do with your lifejacket?
options: Unclip the crotch strap to turn more easily
Take it off and hold it in front of you
Let some air out so you sit lower
Pull its sprayhood down over your face
questions.why: The sprayhood keeps breaking water out of your mouth and nose.

questions.q: At the charter base you check the gas lifejackets before signing for them. What do you look at?
options: Cylinder tight and unfired, indicators green
Pull each toggle once to test the cylinder
Only that each one has a whistle and light
Only the colour, so they show up in the water
questions.why: A loose or fired cylinder means no inflation; firing one to test it leaves it useless.

questions.q: You are checking the safety gear against your crew list. What do you need before sailing?
options: Nothing, if she stays in the cockpit
A child's lifejacket sized for her weight
A swimming ring for when she is on deck
An adult jacket with the straps pulled tight
questions.why: Lifejackets are sized by weight; an adult jacket slips straight off a child.

questions.q: You are putting on foul-weather gear for the night watch. Where does the lifejacket go?
options: Under the jacket, to keep it dry
Clipped to the binnacle within reach
Over the jacket, as the outer layer
Under the fleece, next to the body
questions.why: Worn underneath, the bladder cannot inflate properly and may crush your chest.

questions.q: You are coming up from below to start your watch. When do you clip on?
options: Once you are sitting at the helm
When the skipper tells you to clip on
Only if you go forward of the mast
Before you leave the companionway
questions.why: Clip to a strong point from the hatch so you are never on deck unattached.

questions.q: You are on the foredeck on a two-legged tether and need to move from the jackstay to the strong point at the mast. How do you change over?
options: Clip the second hook on, then unclip the first
Stay on the jackstay and stretch across
Unclip, step across quickly, then clip on again
Unclip and hold on to the mast with both hands
questions.why: Always one hook attached: make the new clip before you release the old one.

questions.q: You are rigging jackstays at the base before a night crossing. How do you lead them?
options: Outside the shrouds, along the toerail
Bow to cockpit on deck, inboard and taut
From the mast to the pulpit, slack
Along the guardrails at waist height
questions.why: Tight, inboard jackstays stop a tethered crew reaching the water; guardrails are not strong points.

questions.q: You are alone on watch at 03:00 in a calm sea while everyone else sleeps. Do you clip on?
options: Only if you leave the cockpit
No — the sea is calm
Yes, for the whole watch
Only if the wind rises above 20 knots
questions.why: Alone at night nobody would see you go over: clip on whatever the weather.

questions.q: You will helm this boat at night with a 2 m tether. Where do you clip on?

figure.title: Cockpit layout
lines: Strong points: at the hatch and the transom
Helm seat 1.5 m from the stern edge

options: To the strong point nearest the transom edge
To the guardrail wire beside the helm seat
Anywhere — any tether keeps you aboard
Where the tether cannot reach the open transom
questions.why: A tether only helps if it is too short to let you reach the water.

questions.q: You plan a night crossing on day three of the charter. What do you do about it at check-in?
options: Ask the base for harnesses, tethers and jackstays
Plan to motor so nobody needs to go forward
Nothing — lifejackets are enough at night
Tie spare mooring lines round the crew as tethers
questions.why: Without harnesses and jackstays no one can stay attached on deck at night.

questions.q: The liferaft sits in a cradle on the pushpit with a hydrostatic release. The yacht sinks before anyone can launch it. What happens?
options: It only releases if someone cuts the lashing first
It is freed at a few metres, floats up and inflates
It inflates on deck as soon as it gets wet
Nothing — it goes down with the yacht
questions.why: The HRU lets the raft float free; the taut painter fires the inflation, then a weak link breaks.

questions.q: You are checking the liferaft before a week on charter. What do you do?
options: Accept it — a sealed raft lasts for years
Open the canister to check it yourself
Ask the base for a raft that is in service
Inflate it on the pontoon to test it works
questions.why: An out-of-date raft may not inflate; only an approved station services one.

questions.q: During check-in you find the valise liferaft at the bottom of the cockpit locker, under fenders, lines and the outboard fuel. What do you do?
options: Leave it — it is dry and protected down there
Move it to the forepeak, out of the way
Lash it down hard at the bottom of the locker
Restow it on top so it can be lifted out fast
questions.why: A liferaft must be reachable and launchable in seconds.

questions.q: You find the canister raft on the coachroof like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-in: coachroof
lines: Base has added two rope lashings over it

options: Remove the extra ropes so it can float free
Add a padlock so it cannot be stolen
Untie the painter from the cradle as well
Leave them — now the raft can never be lost
questions.why: Extra lashings defeat the hydrostatic release; the raft would sink with the yacht.

questions.q: Which extinguisher do you reach for?

figure.title: Aft deck
lines: Petrol spilt filling the outboard tank
Now burning in a pool on deck

options: The deck-wash hose
Dry powder or foam
A bucket of sea water
A wet towel to beat it out
questions.why: Burning fuel is a Class B fire: water spreads it, powder or foam smothers it.

questions.q: You are first to the chart table. What is your plan?

figure.title: Chart table
lines: Smoke from behind the switch panel

options: Throw a bucket of water over the panel
Open the panel to find the burning wire first
Isolate the batteries, then use CO2 or powder
Spray foam into the panel at once, then isolate
questions.why: Cut the power so it cannot re-ignite; never water or foam on live electrics.

questions.q: You are at the helm when this starts. How do you fight it?

figure.title: Motoring
lines: Engine alarm, smoke from the engine box
Small hole in the box marked FIRE PORT

options: Open the hatches below to let the smoke out
Lift the engine box and spray straight at the flames
Keep the engine running so the fan clears the smoke
Stop engine and fuel, discharge through the fire port
questions.why: Opening the box feeds the fire with air; the fire port floods the space while it stays shut.

questions.q: What is wrong with this galley?
options: You must reach over the flames to get the blanket
It belongs in the cockpit, ready for deck fires
Nothing — it is as close to the fire as possible
It should be inside a locker to keep it dry
questions.why: Mount the blanket near the galley but to one side, so you never lean over a burning pan.

questions.q: How do you put this fire out?

figure.title: Forecabin
lines: Candle knocked over onto a cushion
Galley tap and buckets close by

options: Open the forehatch to clear the smoke
Douse it thoroughly with water
Use only CO2 — never water below
Shut the cabin door and let it burn out
questions.why: Fabric and foam are Class A: water cools and soaks them so they do not re-ignite.

questions.q: How do the two in the forecabin get out?

figure.title: Fire in the saloon
lines: Two crew asleep in the forecabin

options: Through the saloon, fast, with wet towels
Shut the cabin door and wait inside
Through the forehatch onto the foredeck
Through the companionway once it clears
questions.why: Brief everyone on the escape hatches; never go through a fire to reach the main exit.

questions.q: Heeled on starboard tack, the cook wants to heat soup for the crew. How do you set up the galley?
options: Fill the pan well up so it sits steadier
Stand on the low side, right in front of the stove
Lock the gimbals so the stove stays level
Gimbals free, pan clamps on, cook braced in a strap
questions.why: The stove swings level on its gimbals; scalds come from pans falling onto a cook on the low side.

questions.q: You are checking where the gas alarm sensor is fitted. Where should it be?
options: Low down, near the bilge below the cooker
Beside the companionway at head height
High up, near the deckhead above the cooker
In the cockpit, next to the gas bottle
questions.why: LPG is heavier than air: it sinks and collects in the bilge.

questions.q: You run the daily gas check. What does this tell you?

figure.title: Gas locker
lines: Press the bubble tester: a steady stream

options: The bottle is nearly empty and needs changing
A leak — shut the bottle and do not use the gas
The regulator is working just as it should
All normal — gas is flowing to the cooker
questions.why: With every appliance off no gas should flow; bubbles mean it is escaping somewhere.

questions.q: You are about to leave the boat for dinner ashore. What do you do?

lines: Crew going ashore for the evening

options: Leave it — the cooker knobs are off
Turn it off only before you sleep
Switch the gas solenoid off
Leave it on, ready for breakfast
questions.why: The solenoid is open only while cooking; a closed valve cannot feed a leak.

questions.q: You have just connected a new gas bottle in the locker. How do you check the joint?
options: Sniff it closely for any smell of gas
Light the cooker and listen at the locker
Hold a lighter near it to look for a flame
Brush soapy water on it, watch for bubbles
questions.why: Soapy water shows the smallest leak without any flame.

questions.q: You are told this over breakfast. What do you suspect, and what do you do?

figure.title: Morning after rafting up
lines: Motor yacht alongside: generator all night
Its exhaust beside your aft cabin port
Two crew from that cabin: headache, nausea

options: Carbon monoxide — fresh air and medical advice
Dehydration — plenty of water and back to bed
Seasickness — a tablet each and lie them down
Food poisoning — let them sleep it off below
questions.why: Headache and nausea in a cabin near an exhaust is CO until proved otherwise.

questions.q: The alarm wakes you. How do you respond?

lines: No smell, nobody feels ill yet

options: Ignore it — you would smell a real leak
Get everyone into fresh air, find the source
Take the battery out and go back to sleep
Reset it and check it in the morning
questions.why: Carbon monoxide has no smell; sleepers can be poisoned before they notice symptoms.

questions.q: An hour out of Lavrio a crew member feels queasy. What do you suggest?
options: Go below and lie down in the forecabin
Eat a large, rich lunch to settle her stomach
Stay on deck, take the helm, watch the horizon
Read the pilot book to take her mind off it
questions.why: Fresh air, the horizon and a job help; the forecabin has the most motion.

questions.q: At night a seasick crew member needs to be sick. Where?
options: Windward rail, clipped on, so it blows clear
At the leeward rail, unclipped for comfort
Alone at the stern, out of everyone's sight
Leeward side, clipped on, someone watching
questions.why: Seasick crew are a classic overboard risk: leeward, clipped on and in sight.

questions.q: A crew member who gets seasick asks when to take her tablets for tomorrow's crossing. What do you tell her?
options: Before you leave, as the packet says
As soon as you start to feel sick
Halfway across, if it gets rough
Only if the wind is above Force 5
questions.why: Seasickness tablets need time to work; once vomiting starts they barely stay down.

questions.q: You are skipper on this passage. How do you treat this crew member?

figure.title: Passage, day 2
lines: Drowsy, dark urine, dizzy on standing

options: Normal seasickness — she will adapt by tomorrow
As serious: frequent sips, consider diverting
Keep her on the helm to take her mind off it
A large glass of water in one go, then sleep
questions.why: Prolonged vomiting causes dangerous dehydration; give sips often and seek help early.

questions.q: A crew member calls you to the cockpit. What is wrong, and what do you do?

figure.title: Anchored, 14:00
lines: Crew member swam, then slept in the sun
Hot, red, dry skin; very hot to touch

options: Chill from the swim: wrap them up in a blanket
Sunburn: after-sun cream and a sleep in the cabin
Heatstroke: shade, cool with water and air, get help
Heat exhaustion: rest below with a cold beer
questions.why: Hot dry skin and confusion mean heatstroke — cool fast and get medical help.

questions.q: How do you look after this crew member?

figure.title: Motoring, no wind
lines: Crew member pale and sweating heavily
Dizzy, headache, cramps in the legs

options: Keep them working and make them drink at dinner
Wrap them in a foil blanket and let them sleep
Strong coffee to perk them up, then back to work
Shade, rest, sips of water with rehydration salts
questions.why: Heat exhaustion: a cool place, fluids and salts — before it becomes heatstroke.

questions.q: How do you plan the day for the crew?
options: Bimini up, regular water, hats and sunscreen
Cold beer through the day instead of water
Sprayhood down for the breeze, hats off
Hourly swims, so drinking matters less
questions.why: Shade, steady drinking and sun cover prevent sunburn, dehydration and heat illness.

questions.q: You fall in on an April delivery trip. The water is 15 °C and you are gasping uncontrollably. What do you do for the first minute?
options: Swim hard for the boat straight away
Lean back, float and let your breathing settle
Shout and wave continuously so they hear you
Kick off your boots and pull off your jacket
questions.why: Cold-water shock passes in about a minute; float until you control your breathing.

questions.q: You come up to check on the watch. What do you do for the helm?
options: Keep them helming so they stay active and warm
Rub their arms and legs hard to get blood flowing
Relieve them: dry clothes below, warm sweet drink
A tot of brandy to warm up, then back on watch
questions.why: Early hypothermia: shelter, dry insulation and warm sweet drinks; no alcohol.

questions.q: You are the nearest crew member. What is your first aid?

figure.title: Galley, under way
lines: Kettle tipped over in a wave

options: Spread butter on it to soothe the pain
Hold ice straight on the skin until numb
Pop the blisters so the skin can heal
Cool it under running water for 20 minutes
questions.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the damage; no ice, fats or bursting blisters.

questions.q: You have cooled a scald on a crew member's hand for 20 minutes. How do you cover it?
options: A loose layer of cling film, no creams
Antiseptic cream under a large plaster
A fluffy cotton-wool pad, taped down
A tight bandage to stop the swelling
questions.why: Cling film laid on loosely protects a burn and does not stick to it.

questions.q: You grab the first-aid kit. What do you do first for this wound?

figure.title: Foredeck
lines: Knife slipped while cutting a line

options: Rinse it in the sea and leave it open
Press firmly on it with a clean pad
Tie a tourniquet above the wrist
Pull the edges apart to clean it out
questions.why: Firm direct pressure stops most bleeding; a tourniquet is for life-threatening limb bleeding only.

questions.q: How do you manage this casualty?

figure.title: Accidental gybe
lines: Boom hit a crew member's head
Knocked out for a few seconds

options: A stiff drink to steady them, then carry on
Nothing more — they are awake and talking
Watch them closely and get medical advice
Painkillers and let them sleep alone below
questions.why: Any loss of consciousness needs medical advice; signs of brain injury can appear hours later.

questions.q: You check on the casualty from the morning. What do you conclude?

figure.title: Later that evening
lines: Hit by the boom this morning
One pupil larger than the other

options: Seasickness — a tablet and some rest below
Tiredness after the shock — let them sleep it off
Dehydration — plenty of fluids and an early night
Serious head injury — get urgent medical help
questions.why: Repeated vomiting, drowsiness and unequal pupils point to pressure on the brain.

questions.q: You are sailing like this and the boat is rolling. How do you protect the crew?

figure.note: Dead run in a swell, crew in the cockpit

options: Rig a preventer, keep heads clear of the boom
Steer slightly by the lee to keep the sail full
Ease the mainsheet fully and let the boom swing
Let the crew sit up on the coachroof
questions.why: An accidental gybe swings the boom across hard; a preventer holds it.

questions.q: Coming stern-to in Hydra, the transom is about to touch the quay. A crew member stretches a foot out to push off. What do you tell her?
options: Push off with your hand instead of a foot
Keep your feet in — use a roving fender
Push only once the boat has stopped moving
Sit on the transom and brace with both feet
questions.why: Never put a limb between boat and quay; several tonnes will crush it.

questions.q: A crew member presses the electric winch button to hoist the main while another feeds the halyard. What is the rule?
options: Press in long bursts so it is over quickly
Leave the clutch open in case it jams
The one pressing watches, ready to stop
The feeder keeps a hand close to the drum
questions.why: Electric winches crush fingers and break gear; the operator watches and stops at any snag.

questions.q: Weighing anchor, a crew member wants to guide the chain onto the windlass by hand while you press the button. What do you say?
options: Fine, as long as you wear sailing gloves
Fine, but only at slow speed
Hold it on the gypsy with your foot instead
Hands clear — signal to me and I will stop
questions.why: A windlass will not stop for fingers; hands and feet stay away from the gypsy.

questions.q: The swimmer seems well again. What do you do?
options: Get her checked by a doctor today
Another swim to rebuild her confidence
Nothing — she's fine now
A hot shower and an early night
questions.why: Water in the lungs can cause breathing problems hours later; anyone who inhaled water needs checking.

questions.q: You pull a swimmer from the water. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. How do you start CPR?
options: Hold him upside down to drain the water first
Five rescue breaths, then 30 compressions to 2
Recovery position and wait for him to breathe
30 compressions to 2 breaths, compressions first
questions.why: Drowning is a lack of oxygen, so CPR starts with five rescue breaths.

questions.q: You reach the casualty. How do you look after him?

figure.title: Anchored, afternoon
lines: Crew member fainted in the cockpit
Does not respond to your voice

options: Sit him upright on the cockpit seat to recover
Splash him with cold water and leave him there
Recovery position, keep checking the breathing
Start chest compressions at once
questions.why: Unresponsive but breathing: the recovery position keeps the airway open.

questions.q: Your charter crew are mostly friends of friends. Before sailing, what do you ask them about their health?
options: Only whether they can swim well
Nothing — their health is private
Only whether they get seasick
Conditions, allergies and medicines
questions.why: The skipper must know medical needs before a problem happens miles from help.

questions.q: How do you treat the sting?

figure.title: Swimming off Vis
lines: Crew member stung on the arm
Pieces of tentacle still on the skin

options: Rinse with sea water, lift tentacles off
Rub wet sand on it to scrape it clean
Rinse with fresh water and rub it dry
Pour urine on it to stop the stinging
questions.why: Fresh water and rubbing make the stinging cells fire; rinse with sea water, no rubbing.

questions.q: What is likely, and how do you treat it?

figure.title: Wading ashore, sandy bay
lines: Sudden, intense pain in the foot
One small puncture, no spines in it

options: Jellyfish — rinse it with fresh water
Weever fish — soak the foot in hot water
Sea urchin — dig the spine out with a knife
Weever fish — pack the foot in ice
questions.why: Weever venom is broken down by heat; water as hot as is bearable, without scalding, eases it.

questions.q: What do you do before anyone goes in?
options: Let them jump, lower the ladder later
Keep the engine on, swim from the bow
Stop the engine and lower the ladder
Put the engine in neutral and let them go
questions.why: No swimming with the engine running; the ladder goes down before anyone jumps.

questions.q: Your crew want to swim off the stern. What do you rig first?

figure.note: At anchor · wind 15 kn · current setting south

options: The tender, tied up alongside the bow
A line from the bow to the shore
Nothing — the anchor holds the boat still
A floating line streamed astern
questions.why: A trailing line gives a tired swimmer something to grab before being carried away.

questions.q: A crew member wants to swim from the yacht to the beach. What do you insist on?

figure.note: Y: your yacht, 300 m off the beach

options: A bright tow float, clear of the tender route
Nothing — rib drivers will see her head
The tender route, as it is the shortest way
Going at dusk, when the water is calmer
questions.why: A swimmer's head is almost invisible to a rib driver; a bright float and a clear route save lives.

questions.q: After dinner aboard with wine, two crew want a moonlit swim off the stern. What do you say?
options: Fine, as long as they stay near the ladder
No swimming after drinking or in the dark
Fine, if the deck lights are on
Fine, if they wear masks and fins
questions.why: Alcohol slows reactions, and in the dark nobody sees a swimmer in trouble.

questions.q: How do you get them ashore?

figure.title: Tender
lines: 6 crew want to go ashore for dinner
Calm bay, 200 m to the quay

options: One trip, the heaviest at the bow
One trip, two sitting on the tubes
Two trips
One trip — it is calm and close
questions.why: The builder's plate is the limit; overloaded tenders swamp and capsize.

questions.q: What do you need for the trip back to the yacht?

figure.title: Back from the taverna
lines: Crew have had wine with dinner

options: Nothing — the anchor lights will show the way
All torches off to keep your night vision
Full speed, to spend less time on the water
A torch to show, lifejackets on, a sober driver
questions.why: An unlit tender is invisible to other tenders; darkness and drink cause many accidents.

questions.q: You are passing the outboard down from the pushpit into the tender. How do you do it?
options: Safety line on until it is clamped and secured
Drop it on the floor and clamp it on later
Carry it down the ladder in one hand
Hand it across without a line — it is quicker
questions.why: Outboards are easily dropped overboard; keep a line on until clamped and secured.

questions.q: You are about to start the outboard. What do you do before pulling the cord?

figure.title: Starting the outboard
lines: Two crew swimming next to it

options: Start it in forward so it moves off quickly
Neutral, and wait until the swimmers are clear
Ask the swimmers to hold on to the transom
Pull it now — the tender is tied to the yacht
questions.why: A propeller turning near swimmers causes terrible injuries; neutral and clear water first.

questions.q: You are taking the crew ashore. What must be in the tender?

figure.title: Going ashore
lines: Wind 15 kn blowing off the beach

options: Nothing extra, the trip is short
Only the fuel tank — the engine is new
Oars, a bailer and a phone in a dry bag
A spare anchor and chain for the yacht
questions.why: If the outboard fails in an offshore wind you drift out to sea; carry oars and a way to call.

questions.q: You buy a 5-litre can of petrol for the outboard in Fethiye. Where do you stow it?
options: In the engine bay beside the diesel
In the forepeak locker with the fenders
In the bilge, where it stays cool and dark
On deck or in a locker draining overboard
questions.why: Petrol vapour, like gas, sinks and can explode below; keep it outside the hull.

questions.q: At night a male crew member heads to the stern rail to relieve himself over the side. What do you tell him?
options: Use the heads below instead
Do it at the bow instead
Clip on to the guardrail first
Fine, as long as the sea is calm
questions.why: Relieving yourself over the rail is a classic cause of falling overboard, above all at night.

questions.q: The horseshoe is thrown and a spotter is pointing. What do you do at the plotter?
options: Write the position down in the log book
Press the MOB button to mark the spot
Zoom out to find the nearest port
Switch the display over to radar
questions.why: The MOB button fixes the position at once — vital if you lose sight of the casualty.

questions.q: You find this on your check-in walk round. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-in: pushpit
lines: Held on with three cable ties
Danbuoy line tangled round its flag

options: Add more ties so nothing blows off at sea
Stow both in the cockpit locker for now
Cut the ties and clear the danbuoy line
Leave them — the ties stop theft in port
questions.why: Throwable gear must leave the boat in seconds: no ties, no tangles.

questions.q: You are going forward in daylight to check the anchor locker, the boat pitching in a short sea. How do you move?
options: Leeward side, sheltered by the sails
Along the outside of the guardrails
Upright and quick, to spend less time there
Windward side, low, one hand always holding
questions.why: One hand for yourself, one for the boat; to windward you fall into the boat, not over the side.

questions.q: What is your rule?

figure.title: Lunch stop, Hvar
lines: Crew have had a few beers

options: Whoever helms or keeps watch stays off alcohol
Fine to drink once the sails are up
Two beers each is fine for everyone aboard
Anyone may drink if the skipper stays sober
questions.why: Alcohol slows reactions and raises the risk of going overboard; helm and watch stay sober.

questions.q: How do you plan the night?

figure.title: Overnight passage
lines: Crew of 6, you the only skipper

options: Everyone stays up — it is only one night
Set watches so everyone sleeps, including you
Sort out watches once people get tired
Stay on deck all night yourself to be safe
questions.why: A tired skipper makes poor decisions; a watch system gives everyone rest.

questions.q: How do you split the watches?

figure.title: Crew for the night crossing
lines: Ben, Chris, Dana: first night sail

options: Novices on deck, you two asleep below
You and Anna together, the novices together
One led by you, one by Anna, novices shared
Everyone on deck together all night
questions.why: Each watch needs an experienced leader; novices learn and are never left alone.

questions.q: You are at the helm. How do you handle the crew?

figure.title: Halfway across
lines: Wind up from F4 to F6

options: Tell them it will soon die down
Send everyone below until it is over
Say nothing so as not to alarm them
Tell them what's happening and the plan
questions.why: Crew who know the plan stay calmer and can help; uncertainty breeds fear.

questions.q: In your safety briefing, who do you show how to stop the boat, use the VHF and start the MOB drill?
options: At least one other crew member
Nobody — the skipper does all that
Whoever happens to be helming
Only the person who booked the boat
questions.why: If the skipper goes overboard or is hurt, someone else must be able to take charge.

questions.q: Your rule is lifejackets on deck at night. A crew member says they are for beginners and refuses. What do you do?
options: Let him off if he is a strong swimmer
Insist — the skipper's rule stands
Let him decide for himself
Let him wear it, unfastened
questions.why: The skipper is responsible for everyone aboard and sets the safety rules.

questions.q: You review the rota after dinner. What do you change?
options: Let the autopilot steer while he dozes
Nothing — the tablets stop him being sick
Pair him up or take him off the solo watch
Give him strong coffee and keep the rota
questions.why: Many seasickness tablets cause drowsiness; a sleepy lone watchkeeper is a danger.

questions.q: You must decide on tonight's landfall. What do you do?

figure.title: Approaching Turkey
lines: You have been up since 06:00; now 23:00
Crew tired, light wind, plenty of sea room

options: Go in now, before you get even more tired
Go in now with everyone on deck as lookouts
Feel your way in and anchor at the entrance
Stay offshore, rest in turns, enter at dawn
questions.why: Fatigue and an unknown, unlit entry don't mix; with sea room, wait for daylight.

questions.q: When do you reef?
options: Before leaving the harbour
When the boat starts heeling hard
When the wind reaches F6
Halfway, once you see how it goes
questions.why: Reef early: it is easy in shelter and hard once you are overpowered.

questions.q: What do you do below before leaving?

figure.title: Before the crossing
lines: Floorboards loose, tins in an open locker

options: Leave everything out so it is close to hand
Lock floorboards and lockers, stow heavy items
Pile the heavy bags on the saloon table
Open the hatches for fresh air below
questions.why: In a knockdown loose heavy items become missiles and floorboards fly.

questions.q: You expect six hours of rough beating. What do you do about food?
options: Plan a hot fry-up halfway across the passage
Skip food altogether until you arrive
Make sandwiches and fill flasks before you go
Cook a full hot meal once it gets rough
questions.why: Cooking in rough weather is hard and risky; hungry crew tire and get seasick faster.

questions.q: What do you do with the washboards?

figure.title: Running before a big sea
lines: Two crew in the cockpit, one below

options: Fit them only once water has come below
Leave them stowed in the locker below
Leave them out so crew get below quickly
Fit the lower ones, keep the rest at hand
questions.why: If a wave fills the cockpit, the washboards stop it pouring below.

questions.q: Your novice crew are due to cross 25 miles of open water tomorrow. What do you do?

figure.note: Tomorrow: NW F7 from dawn, all day

options: Stay in harbour until it passes
Go under engine and motor through
Leave at first light, before it builds
Go, and reef once it gets rough
questions.why: The best heavy-weather tactic for a charter crew is not to be out in it.

questions.q: Conditions are as shown. What do you decide?

figure.title: Beating to windward
lines: Wind F6 on the nose, 18 miles to go
Two of five crew seasick, one exhausted

options: Send the sick crew below and carry on
Bear away for the sheltered bay
Start the engine and motor into it
Press on — it is the plan
questions.why: A tired, sick crew is a hazard; turn for shelter while you still can.

questions.q: Your crew are going on night watch for the first time. How do you protect their night vision?
options: White cabin lights on for safety
Head torch on full beam on deck
Red lights below, dimmed screens
Bright plotter screen for detail
questions.why: Night vision takes many minutes to come back after white light.

questions.q: You are on watch with the skipper asleep below. What do you do?
options: Alter course quietly
Wait until it is closer
Shine a torch at it
Wake the skipper now
questions.why: A steady bearing means risk of collision: call the skipper early, never late.

questions.q: At night you need to go forward to clear a fouled furling line. What do you do first?
options: Tell the helm, clip on, take a head torch
Unclip so you can move faster forward
Go without a light to keep night vision
Go quietly so you wake nobody below
questions.why: Nobody goes forward at night without the helm knowing, clipped on and with a light.

questions.q: You are finishing the grab bag. Which item is most worth adding?

figure.title: Grab bag so far
lines: Copies of passports and boat papers

options: A saucepan and a gas canister
A handheld VHF in a waterproof pouch
The boat's toolbox and spare fuses
Paper charts of the whole cruising area
questions.why: In a liferaft, a way to talk to rescuers matters more than anything else.

questions.q: Where do you keep the grab bag during a charter week?
options: Under the forecabin bunk, out of the way
In the cockpit locker under the lines
By the companionway, known to all
In the skipper's cabin, locked
questions.why: In an emergency you have seconds; the grab bag must be on the way out.

questions.q: You are packing drinking water for the grab bag. How?
options: Glass bottles, to keep it fresh
None — the liferaft has enough
One full 5-litre can
Small bottles, not quite full
questions.why: Part-filled small bottles float if dropped and are easy to share out.

questions.q: You are checking the fire gear at the base. What do you do?
options: Have it replaced before you leave
Shake it to bring the needle back
Sign for it, report it at the end
Accept it — red is normal for powder
questions.why: A needle in the red means low pressure; the extinguisher may not work.

questions.q: You count the lifejackets at check-in. What do you do?
options: Share them — not all are on deck at once
Get two more from the base before sailing
Sail; the two best swimmers go without
Use cockpit cushions for the other two
questions.why: There must be a lifejacket of the right size for every person aboard.

questions.q: Crossing the Saronic Gulf at midday, the whole crew wants to eat lunch below. What does Rule 5 require?

figure.title: Midday passage
lines: Ferries and fast boats on the route

options: A lookout is only required at night
A quick look round every 15 minutes will do
Someone keeps a lookout on deck at all times
The autopilot alarm is enough in daylight
questions.why: Rule 5: a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times.

questions.q: How do you keep a proper lookout, sailing like this?
options: Rely on the AIS alarm to warn you
Leave it to others — they can see you
Watch ahead and to windward only
Look under the genoa to leeward regularly
questions.why: Rule 5: the genoa hides the leeward bow — that is where you must look.

questions.q: You are approaching this harbour at night. What does the scene mean for your speed?

figure.note: Night · harbour entrance against the town lights

options: Slow down — shore lights hide other vessels
Keep speed to clear the entrance quickly
Speed only matters in poor visibility
Keep to the harbour limit, nothing more
questions.why: Rule 6: background light is a factor in choosing a safe speed.

questions.q: Fog comes down while you are motoring along the Croatian coast. What speed do you choose?
options: Full speed to get out of it sooner
Slow enough to stop well within 200 m
Any speed — others must avoid you
Exactly half your usual cruising speed
questions.why: Rules 6 and 19: a safe speed lets you stop within the distance you can see.

questions.q: You are entering this harbour under power. How fast do you go?
options: Fast, to spend less time in everyone's way
Cruising speed — the visibility is good
Slowly — traffic density sets a safe speed
Any speed you like — others will avoid you
questions.why: Rule 6: the density of traffic is a key factor in safe speed.

questions.q: You are motoring in fog with this radar picture. What does Rule 6 say about relying on it?

figure.title: Fog, short steep sea
lines: Radar: sea clutter out to 0.5 M

options: Nothing is there — keep your speed
With radar on you may keep cruising speed
Turn up the gain until the clutter clears
Small boats may hide in the clutter — go slower
questions.why: Rule 6(b): radar limits, sea state and clutter count in choosing a safe speed.

questions.q: How do you keep a proper lookout by hearing in these conditions?
options: Post someone forward and stop now and then to listen
Keep the engine loud so that others can hear you
Listen from the cockpit, right beside the engine
Hearing does not count — only sight matters
questions.why: Rule 5: lookout by sight and hearing — get away from the engine noise.

questions.q: You take three hand-bearing compass bearings of a ship. What do they tell you?
options: She will pass astern of you
Risk of collision exists
No risk — the bearing moved 1°
She will pass ahead of you
questions.why: Rule 7: a steady compass bearing with the range closing means risk of collision.

questions.q: You take these bearings of a ship on your port bow. What will she do?
options: Hit you — the bearing is steady
Pass ahead of you — the bearing is drawing forward
Pass astern of you — the bearing is drawing aft
Cross ahead — she is on your port bow
questions.why: Rule 7: a bearing drawing aft means she will pass astern; keep checking.

questions.q: The bearing of this cruise ship is changing. Can you relax?
options: Yes — a ship that size is bound to have seen you
Only once the bearing has moved by 10° or more
Yes — any change of bearing means there is no risk
No — so close to a big ship, risk may still exist
questions.why: Rule 7(d)(ii): risk can exist with a changing bearing when close to a large vessel.

questions.q: What does Rule 7 say about this radar echo?

figure.title: Radar, haze at dusk
lines: One echo at 4 M on the starboard bow

options: Plot it over time before deciding it will pass
Turn to port now to open the range
It is far off — ignore it until it is seen
Assume it is a buoy until it moves
questions.why: Rule 7(c): no assumptions on scanty information, especially radar.

questions.q: You cannot tell whether the bearing of this motorboat is changing. What do you assume?

figure.note: Bearing hard to read in the swell

options: That she has seen you
That risk of collision exists
Nothing until you are sure
That she will pass clear
questions.why: Rule 7(a): if in doubt, risk of collision is deemed to exist.

questions.q: Your plotter shows this AIS target. What do you make of it?

figure.title: AIS target
lines: Not yet in sight in the haze

options: She has AIS, so she has seen you
Wait until she is in sight to decide
Risk of collision — plan early action now
No risk — 0.1 M is a clear pass
questions.why: Rules 7 and 8: a CPA near zero means risk of collision; act early.

questions.q: Can you rely on the AIS screen for your lookout here?

figure.title: Haze, visibility 1 mile
lines: AIS screen: no targets within 10 M
Radar: switched off to save power
Fishing boats often work this coast

options: Yes, as long as it is daylight
Yes, for anything inside 10 M
Yes — every vessel must carry AIS
No — many boats carry no AIS at all
questions.why: Rules 5 and 7: AIS is only an aid; yachts and fishing boats often have none.

questions.q: You must give way to this ship. What kind of alteration does Rule 8 want?
options: One early turn, big enough to see on radar
A late turn once she is close
A small change of speed only
Several small 5° nudges as she closes
questions.why: Rule 8: early, substantial, readily apparent — not a series of small alterations.

questions.q: You are the give-way vessel but cannot turn to starboard. What do you do?

figure.note: Shoal water close on your starboard side

options: Turn to port and cross ahead of her
Slow down or stop and let her pass ahead
Hold course and speed — you have no choice
Speed up to get across her bow
questions.why: Rules 8(e) and 16: slowing or stopping is a proper give-way action.

questions.q: You have turned 40° to starboard to pass astern of this boat. What does Rule 8 require now?
options: Return to your original course at once
Sound one short blast every minute until clear
Check her bearing until she is past and clear
Nothing more — the turn itself was enough
questions.why: Rule 8(d): check the action until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

questions.q: Under sail in this channel, risk of collision with the tanker now exists. Does your duty change?

figure.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the deep water

options: No — but only if she sounds five short
Yes — you become stand-on and hold course
Yes — the duty ends once she is close
No — you must still act early not to impede her
questions.why: Rule 8(f): the duty not to impede continues when risk of collision develops.

questions.q: You want to cross this buoyed channel ahead of the ship. What does Rule 9 say?

figure.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the channel

options: Do not cross if it will impede her — wait
Cross now — she must give way to you
Cross diagonally to save time
Cross at speed — she can slow down
questions.why: Rule 9(d): do not cross a narrow channel if it impedes a vessel confined to it.

questions.q: You are motoring up a winding channel and nearing a bend where high ground hides what is coming. What sound signal do you give?
options: Five short blasts
One prolonged blast
One short blast
Two prolonged blasts
questions.why: Rule 34(e): one prolonged blast when nearing a bend that may hide other vessels.

questions.q: Close to a blind bend in a narrow channel, you hear a prolonged blast from behind the headland. What do you do?
options: Reply with one short blast and cut the corner
Reply with five short blasts
Reply with one prolonged blast and keep right
Stay silent and speed up round the bend
questions.why: Rule 34(e): a prolonged blast from round the bend is answered with one prolonged.

questions.q: In this narrow channel you want to overtake on her port side. What do you sound first?

figure.note: Narrow channel · you are the faster boat

options: Two short blasts
Long, short, long, short
Two prolonged then one short blast
Two prolonged then two short blasts
questions.why: Rule 34(c): two prolonged + two short = I intend to overtake on your port side.

questions.q: After your overtaking signal in a channel, the boat ahead replies like this. What does it mean?
options: She agrees — overtake with care
She is altering to starboard
She objects — stay astern
She is going astern
questions.why: Rule 34(c)(ii): prolonged, short, prolonged, short = agreement.

questions.q: In a narrow channel you signal that you want to overtake. The boat ahead answers with five short blasts. What now?
options: Overtake at once — she has heard your signal
Stay astern until it is safe and she agrees
Sound five short back, then overtake
Overtake her on the other side instead
questions.why: Rule 34(d): five short = doubt; do not overtake yet.

questions.q: In a narrow channel this motor vessel astern sounds two prolonged and two short blasts. What do you do?

figure.note: Narrow channel · she is closing from astern

options: Nothing — she must keep clear of you
Move to port and hold your speed
Sound agreement and move over to starboard
Speed up so she cannot pass
questions.why: Rule 9(e): if you agree, answer long-short-long-short and make room.

questions.q: You must cross this traffic separation scheme. How do you steer?
options: On a track at right angles, heading into the stream
At a shallow angle, going with the traffic flow
Straight across towards your destination
On a heading at right angles, whatever the stream
questions.why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the flow.

questions.q: You want to follow the eastbound lane along the coast. How do you join it?
options: At its end, or from the side at a small angle
Anywhere along it, in either direction
From the side, at right angles to the lane
Straight across the separation zone into it
questions.why: Rule 10(b)(iii): join at the end, or from the side at as small an angle as practicable.

questions.q: Your 13 m yacht is going from one bay to the next along this coast. May you use the inshore traffic zone?
options: No — it is for fishing vessels only
Yes — under 20 m and sailing vessels may
No — you must use the lane
Only with permission from VTS
questions.why: Rule 10(d): vessels under 20 m, sailing vessels and fishing vessels may use it.

questions.q: Your planned track runs straight down the middle of the separation zone. Is that acceptable?
options: Yes, but only in good daylight visibility
Yes — it is the safe space between the ships
No — enter it only to cross or in an emergency
Yes, provided you show a cone by day
questions.why: Rule 10(e): keep out of a separation zone except to cross, join, leave or in an emergency.

questions.q: You are in this lane of a traffic separation scheme. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — lanes are two-way for yachts
Nothing, if you keep to the edge
You should be in the separation zone
You are going against the traffic flow
questions.why: Rule 10(b)(i): in a lane, go in the general direction of traffic flow.

questions.q: Your route passes close to where this scheme ends. What do you expect there?
options: Ships changing course and converging
Ships slowing down to anchor
Ships giving way to yachts there
No traffic — ships have left the lanes
questions.why: Rule 10(f): navigate with particular caution near the ends of a scheme.

questions.q: Crossing the lane under sail, this ship following the lane is closing on a steady bearing. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Crossing a TSS lane under sail

options: Nobody — both hold course inside the scheme
You — you must not impede a ship in the lane
The ship — power always gives way to sail
The ship — you are crossing at right angles
questions.why: Rule 10(j): sail and vessels under 20 m must not impede power vessels in a lane.

questions.q: To cross this scheme at right angles under sail you would be head to wind. What do you do?
options: Cross on a diagonal — ships give way to sail
Sail along the lane until the wind frees
Motor-sail to hold a heading near right angles
Tack across at whatever angle the wind allows
questions.why: Rule 10(c): cross as nearly at right angles as practicable — use the engine.

questions.q: This yacht to windward is running downwind and you cannot see her mainsail. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Her mainsail is hidden behind the genoa

options: She does — she is running free
She does — she is to windward
Neither, until you know her tack
You — you cannot be sure of her tack
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, if unsure of a windward boat's tack, keep clear.

questions.q: Both yachts are close-hauled on port tack and converging. What do you do?
options: Hold course and speed — she is to windward
Bear away — you are the leeward boat
Give way — she is on your port side
Tack at once onto starboard
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, windward keeps clear; you stand on (Rule 17).

questions.q: You are to windward of this yacht. Who gives way?
options: You do — you are to windward
She does — she is on port tack
You do — she is close-hauled
Whichever boat is faster
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(i): on different tacks, port keeps clear; windward only counts on the same tack.

questions.q: You are running dead downwind with the mainsail out to port. This yacht is converging. Who keeps clear?
options: You do — she is on your starboard side
You do — running, you have no tack
She does — you count as starboard tack
Neither — pass each other port to port
questions.why: Rule 12(b): the windward side is opposite the mainsail, so main to port = starboard tack.

questions.q: You are stand-on to this port-tack yacht a mile away. Your crew want to tack away now, just in case. What do you do?
options: Luff up and slow right down for her
Bear away now to pass astern of her
Tack now so as to be on the safe side
Hold course and speed so she can keep clear
questions.why: Rule 17(a)(i): the stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed.

questions.q: This motor yacht is coming up from here, faster than you. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: She is closing from your starboard quarter

options: She does — she is overtaking you
Both alter course to starboard
You do — she is the faster boat
You do — she is on your starboard side
questions.why: Rule 13: from more than 22.5° abaft your beam she is overtaking, whatever the side.

questions.q: You are catching this motorboat up and cannot be sure whether you are overtaking or crossing. What do you do?

figure.note: You are faster · about 20° abaft her beam

options: Pass close ahead of her as stand-on
Assume you are overtaking and keep clear
Hold course and speed until it is clear
Treat it as crossing: she gives way to you
questions.why: Rule 13(c): in doubt, assume you are overtaking and keep out of the way.

questions.q: You started overtaking this boat from astern; now she is converging with you. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Bearing now forward of your beam

options: Neither — you are now abreast
She does — she is the slower boat
You — until you are past and clear
She does — she is now crossing from port
questions.why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing does not end the overtaking vessel's duty.

questions.q: Motoring at night, this is the only light ahead and you are gaining on it. What do you do?
options: Hold course — it must get out of your way
Pass close down either side at speed
Stand on and flash your spotlight
Keep clear — you are coming up from astern
questions.why: Rule 13: seeing only her sternlight, you are overtaking and keep clear.

questions.q: Sailing downwind, you are catching up this yacht. Who keeps clear?
options: You — overtaking beats the tack rules
She does — she is to leeward
Neither — both boats are running
She does — she is on port tack
questions.why: Rule 13 overrides Rule 12: an overtaking sailing vessel keeps clear.

questions.q: Under sail, you see this motor yacht coming up from astern. What do you do?

figure.note: She is faster, closing from astern

options: Slow down so she passes quickly
Hold course and speed — she keeps clear
Alter course to let her pass
Give way — she is the faster vessel
questions.why: Rules 13 and 17: she is overtaking and keeps clear; you stand on.

questions.q: Looking astern at night, you see these lights closing on you. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · dead astern of you, closing fast

options: Turn to port to let her pass
Turn to starboard as for head-on
Hold course and speed and watch her
Speed up to stay ahead of her
questions.why: Rules 13 and 17: a vessel coming up from astern is overtaking; you stand on.

questions.q: Motoring at night, these lights appear fine ahead on a steady bearing. What do you do?
options: Alter course to port
Hold course and speed
Stop and wait for her to act
Alter course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 14: masthead lights in line and both sidelights = head-on; both turn to starboard.

questions.q: Motoring, you meet this yacht under sail end-on. Who takes action?
options: You alone — power keeps clear of sail
She does — sail is more agile than power
Both of you — each turns to starboard
Neither — you pass port to port as you are
questions.why: Rule 14 is for two power vessels; Rule 18 makes power keep clear of sail.

questions.q: This vessel is nearly ahead and her red light comes and goes. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · fine on your starboard bow, closing

options: Alter to port to open the gap
Treat it as head-on and alter to starboard
Wait until both sidelights are steady
Hold on for a starboard-to-starboard pass
questions.why: Rule 14(c): if in doubt whether it is head-on, assume it is and act.

questions.q: Motoring by day, you see this ship ahead with her masts in line. What do you do?
options: Stop and wait for her
Hold your course and speed
Alter course to starboard
Alter course to port
questions.why: Rule 14: masts in line by day = head-on; both turn to starboard.

questions.q: Motoring, you see this boat crossing. What do you do?
options: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Slow down to let her cross ahead
Turn to starboard to give way
Hold course and speed, and watch her
questions.why: Rules 15 and 17: you are on her starboard side, so you stand on.

questions.q: In open water, this high-speed ferry is closing on a steady bearing. Who gives way?

figure.note: Ferry at 30 knots · you are motoring

options: The ferry — you are on her starboard side
You — the bigger vessel has right of way
You — high-speed craft have priority
Both of you alter to starboard
questions.why: Rule 15: a high-speed craft is a power-driven vessel with no special priority.

questions.q: You are motoring. These lights are on your port bow on a steady bearing. Your action?
options: Stop — she has the right of way
Hold course and speed, ready to act
Turn to port to pass astern of her
Turn to starboard and give way
questions.why: Rules 15 and 17: you see her green, so she has you to starboard and gives way.

questions.q: You are the stand-on vessel and she shows no sign of giving way. What do you do first?

figure.note: Steady bearing, half a mile, no action

options: Turn to port across her bow
Sound one prolonged blast
Sound at least five short blasts
Keep silent and hold on
questions.why: Rule 34(d): five short blasts when in doubt the other is taking enough action.

questions.q: She still does nothing after your five short blasts. You decide to act. Which way?
options: Hold on — stand-on may never act
Turn to port to pass astern of her
Speed up to cross ahead of her
Turn to starboard, not to port
questions.why: Rule 17(c): do not turn to port for a power vessel on your own port side.

questions.q: She is now so close that her action alone cannot avoid a collision. What does Rule 17 require?
options: You must take the best action to avoid her
Wait — she is the give-way vessel
Hold course and speed to the end
Sound five short and do nothing else
questions.why: Rule 17(b): when the give-way vessel alone cannot avoid collision, you must act.

questions.q: Under sail, you are stand-on to this container ship. Why do you still watch her closely and act early if she does not alter?

figure.note: Open water · she is not restricted

options: Because she is crossing from your starboard side
She may not see you, and can't turn or stop fast
Ships always have the right of way over yachts
Ships are not allowed to alter course for yachts
questions.why: Rules 2 and 17: big ships have blind arcs and long stopping distances.

questions.q: You are under sail and converging with a ship showing these shapes. Who keeps clear?
options: Neither — she is at anchor
She does — power gives way to sail
You — she is not under command
Whoever has the other on her port side
questions.why: Rule 18: sail keeps clear of a vessel not under command (two balls).

questions.q: Motoring past a dredger working in the harbour approach, you see these shapes. What do you do?
options: Keep clear only if she is to starboard
Pass close to read her signals
Hold course — she is just a power vessel
Keep clear — she is restricted in manoeuvre
questions.why: Rule 18: ball-diamond-ball = restricted in ability to manoeuvre.

questions.q: Under sail, you are converging with a deep-laden tanker showing this shape. What do you do?
options: Keep out of her way — avoid impeding her
Hold on — she gives way to sail
Pass close ahead — she can slow down
Nothing — the shape is for fishing boats
questions.why: Rule 18(d): all but NUC and RAM avoid impeding a vessel constrained by her draught.

questions.q: Motoring, you see this boat crossing on a steady bearing. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Trolling lines astern, no day shape

options: Neither — both of you should slow down
She does — trolling is not "engaged in fishing"
You — fishing boats always have the priority
You — she has fishing lines in the water
questions.why: Rule 3(d): trolling lines do not restrict manoeuvring, so Rule 15 applies.

questions.q: Under sail near Corfu, this seaplane is taxiing towards your track. Who keeps clear?
options: Neither — it is about to take off
You — aircraft always have priority
The seaplane — it keeps clear of vessels
You — it is on your starboard side
questions.why: Rule 18(e): a seaplane on the water keeps well clear of all vessels.

questions.q: You are sailing like this with the engine running in gear. What do you hoist?
options: Nothing — the sails say you are sailing
A black ball forward
Two cones, points together
A cone, point down, forward
questions.why: Rule 25(e): under sail and engine, show a cone apex down; you are power-driven.

questions.q: You are under sail alone, on port tack. This yacht on starboard tack is crossing your course. Who keeps clear?
options: She does — she is power-driven
You do — she is on starboard tack
Neither — both have sails up
Whichever boat is to windward
questions.why: Rule 18: the cone shows she is motor-sailing, so she keeps clear of sail.

questions.q: This vessel lies across your planned route into a Croatian bay. What do you do?
options: Stand by — she is not under command
Keep well clear — she is aground in shallows
Pass either side — she is fishing
Pass close astern — she is only at anchor
questions.why: Rule 30(d): three balls = aground; there is shallow water round her.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see these lights. Where do you pass?
options: Just astern of the tug, ahead of the tow
Between the tug and the lit tow
Well astern of the tow, never between
Close ahead of the tug, then clear
questions.why: Three masthead lights: a tow over 200 m long, behind the tug — never cut between.

questions.q: Off this beach, what does good seamanship ask of you?

figure.title: Off a beach on Paros
lines: Your route passes 300 m off the beach

options: Hold course — they must keep clear
Speed up to get through quickly
Sound five short and carry on
Slow down, keep well off and watch them
questions.why: Rules 2, 5 and 6: fast, unpredictable craft call for a wide berth and safe speed.

questions.q: Motoring, you meet this windsurfer crossing ahead. Who keeps clear?
options: You — treat her as a sailing vessel
She does — she is on your port side
She does — she is far more agile
Neither — she is not a vessel
questions.why: Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail; give boards a wide berth.

questions.q: Motoring, you see this trawler crossing from your port side. Who keeps clear?
options: Both of you alter to starboard
You — she is engaged in fishing
She does — you are on her starboard side
She does — she is power-driven too
questions.why: Rule 18(a): power keeps clear of a vessel engaged in fishing, from any side.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see only these two lights, close together, on a steady bearing. What do you do?
options: Turn to port across her bow
Hold course — she must give way to you
Keep clear — she is a yacht under sail
Stand on — she is only a small boat
questions.why: No masthead light: a sailing vessel; power keeps clear of sail (Rule 18).

questions.q: You are under sail alone and see these lights on a steady bearing. What do you do?
options: Give way — she is on your starboard side
Turn to port to pass astern of her
Tack at once to keep clear of her
Hold course and speed, watching her closely
questions.why: Masthead light and red = power vessel crossing; she keeps clear of sail (Rule 18).

questions.q: Under sail at night, you see these lights converging. Who keeps clear?
options: You — she is restricted in manoeuvre
She does — she is on your port side
Neither — she is at anchor
She does — power gives way to sail
questions.why: Red-white-red all-round = restricted in ability to manoeuvre; sail keeps clear.

questions.q: You must pass this fishing vessel. Which side do you choose?
options: Either side — she is not making way
The right-hand side, away from the extra white
The left-hand side, by the extra white
Close past her, whichever side is shorter
questions.why: Rule 26(c): an extra all-round white shows the direction of outlying gear.

questions.q: You hear this signal. What does Rule 19 require you to do?

figure.title: Fog, no radar
lines: Heard: one prolonged blast every 2 min
It seems to come from your port bow

options: Keep speed and sound one short blast
Hold course and speed — you stand on
Slow to steerage way, and stop if needed
Turn to starboard and keep your speed
questions.why: Rule 19(e): a fog signal heard forward of the beam — cut to bare steerage way.

questions.q: In fog, radar shows this target closing. Which alteration is right?

figure.note: Fog · radar only, bearing steady, closing

options: None — hold on as the stand-on vessel
Speed up to pass ahead of the target
A turn to port, away from the target
A bold turn to starboard, or slow down
questions.why: Rule 19(d)(i): avoid turning to port for a vessel forward of the beam.

questions.q: In fog, radar shows this target closing from your starboard quarter. What do you do?

figure.note: Fog · not in sight, she is faster

options: Alter to port, away from her
Alter to starboard, the usual way
Turn towards her to pass under her stern
Hold on — she is overtaking, so she keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid turning towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.

questions.q: In fog, radar shows this vessel closing from your port bow. Are you the stand-on vessel?

figure.note: Fog · not in sight of each other

options: No — you are the give-way vessel
No — out of sight, both must act
Yes, until she is within a mile
Yes — she is on your port side
questions.why: Rule 19: vessels not in sight have no stand-on or give-way; each avoids close quarters.

questions.q: You were tracking this motor yacht by radar in fog. Now she is in sight. Which rule applies?

figure.note: She has just come into sight, 200 m off

options: You stand on — she is the faster boat
Both of you turn to port to open up
The crossing rule — you give way to her
Still Rule 19 — nobody is stand-on
questions.why: Rules 11 and 15: once in sight of each other, the steering rules apply.

questions.q: Motoring at 5 knots in fog, what sound signal do you make?
options: Five short blasts every minute
Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes
One prolonged and two short every 2 minutes
One prolonged blast every 2 minutes or less
questions.why: Rule 35(a): power-driven, making way — one prolonged at intervals of 2 minutes or less.

questions.q: Fog closes in while you are under sail alone. Which signal do you give, and how often?
options: One prolonged and two short, every 2 minutes
One prolonged, every 2 minutes
Two prolonged, every 2 minutes
Rapid ringing of the bell, every minute
questions.why: Rule 35(c): a sailing vessel sounds one prolonged followed by two short.

questions.q: In thick fog you stop the engine and drift, sails furled, to listen. What signal now?
options: None — you are not making way through the water
Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes or less
One prolonged blast every 2 minutes or less
One prolonged, two short, every 2 minutes
questions.why: Rule 35(b): under way but not making way — two prolonged blasts.

questions.q: In fog you hear three separate strokes of a bell, rapid ringing, then three strokes again, ahead of you. What do you do?
options: Ignore it — it is a church bell ashore
Pass close — it is just a vessel at anchor
Keep well clear — a vessel aground, shoal water
Hold on — a vessel under way must give way
questions.why: Rule 35(h): three strokes, rapid ringing, three strokes = vessel aground.

questions.q: Motoring slowly along the coast in fog, you hear rapid ringing of a bell for about five seconds, once a minute. What is it?
options: A sailing vessel under way
A fishing boat hauling her nets
A vessel aground — the water is shallow
A boat at anchor — slow down and avoid her
questions.why: Rule 35(g): rapid bell ringing for 5 seconds each minute = vessel at anchor.

questions.q: Creeping into a bay in fog, you hear one short, one prolonged and one short blast close ahead. What does it mean?
options: An anchored boat warns you are closing on her
A ship astern intending to overtake you
A vessel aground somewhere ahead of you
A sailing vessel under way close by
questions.why: Rule 35(g): an anchored vessel may sound short-prolonged-short as a warning.

questions.q: A motor yacht you can see clearly sounds two short blasts. What is she doing?
options: Asking you to keep clear
Altering her course to port
Altering her course to starboard
Going astern
questions.why: Rule 34(a): two short = I am altering my course to port.

questions.q: In a busy island harbour, a ferry near the quay sounds three short blasts. What does it mean?
options: She is altering course to starboard
She is about to leave — clear the way
Her engines are going astern
She doubts what you are doing
questions.why: Rule 34(a): three short = I am operating astern propulsion.

questions.q: You are near a ship in clear weather when she sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does she mean?
options: She is going astern
She is altering course to port
She is about to overtake you
She doubts you are keeping clear
questions.why: Rule 34(d): at least five short = I doubt your intentions or action.

questions.q: Motoring in sight of this ship, you are about to alter to starboard to give way. What signal do you give?
options: One short blast as you turn
None — signals are for ships only
One prolonged blast
Two short blasts as you turn
questions.why: Rule 34(a): power vessels in sight signal alterations — one short = to starboard.

questions.q: You have not yet altered for this ship. She flashes a white light five times, rapidly. What does she mean?
options: She wants you to hold course and speed
She doubts you are keeping clear — act now
She is turning to starboard to avoid you
She is altering her course to port
questions.why: Rule 34(d): five short, rapid flashes = doubt; give way clearly now.

questions.q: This ship flashes her all-round white light twice. What is she doing?
options: Operating astern propulsion
Warning you of danger ahead
Altering her course to port
Altering her course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 34(b): two flashes, like two short blasts = altering to port.

questions.q: There is no room to turn to starboard for this motorboat. What do you do?

figure.note: Narrow passage · rocks close to starboard

options: Turn to port and pass starboard to starboard
Turn to starboard anyway — Rule 14
Hold course and speed — she will move
Slow down or stop until she has passed
questions.why: Rules 2(b) and 8(e): when the rule cannot be followed, slow or stop.

questions.q: Your plotted position lies three-quarters of the way up from the lower parallel to the upper one. What is your latitude?

figure.note: Parallels of latitude on the chart

questions.why: The parallels are 10' apart; three-quarters up is 7.5' north of 37°40'.

questions.q: You span the dividers between the harbour and tonight's anchorage, then move them to the side of the chart. How far is it?
