options: About 33 nautical miles
18 nautical miles
About 10 nautical miles
18 kilometres
questions.why: On the latitude scale one minute = one nautical mile: 43' − 25' = 18'.

questions.q: Your crew reads a position off a phone app. What latitude do you plot on the paper chart?
questions.why: 0.75 of a degree × 60 = 45 minutes.

questions.q: The log shows a steady 6 knots. How far through the water do you go in one hour?
options: 6 kilometres
11 nautical miles
6 statute miles
6 nautical miles
questions.why: A knot is one nautical mile (1,852 m) per hour.

questions.q: You sail due north as shown, with no tide or leeway. What latitude do you reach?
A navigation warning reports a drifting container. Is its position on the chart you have open?
options: No — just north of the top edge
No — just west of the chart's left edge
Yes — in the upper half of the chart
No — just east of the right edge
questions.why: 019°55'E is 5' west of 020°00'E, the chart's western limit.

questions.q: You anchor at high water. How much water will be under the keel at low water tonight?
questions.why: At LW the depth falls by the range: 4.0 − 1.6 = 2.4 m, then minus the 1.8 m draft.

questions.q: The rock off the point carries this drying height. What do you see as you pass at the time shown?
options: 0.9 m of water over the rock
2.1 m of water over the rock
The rock just awash
The rock showing 0.9 m above water
questions.why: Drying height 1.5 m above datum − 0.6 m of tide = 0.9 m still uncovered.

questions.q: Your track crosses this drying patch. How much water is over it at the time shown?
options: None — it is dry
questions.why: Depth over a drying patch = height of tide − drying height: 1.6 − 0.4.

questions.q: You approach a fixed bridge in the northern Adriatic. What is the clearance under it right now?

figure.title: Fixed bridge
lines: HAT is 1.1 m above chart datum

questions.why: Clearance = charted clearance + (HAT − height of tide) = 12.0 + 0.7.

questions.q: Feeling your way into a shallow bay, how much water is really under your keel?
questions.why: Depth = 2.3 + 0.5 = 2.8 m below the surface; minus the 1.9 m draft.

questions.q: On your metric chart a depth is printed as a large 2 with a small 5 set low beside it. What depth is that?
options: 2 fathoms 5 feet
questions.why: Metric charts show decimetres as a small figure: 2 with a small 5 = 2.5 m below chart datum.

questions.q: Planning where to anchor, you find this printed in the bay. What is the seabed?
options: Sand and shells
Stones and shingle
Soft shingle
Shallow shoal
questions.why: Seabed abbreviations: S = sand, Sh = shells.

questions.q: Off the headland the chart shows a small rock with this figure beside it. What is it?
options: A wreck with 4 m of water over it
A rock that never covers, 4 m high
A rock 4 m below the surface
A rock that dries 4 m at low water
questions.why: A height in brackets beside a rock marks an islet that never covers.

questions.q: The chart prints 'Foul' in the corner of the bay where you planned to drop anchor. What do you do?
options: Anchor there with extra scope for weed
Avoid it at low water only — it dries
Anchor elsewhere — debris may trap the anchor
Anchor there — 'Foul' means soft mud
questions.why: Foul ground is no danger to passing boats but is to be avoided for anchoring.

questions.q: The best-sheltered spot in the bay lies on this charted line. Where do you anchor?
options: On it, with a tripping line
On it, if you leave at dawn
On it — cables are buried
Well clear of the cable
questions.why: Never anchor over a charted cable: the anchor can snag or damage it.

questions.q: Well offshore you pass the buoy labelled on the chart like this. What is it?

figure.note: Depths in metres · 20 M off the coast

options: A data buoy recording weather and sea
A wreck marker buoy
A diving-area buoy
An offshore mooring buoy
questions.why: ODAS = Ocean Data Acquisition System: a yellow data buoy; keep clear of it.

questions.q: Your planned route crosses this charted area. What do you do before you go?
options: Nothing — yachts may always cross
Check navigational warnings for firing times
Call the charter base for permission
Cross only at night when it is quiet
questions.why: Firing areas are live only at notified times: check NAVTEX and coast radio warnings.

questions.q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour with rocks off the entrance, which of these charts do you use?
options: Chart 2 — a balance of area and detail
Chart 1 — the bigger number, more detail
Chart 3 — the largest scale, most detail
Any — they all show the same dangers
questions.why: Use the largest-scale chart for pilotage: 1:12 500 shows the most.

questions.q: Your charter boat's chart and this season's pilot book disagree about the harbour. Which do you trust?

figure.title: Harbour of Vathi
lines: with a light on its head

options: The chart — pilot books are not surveyed
The chart — it is the official document
Neither — follow the plotter track
The newer pilot book — and check by eye
questions.why: Harbours change: use the most recent information and confirm it visually.

questions.q: You want to know how up to date the paper chart aboard is. Where do you look?
options: The edition date and corrections in the margin
The latitude scale on the side
The scale line in the title block
The year printed on the compass rose
questions.why: Edition date and Notices to Mariners corrections are printed in the bottom margin.

questions.q: Your chart of a remote Dodecanese bay gives this source information. How do you treat its depths?

figure.title: Source diagram
lines: Surveyed in the 1880s by lead line

options: As exact — old charts are re-checked
With caution — unsurveyed rocks may exist
As too shallow — old surveys under-read
As exact — seabeds never change
questions.why: Old lead-line surveys can miss isolated rocks between soundings.

questions.q: You take the variation from the chart's compass rose. What variation do you use?
Your chart's compass rose reads as shown. What variation do you use?
Close to your track the chart shows a small cross inside a dotted circle, with no depth given. What is it?
options: A rock of unknown depth, dangerous to you
A rock awash at chart datum
A wreck with over 20 m on it
A former buoy position
questions.why: A dotted danger line round a symbol marks a danger to surface navigation: keep clear.

questions.q: An isolated rock near your route is marked 'PA' on the chart. How do you treat it?
options: It is a private area — keep out
Its position is approximate — give it room
It has been removed — ignore it
Its depth is approximate — pass close
questions.why: PA = position approximate: the danger may lie some way from where it is drawn.

questions.q: Near the strait the chart shows a stream arrow with feathers on one side of its shaft and '2kn' beside it. What does it tell you?
options: Ocean current, 2 knots all year
Ebb stream, about 2 knots that way
Flood stream, about 2 knots that way
Prevailing wind, force 2 that way
questions.why: Feathered arrow = flood stream, plain arrow = ebb; the figure is the spring rate.

questions.q: Your plotted course is shown. What compass course do you give the helmsman?
questions.why: True to compass: subtract east, add west: 120 − 3 + 2 = 119.

questions.q: You take a bearing of the lighthouse for a fix. What true bearing do you plot?

figure.title: Fix at 10:40
lines: You stand aft, clear of the engine

questions.why: The deviation card is for the steering compass only: 310 + 4°E variation = 314.

questions.q: You are steering 090° by the steering compass. What is your true heading?
questions.why: Compass to true: add easterly errors: 090 + 2°E deviation + 5°E variation.

questions.q: In flat calm with no tide, the steering compass and the GPS disagree as shown. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Motoring in flat calm
lines: in the locker under the compass

options: Variation has changed since this morning
Leeway pushing the boat sideways
Deviation from the metal and magnets stowed
The GPS has lost its satellite fix
questions.why: Iron and magnets near the compass add deviation: keep them well away.

questions.q: You arrive in a new sailing area and need the local magnetic variation. Where do you find it?
options: On the boat's deviation card
In the tide tables
On the steering compass card
On the compass rose of the chart
questions.why: Variation depends on place and year; the compass rose gives both.

questions.q: You motor straight down this transit to check the steering compass. What is the deviation on this heading?
questions.why: 315°T − 3°E = 312°M; the compass reads 317°, 5° more, so deviation is 5°W.

questions.q: You take this bearing of the lighthouse. Which line do you draw from the light on the chart?
options: A line from the light on 140°T
A line from the light on 230°T
A line from the light on 320°T
A line from the light on 050°T
questions.why: You lie on the reciprocal as seen from the light: 050 + 180 = 230.

questions.q: You can identify these four objects. Which three give the best fix?

figure.note: B is a summit far inland, directly behind A

options: B, C and D
A, B and C
A, C and D
A, B and D
questions.why: Choose objects near you and about 60°–120° apart; A and B lie on one line.

questions.q: You are motoring east along the coast to take a three-point fix. In what order do you take the bearings?
options: Nearest first: Q, then P, then R
Any order — speed matters more
Q on the beam first, then P and R
P and R first, Q on the beam last
questions.why: Beam bearings change fastest, so take them last; ahead and astern change slowly.

questions.q: Your three bearings off Kythnos plot like this, a triangle almost a mile across. What do you do?
options: Re-take the bearings; assume the worst position
Drop one bearing and use the other two
Plot the centre and carry on
Average it with the GPS position
questions.why: A large cocked hat means an error: wrong object, misread compass or deviation.

questions.q: To pass safely south of the reef, what bearing of the church do you keep?
options: Between 060°T and 090°T
Less than 060°T
More than 060°T
Exactly 060°T all the way
questions.why: South of the line the church bears less than 060°; more means you are on the reef side.

questions.q: Approaching on a leading line at night, you see the two lights like this. Which way do you alter?
options: Slow down until they line up
To port, until they line up
To starboard, until they line up
Hold course; they line up closer in
questions.why: Move towards the front light: rear showing left of front means you are left of the line.

questions.q: You have only one landmark in sight. How do you turn these bearings into a running fix?
options: Move the 10:00 line 5 M along 240°T
Cross the two bearings as they are
Move the 10:00 line 5 M along 030°T
Move the 10:00 line 5 M along 060°T
questions.why: Transfer the first position line by the run between bearings, then cross it with the second.

questions.q: You have this range and bearing of the headland. Where are you?
options: 2.5 M due west of the headland
2.5 M due north of the headland
2.5 M due east of the headland
Somewhere on a 2.5 M circle
questions.why: The headland bears 090° from you, so you lie 2.5 M along 270° from it.

questions.q: Your pilotage plan uses this clearing bearing. What does the bearing you have just taken tell you?

figure.title: Clearing bearing
lines: (not less than) to clear the shoal

options: You are safe — 5° is within error
You are on the dangerous side — alter away
You are exactly on the clearing line
Your compass needs a deviation check
questions.why: NLT 190°: anything less than 190° puts you on the shoal side of the line.

questions.q: In haze you get one bearing of the light, and the echo sounder (corrected to chart datum) reads 20 m. What do you have?
options: A full fix, as good as three bearings
Only a position line — depth adds nothing
A rough fix where the bearing meets the 20 m line
A dead-reckoning position
questions.why: A sounding gives a depth-contour position line; crossed with a bearing it gives a rough fix.

questions.q: You take one bearing of a lighthouse and draw it on the chart. What do you have?
options: A course to steer
An estimated position
A fix — your exact position
A position line — you are somewhere on it
questions.why: One bearing gives one position line; you need a second line to cross it.

questions.q: Your crew has marked the 14:00 position on the chart as a small circle round a dot. What kind of position is it?
options: A fix — an observed position
A waypoint
A dead-reckoning position
An estimated position
questions.why: Chartwork symbols: circled dot = fix, triangle = EP, square = waypoint.

questions.q: You plot your course and log distance from the last fix, then add the tidal stream and leeway. What do you have?
options: A fix
An estimated position (EP)
A running fix
A dead-reckoning (DR) position
questions.why: DR uses course and distance only; an EP adds tidal stream and leeway.

questions.q: You leave the 10:00 fix as shown. Where is your 11:00 estimated position?

figure.note: Fix at the boat · no leeway

options: 4.5 M east of the fix
7.5 M east of the fix
6 M east and 1.5 M south of the fix
6 M east and 1.5 M north of the fix
questions.why: Plot the water track 6 M along 090°, then the tide 1.5 M towards 180°.

questions.q: You leave at the time shown. When do you arrive?
You must reach the anchorage before dark. What average speed do you need?
options: 6.0 knots
5.3 knots
6.4 knots
7.0 knots
questions.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 21 ÷ 3.5 h.

questions.q: You are close-hauled as shown. What water track do you make?
questions.why: Leeway pushes you downwind: wind on the port bow sets you to starboard, 040 + 5.

questions.q: You want to make good the water track shown. What heading do you steer?
questions.why: Leeway sets you north, downwind; steer 6° up into the wind to compensate.

questions.q: Over an hour in open water, on several different headings, you see these readings. What is wrong?
options: Leeway is adding to your speed
The GPS over-reads in open water
A 1.2 kn current is helping you
The log under-reads — clean or calibrate it
questions.why: A difference that stays the same on every heading is a log error, not a current.

questions.q: Where is your DR position at 15:30?

figure.note: Fix at the boat · no tide, no leeway

options: 6.0 M west of the fix
5.2 M west of the fix
4.0 M west of the fix
6.0 M east of the fix
questions.why: 1.5 h × 4 kn = 6 M along the course; a DR ignores tide and leeway.

questions.q: Which tidal stream do you take from this table?
options: 280°T at 1.1 knots
270°T at 0.9 knots
270°T at 1.8 knots
090°T at 0.9 knots
questions.why: Read the HW−2 line at the neap rate; the direction is where the stream goes.

questions.q: You want to cross the channel along the track shown. What course do you steer?

figure.note: Same stream for the whole crossing

options: About 080°T
About 070°T
About 110°T
questions.why: Aim up-tide about 20°: 2 kn ÷ 6 kn × 60 (1-in-60), so 090 − 20.

questions.q: Steering exactly the planned heading, you see the cross-track error grow as shown. What do you do?

figure.title: Chartplotter
lines: XTE 0.3 M, right of the track

options: Steer a few degrees to starboard of the track
Turn 90° to port until XTE is zero
Hold the heading; XTE corrects itself
Steer a few degrees to port to regain the track
questions.why: A steady drift to starboard is a set; aim off to port to counter it.

questions.q: The plotter and the compass show this. What is happening?
options: A stream or leeway is setting you east
The GPS has lost its satellite fix
The compass has 15° of deviation
A stream or leeway is setting you west
questions.why: COG is your track over the ground; it lies to starboard of the heading, so you are set east.

questions.q: Motoring north through a narrow strait, you read these speeds. What is the current doing?
options: About 1.7 kn with you
About 1.7 kn against you
About 9.3 kn against you
About 3.8 kn against you
questions.why: SOG = speed through water ± current: 5.5 − 3.8 = 1.7 kn on the nose.

questions.q: How long will this passage take?

figure.title: Passage up the channel
lines: Foul stream 1.0 kn all the way

options: 2 h 00 min
2 h 45 min
3 h 00 min
2 h 24 min
questions.why: Speed over ground = 5 − 1 = 4 kn; 12 ÷ 4 = 3 h.

questions.q: You check the tidal stream atlas for your route. What do the figures beside the arrow mean?
options: 1.2 kn at springs, 2.4 kn at neaps
Stream turns from 120° to 240°
1.2 kn at HW, 2.4 kn at LW
1.2 kn at neaps, 2.4 kn at springs
questions.why: Atlas rates are in tenths of a knot, neap rate first, then spring rate.

questions.q: Planning a cruise in Greece, where do you most need to work out the tidal stream before you go through?
options: The narrow Evripos strait at Chalkis
The open Aegean between Mykonos and Naxos
Any large bay, such as the Saronic Gulf
Nowhere — the Mediterranean has no tide
questions.why: Med tides are small, but in narrow straits like the Evripos the stream runs at several knots.

questions.q: Full moon was two days ago. What tides do you expect this week?
options: Neaps — smaller range, weaker streams
Springs — bigger range, stronger streams
Neaps — bigger range, stronger streams
Springs — smaller range, weaker streams
questions.why: Spring tides follow new and full moon by a day or two.

questions.q: You must cross a shallow bar near low water. At which low water is there least water over it?
options: There is no difference
Low water at neaps
Low water at springs
Low water between springs and neaps
questions.why: Springs have the biggest range: the highest highs and the lowest lows.

questions.q: Using the rule of twelfths, what is the height of tide now?
questions.why: Range 1.8 m; two hours after LW = 3/12 of it (0.45 m) + 0.4 m LW.

questions.q: What is the earliest time you can cross the bar with the clearance you want?
questions.why: Tide needed 2.0 + 0.5 − 0.6 = 1.9 m: a 1.5 m rise, half the range, 3 h after LW.

questions.q: Heading into a marina in the Venetian lagoon, what do you expect of the water level compared with the tide tables?
options: Lower — the wind blows water out
Higher than predicted — a surge
Exactly as predicted
Lower — low pressure lowers the sea
questions.why: Low pressure and a long scirocco pile water into the northern Adriatic: acqua alta.

questions.q: When is high water at your harbour?
questions.why: Apply the time difference to the standard port: 10:40 − 35 min.

questions.q: You plot GPS positions on this paper chart. What do you do?
options: Move them 0.05' S and 0.07' W
Apply the magnetic variation first
Nothing — every chart uses WGS84
Apply the shift in the note before plotting
questions.why: GPS gives WGS84 positions; on an older-datum chart apply the stated shift.

questions.q: Entering this Cycladic bay, the plotter shows your boat here. What do you do?
options: Navigate by eye, depth and bearings
Reboot the plotter and wait
Steer until the screen shows water
Trust the plotter and turn back out
questions.why: Electronic charts of small Greek bays can be offset; the depth and the view are real.

questions.q: Why do you write the position, log reading and course in the logbook every hour?
options: The coastguard needs an hourly report
To plot a DR if the electronics fail
To calibrate the GPS each hour
The charter company bills by distance
questions.why: Hourly positions let you navigate on from the last known point if the GPS dies.

questions.q: Planning the route on the plotter zoomed out, you see clear water all the way. What do you do before you rely on it?
options: Switch the display to 3D view
Move the route closer to the coast
Zoom in along every leg to check for dangers
Nothing — dangers show at every zoom
questions.why: Plotters hide small rocks and soundings at small zoom levels.

questions.q: You set a GPS waypoint for a night arrival at a small harbour. Where do you put it?
options: Exactly on the harbour entrance
On the end of the breakwater
On the charted position of the light
In safe water off the entrance
questions.why: Waypoints go in clear water; pilot the last part in by eye and by the lights.

questions.q: The plotter shows this bearing to the next waypoint. Ignoring deviation, what magnetic course do you steer?
questions.why: True to magnetic: subtract easterly variation, 200 − 5.

questions.q: Creeping through the marina at half a knot, you see the plotter's COG swing wildly from second to second. Why?
options: The marina's steel pontoons cause deviation
GPS course is unreliable at very low speed
Variation changes inside harbours
The tidal stream keeps changing direction
questions.why: COG comes from successive GPS positions; at walking pace small position errors swamp it.

questions.q: You will enter an unfamiliar harbour at dusk. What do you prepare beforehand?
options: Nothing — the plotter route is enough
Only the harbour's VHF channel
A plan of marks, bearings and turning points
A course straight at the entrance light
questions.why: Write the plan before you arrive: what you will see, bearings to hold, where to turn.

questions.q: What do you do about tonight's anchorage?

figure.title: Planning tonight's stop
lines: winds, swell rolls into the bay'

options: Go anyway with extra chain out
Anchor further in, close to the beach
Go anyway — pilot books are cautious
Choose another one sheltered from the south
questions.why: A pilot-book warning matching the forecast: pick shelter from the forecast wind.

questions.q: You plan a long passage along a rocky coast with few harbours. What must your passage plan include?
options: Ports of refuge along the way
A route as close inshore as possible
Only the waypoints for the autopilot
Only the departure and arrival ports
questions.why: A plan needs bolt-holes in case of weather, breakdown or injury.

questions.q: How do you round this breakwater head to enter the harbour?

figure.note: Harbour plan from the pilot book

options: Close, to save time
Wide, then turn in
Close, on its outer side
Stern-first, for control
questions.why: Breakwater heads often have rubble and shoals off them: round them wide.

questions.q: How do you know when to make the turn in this plan?
options: When the echo sounder falls below 10 m
When the chapel comes abeam to port
When the light bears 090°M by hand-bearing compass
When the plotter shows half a mile to go
questions.why: A planned bearing of an object on the beam is a precise, independent turning cue.

questions.q: The pilot book says to approach the harbour from the south-west. Roughly what heading do you steer on the final approach?
options: About 315°
About 225°
About 135°
About 045°
questions.why: Coming from the south-west means heading north-east, 045°.

questions.q: You lay your plotting instrument along the course line and line its grid up with a meridian. What kind of course do you read?
options: True
Relative to the bow
Magnetic
Compass
questions.why: Meridians run to true north, so the course is true; then apply variation and deviation.

questions.q: You read your course off the inner magnetic ring of the chart's compass rose, which is up to date. What must you still apply?
options: Variation for the area
Deviation for that heading
Nothing — it is ready to steer
Variation, then deviation
questions.why: The inner ring already includes variation; only deviation remains.

questions.q: Your GPS position and the echo sounder disagree like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Cross-check
lines: Chart depth at GPS position: 30 m

options: Trust the GPS — the sounder is wrong
Carry on — 8 m is plenty for you
Slow down, head for deep water, take bearings
Reset the echo sounder offset
questions.why: When GPS and depth disagree, doubt the position and check it another way.

questions.q: Your track passes over this charted wreck. What do you do?

figure.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

options: Pass only at high water
Alter course — every wreck is a danger
Stop and sound the depth by hand
Carry on, but don't anchor near it
questions.why: A wreck with 25 m over it is no danger to a yacht; just keep your anchor off it.

questions.q: How far off the light are you when it comes abeam?

figure.title: Doubling the angle
lines: Speed over ground 6.0 kn, no stream

questions.why: Doubling the angle (45° to 90°): distance off = distance run = 0.5 h × 6 kn.

questions.q: The chart prints 'Local magnetic anomaly' beside the island you are passing. What do you do?
options: Re-swing the compass on arrival
Distrust the compass; cross-check by GPS and marks
Add an extra degree of variation
Nothing — it affects only big ships
questions.why: A local anomaly can throw the compass several degrees off; navigate by other means.

questions.q: Can you motor under this cable?
options: Yes — the mast is only 16.5 m
Yes — at low water you gain enough
No — your air draft is 17.5 m
Yes — mid-span the cable is higher
questions.why: Air draft includes aerials, and the safe clearance must exceed it with room to spare.

questions.q: Sailing to windward, how do you estimate your leeway?
options: Log speed compared with GPS speed
From the deviation card
Compass heading compared with variation
Angle between the wake and the centreline
questions.why: Leeway is the angle between heading and water track, shown by the wake.

questions.q: The marina's website says the next bay is 9 km away. How far is that in nautical miles?
options: About 4.9 M
About 9.0 M
About 16.7 M
About 5.6 M
questions.why: One nautical mile = 1.852 km: 9 ÷ 1.852 ≈ 4.9.

questions.q: How far off the intended track will you be at the end of the run?
options: About 3 M
About 1 M
About 0.15 M
About 6 M
questions.why: 1-in-60 rule: 3° off over 60 M = 3 M off, so over 20 M = 1 M.

questions.q: Leaving the marina at Kalamata for the open sea, you have this buoy ahead. On which side do you leave it?

figure.note: You are heading out to sea

options: On your starboard side
Either side, it is a safe water mark
On your port side
On whichever side is deeper
questions.why: Region A: a green cone marks the starboard side going in, so it stays on your port side going out.

questions.q: You are returning to Road Town, Tortola (BVI), from sea. This buoy is ahead. Which side do you leave it?

figure.note: IALA region B · returning from sea

options: On your port side
Pass close north of it
Either side, it marks a danger
On your starboard side
questions.why: Region B (the Americas): red, conical, kept to starboard returning — "red right returning".

questions.q: Entering English Harbour, Antigua, from the sea, you see this buoy. What is it?

figure.note: IALA region B · entering from sea

options: A port-hand mark: leave it to port
A wreck mark: keep well clear
A starboard-hand mark: leave it to starboard
A special mark: check the chart
questions.why: Region B: green and can-shaped marks the port side when entering.

questions.q: Entering Kos harbour at night, you see this light ahead, low on the water. On which side do you leave it?
options: Steer for it, it marks mid-channel
On your starboard side
Either side, keeping 50 m off
On your port side
questions.why: Region A: a green light is a starboard-hand mark; keep it to starboard going in.

questions.q: Near the entrance to Fethiye at night, you see this light low on the water. What is it?

figure.note: Night · light low on the water

options: An isolated danger mark
A yacht at anchor
A port-hand lateral mark
A preferred-channel mark
questions.why: A red light of any rhythm except Fl(2+1) is a port-hand mark; isolated danger is white Fl(2).

questions.q: At dusk you cannot make out colours. Coming in from sea, the buoy ahead is conical with a cone-shaped topmark. On which side do you leave it?
options: On your port side
On the side away from the shore
Either side
On your starboard side
questions.why: Shape gives the side without colour: a cone is a starboard-hand mark, in region A and B alike.

questions.q: You are sailing south through a channel between two islands, with no harbour at either end. How do you know which lateral marks are "port-hand"?
options: From the direction-of-buoyage arrow on the chart
From the direction you happen to sail
Port marks are always on the west side
Port is the side nearer the mainland
questions.why: Lateral marks follow the direction of buoyage: from seaward, or as shown by the arrow on the chart.

questions.q: Coming in from sea, you reach this mark where the channel divides. Where is the main (preferred) channel?

figure.title: Channel fork, entering from sea
lines: Red buoy with one broad green band

options: Straight past it: it is a safe water mark
To starboard: leave the mark to port
To port: leave the mark to starboard
Either way: both are equal
questions.why: Region A: red with a broad green band, Fl(2+1) R, is a modified port mark; the preferred channel is to starboard.

questions.q: Coming in from sea, this light marks a fork in the channel. What does it tell you?

figure.note: Night · channel junction, entering from sea

options: Isolated danger: pass on any side
Special mark: check the chart
Preferred channel to port: leave it to starboard
Preferred channel to starboard: leave it to port
questions.why: Region A: Fl(2+1) G is a modified starboard-hand mark, so the main channel is to port.

questions.q: Your next charter is in the Philippines. Entering a harbour from sea, what colour are the lateral marks you keep on your starboard side?
options: Yellow
Black and yellow
Green
Red
questions.why: The Philippines, like the Americas, Japan and Korea, use IALA region B: red to starboard returning.

questions.q: Entering harbour at night, you have this light fine on your starboard bow. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · entering from sea · light fine to starboard

options: Alter to starboard and leave it to port
Hold on and leave it to starboard
Steer straight for it
Alter to port and pass close to it
questions.why: Region A: a red light is a port-hand mark, so going in it must pass down your port side.

questions.q: On the way into a marina at night, you see this light. What is it?
options: A safe water mark
A starboard-hand lateral mark
A north cardinal mark
A special mark
questions.why: Quick flashing is not only for cardinals: the colour decides, and green is starboard-hand in region A.

questions.q: Sailing along the coast of Lefkada, you see this mark. On which side of it is the safe water?
options: Any side, the danger is right under it
West of it
East of it
North of it
questions.why: East cardinal: black–yellow–black, cones base to base; pass to the east.

questions.q: This mark stands off a reef near Hvar. Where do you pass it?
options: Close on either side
To the east of it
To the south of it
To the west of it
questions.why: West cardinal: yellow–black–yellow, cones point to point; safe water to the west.

questions.q: At night you see this light low on the water ahead. Which side of it is safe?

figure.note: Night · light low on the water

options: The east side
The south side
The west side
Any side
questions.why: Three quick flashes = 3 o'clock = east cardinal.

questions.q: Your track north runs close past this mark. How do you get by it safely?
options: Alter to starboard and pass east of it
Alter to port and leave it to starboard
Pass close on either side
Hold course and leave it to port
questions.why: West cardinal: safe water to the west, danger to the east, which is where your track goes.

questions.q: Approaching the Kornati islands at night, you see this light marking a shoal. Where do you pass it?

figure.note: Night · continuous, about two flashes a second

options: Either side
To the east
To the north
To the south
questions.why: Uninterrupted quick or very quick flashing: north cardinal.

questions.q: At dusk you can only see a dark silhouette on the buoy: two cones, one above the other, base to base. What mark is it?
options: An isolated danger mark
A north cardinal
A west cardinal
An east cardinal
questions.why: Base to base looks like an egg: E. Point to point: W. Both up: N. Both down: S.

questions.q: Counting the quick flashes of a white light, you are not sure whether there were six or nine. What tells you it is a south cardinal?
options: A long flash follows the quick ones
The flashes are red
There is no pause between groups
The pause after the group is shorter
questions.why: South cardinal: Q(6) + LFl; the long flash stops it being mistaken for a west (Q(9)).

questions.q: Bound west along the coast, which way do you take this mark?
options: Alter to port and pass close south of it
Alter to starboard and leave it to port
Hold course and leave it to starboard
Pass close on either side
questions.why: North cardinal: safe water to the north; the danger lies south of it, on your track.

questions.q: Sailing in the Bahamas (IALA region B), you see this mark. What does it mean there?
options: Pass to the north
Pass to the west, colours are reversed in B
Pass to the east, as in region A
It is a starboard-hand mark in B
questions.why: Only lateral marks differ between regions A and B; cardinals are the same worldwide.

questions.q: You want to continue east. Can you pass between these two marks?

figure.note: Depths in metres · you are heading east

options: Yes: the gap between them is the channel
No: go west of both marks
Yes, but only at slow speed
No: go north of the N mark or south of the S mark
questions.why: Cardinals are named for where the safe water is, so the shoal lies between them.

questions.q: Rounding a headland in the Gulf of Corinth, you see this mark off the point. Where is the danger?
options: North of the mark
Right under the mark
East of the mark
South of the mark
questions.why: South cardinal: safe water to the south, so the danger lies to the north of it.

questions.q: You time this light on a buoy off Paros. Where do you pass it?

figure.note: Night · 9 quick flashes, then dark, every 15 s

options: To the south
To the west
To the north
To the east
questions.why: Nine quick flashes = 9 o'clock = west cardinal.

questions.q: The topmark of this buoy has been knocked off. It is painted yellow above black. Which mark is it?
options: A west cardinal: pass west
A north cardinal: pass north
A south cardinal: pass south
An isolated danger: any side
questions.why: Cones point to the black: black at the bottom means both points down, south.

questions.q: At night this light marks a rock in the middle of a bay. What is it?

figure.note: Night · light on a beacon in the bay

options: A south cardinal: pass south of it
A safe water mark: steer for it
A port-hand mark: leave it to port
An isolated danger mark: pass well clear, any side
questions.why: White Fl(2): isolated danger, with navigable water all round.

questions.q: Making landfall at night, you see this light ahead, low on the water, alone in open sea. What is it?
options: A safe water mark
A north cardinal mark
A special mark
An isolated danger mark
questions.why: White Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A): safe water — landfall or mid-channel.

questions.q: At dusk you see a pillar buoy with a single ball as its topmark. What kind of mark is it?
options: A port-hand mark
A safe water mark
A special mark
An isolated danger mark
questions.why: One red ball: safe water. Two black balls: isolated danger.

questions.q: Anchoring off a beach in Zakynthos, you see a line of these buoys between you and the shore. What do they usually mark?

figure.note: Small buoys in a line parallel to the beach

options: The edge of a dredged channel
A channel for yachts to the beach
The edge of a swimming area: stay outside
Moorings you may pick up
questions.why: Yellow special marks along beaches usually mark the bathing zone; check the chart or local rules.

questions.q: Entering a quiet bay in the Gulf of Corinth at night, you see several of these lights in a rough square. What are they most likely marking?

figure.note: Night · four lights, low on the water

options: Yachts at anchor
An isolated danger
A safe channel: steer between them
A fish farm: keep outside them
questions.why: Yellow lights are special marks; in Greek and Turkish bays they often mark fish farms.

questions.q: Off Piraeus you see this new buoy, which is not on your chart. What does it mark?
options: A recent wreck, not yet charted
A ferry waiting position
A traffic separation lane
A diving area
questions.why: Blue and yellow stripes: an emergency wreck-marking buoy over a new, uncharted wreck.

questions.q: At night you see this light, low on the water, where your chart shows nothing. What is it?

figure.note: Night · one light: blue, then yellow, then blue…

options: A hovercraft
An emergency wreck-marking buoy
A special mark on a fish farm
A police patrol boat
questions.why: Alternating blue and yellow flashes: emergency wreck-marking buoy; treat it as a new danger.

questions.q: You see two of these marks close together where your up-to-date chart shows clear water. What does it mean?

figure.note: Two of these, side by side; chart shows clear water

options: The channel runs between them
One of them has dragged: ignore it
A newly found danger, marked with a duplicate
A practice area for buoy tenders
questions.why: IALA: a serious new danger may be marked by duplicating one of the marks until it is charted.

questions.q: The chart shows this light on the cape. What will you see at night?
options: Five flashes, then a pause
Light on 5 s, then off 5 s
One flash lasting 5 seconds
One flash every 5 seconds
questions.why: Fl 5s: a single flash, repeated every 5 s (the period).

questions.q: You are trying to pick out this harbour light among the lights of the town. What pattern do you look for?
options: Mostly on, with two short eclipses every 8 s
Equal light and dark, twice every 8 s
Two long flashes, each lasting 8 s
Mostly dark, with two short flashes every 8 s
questions.why: Oc: light longer than dark; Oc(2) 8s puts two eclipses in each 8-second period.

questions.q: Which chart abbreviation matches the harbour light your crew is timing?

figure.note: Night · 3 s on, 3 s off, repeating

options: LFl 6s
Iso 6s
Fl 3s
Oc 3s
questions.why: Iso = equal light and dark; the period is the whole cycle, 3 + 3 = 6 s.

questions.q: What does the "23m" in this light's description on the chart tell you?
options: The width of the red sector
The height of the tower from its base
The height of the light above sea level
The least depth off the cape
questions.why: Elevation: the height of the light itself above sea level (above MHWS on tidal charts).

questions.q: Planning a night landfall, you read this light on the chart. What is meant by 18/15M?
options: The distance to the next light
The width of its white and red sectors
It is seen only from 15 to 18 miles
The nominal range of its white and red light
questions.why: Nominal range in 10 M visibility: 18 M for the white, 15 M for the weaker red.

questions.q: You time the light you can see. Which lighthouse is it?

labels: 3 flashes, then dark · 15 s per cycle

options: B
You cannot tell without its colour
C
A
questions.why: Fl(3) 15s: a group of three flashes, then dark, the whole cycle taking 15 s.

questions.q: Approaching at night, the light ahead behaves as described. Which charted light is it?

labels: Steady light, briefly dark every 10 s

options: A
B
Any of the three
C
questions.why: Occulting: the light is on longer than it is off; Fl is mostly dark, Iso is half and half.

questions.q: The light shows green. What do you do?

figure.title: Light ahead: Fl WRG 4s
lines: White sector: the safe channel in
Red sector: rocks to the north
Green sector: shoal to the south
You are heading east, towards it

options: Hold course: green means safe water
Alter to starboard until it shows white
Alter to port until it shows white
Stop and wait until it shows red
questions.why: Sectored light: you are in the green sector south of the white channel; north is to port.

questions.q: You take a bearing of the light and correct it to true. Which colour do you see?

figure.title: Chart: Fl WR 5s on the point

options: Nothing: you are in an obscured arc
Red and white alternately
White
Red
questions.why: Sector limits are true bearings of the light as seen from seaward; 120° lies inside 095°–140°.

questions.q: You are coming in on these leading lights and they look like this. Which way do you steer to get back on the line?

figure.note: Night · leading lights into the harbour

options: To port
Steer straight at the rear light
Hold course: near enough
To starboard
questions.why: Move towards the side the front (lower) light has moved to: front left of rear, so go left.

questions.q: Approaching a Greek harbour at night, you see these two lights on the breakwater ends. What do you do?
options: Keep both lights on your starboard side
Enter between them, green to starboard
Keep both lights on your port side
Wait outside: red means the port is closed
questions.why: Region A: red marks the port side and green the starboard side of the entrance.

questions.q: At what distance off do you first see the light itself, not just its loom?

figure.title: Making landfall at night
lines: Your eye: 4 m above the sea

options: About 30 M
22 M, its nominal range
About 19 M
About 12 M
questions.why: Geographical range ≈ 2.08 × (√49 + √4) ≈ 18.7 M, less than the 22 M nominal range.

questions.q: What are you seeing?

figure.title: Night passage, 25 M offshore
lines: A pale glow sweeps the sky over the horizon

options: A light buoy in a swell
A distant ship's searchlight
Lightning far away
The loom of a lighthouse below the horizon
questions.why: The beam lights the sky before the light itself rises above the horizon.

questions.q: You see this light change colour as you hold your course. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing about your position: it alternates
A vessel is passing in front of it
You have entered its red sector
The light is faulty
questions.why: Al WR: the light alternates white and red wherever you are; a sector light changes only with your bearing.

questions.q: What colour is this light on the end of the mole?
options: Green
White
Yellow
Red
questions.why: No colour letter in the chart description means a white light.

questions.q: How is this light written on the chart?

figure.note: Night · 2 flashes, then dark; start to start 10 s

options: Fl(2) 5s
questions.why: Group flashing, two flashes; the period runs from the start of one group to the start of the next.

questions.q: Your crew says you should see the light by now. Should you?

figure.title: Night, hazy
lines: Lighthouse ahead: Fl 5s, nominal range 15 M

options: Yes: it is well within 15 M
No: lights are never seen beyond 5 M
Yes: nominal range already allows for haze
Probably not: in haze its range is far less
questions.why: Nominal range assumes 10 M visibility; in 3 M visibility the luminous range is much shorter.

questions.q: Sailing along the coast at night, the lighthouse you are watching changes colour. What has happened?

figure.note: Night · white for the last hour, now red

options: You have crossed into its red sector
A ship has passed in front of it
You are too close to see the white
The lighthouse has a fault
questions.why: Sectored light: the colour depends on your bearing; red sectors usually cover a danger.

questions.q: What do you do?

figure.title: Directional light ahead: Dir WRG
lines: red sector to the left of the white,

options: Stop: red means the port is closed
Alter to starboard until it shows white
Alter to port until it shows white
Hold course: red is the safe side
questions.why: You are in the red sector, which lies to port of the approach line; come back to starboard.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see these lights ahead. What are you looking at?
options: A vessel at anchor
A sailing vessel heading towards you
A power-driven vessel heading towards you
A power-driven vessel heading away
questions.why: A masthead light over both sidelights: power-driven, bow on.

questions.q: What is this vessel, and which side of her are you seeing?
options: Power-driven; her starboard side
Sailing; her port side
At anchor; her stern
Power-driven; her port side
questions.why: A white masthead light with a red sidelight: power-driven, port side towards you.

questions.q: What do these lights tell you?
options: A large power vessel showing her starboard side
A large power vessel showing her port side
A vessel towing, seen from ahead
Two small vessels in company
questions.why: Two masthead lights, the aft one higher, and a green sidelight: big ship, starboard side on.

questions.q: This light is moving slowly from left to right across your bow. What is it?

figure.note: Night · steady light, no white above it

options: A power vessel showing her starboard side
A sailing vessel showing her starboard side
A starboard-hand buoy
A sailing vessel showing her port side
questions.why: A sidelight with no masthead light above it: a vessel under sail.

questions.q: Close inshore at night, you see only this light, moving slowly from right to left. What is it?

figure.note: Night · single steady red light, high up

options: A port-hand mark
A power vessel, port side on
A yacht under sail with a tricolour
A vessel not under command
questions.why: A red sector high at the masthead: the tricolour of a sailing vessel under 20 m, port side on.

questions.q: These lights are coming towards you. What is it?

figure.note: Night · high up, close together, no white light

options: A power vessel, bow on
A yacht under sail, seen from astern
A vessel at anchor
A yacht under sail, bow on
questions.why: Green and red together at the masthead with no white: a tricolour seen from ahead.

questions.q: Through binoculars you see a yacht with her sails set, showing these lights. What is she under the rules?
options: A power-driven vessel
A vessel not under command
A sailing vessel
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
questions.why: A steaming light means the engine is running: motor-sailing counts as power-driven.

questions.q: In the anchorage off Piraeus you see these lights. What is the ship doing, and which way does she lie?

figure.note: Night · deck lights on, no sidelights

options: At anchor, bow to the right
At anchor, bow to the left
Under way, bow to the right
Aground, bow to the left
questions.why: Rule 30: the forward anchor light is the higher one; under way, the forward masthead light is the lower.

questions.q: Off a reef in the Dodecanese you see these lights. What do they tell you?
options: A vessel not under command, under way
A fishing vessel at anchor
A vessel aground
A pilot vessel at anchor
questions.why: Two all-round reds plus anchor lights: a vessel aground.

questions.q: What is this vessel?
options: Aground
Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Constrained by her draught
Not under command, making way
questions.why: Two all-round reds with sidelights and no masthead light: NUC, moving through the water.

questions.q: In open water you see only these lights. What is the vessel doing?
options: Not under command, stopped in the water
Aground on a shoal
Not under command, making way
Lying at anchor
questions.why: NUC shows sidelights only when making way; aground she would add anchor lights.

questions.q: Crossing the Saronic Gulf at night, you see these lights. What is the vessel?
options: Constrained by her draught
Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, under way
A pilot vessel on duty
Not under command, under way
questions.why: Red-white-red all-round plus masthead light and sidelights: RAM, making way.

questions.q: These lights belong to a ship off Rhodes. What is her status?
options: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre, under way
Not under command, stopped
Restricted in ability to manoeuvre, at anchor
Aground
questions.why: Red-white-red with an anchor light and no sidelights: RAM at anchor.

questions.q: A dredger is working in the channel into Lefkas. On which side can you pass her?
options: On the side with the two red lights
Either side, keeping well clear
Neither: wait until she moves
On the side with the two green lights
questions.why: Rule 27(d): two reds mark the obstructed side, two greens the side where you may pass.

questions.q: About a mile off you see these lights and no others. What is the vessel?
options: A trawler, not making way
A trawler making way towards you
A pilot vessel on duty
A vessel fishing with nets, stopped
questions.why: Green over white = trawling; no sidelights means she is not making way.

questions.q: Off Kalymnos at night, a boat shows these lights. What is she?
options: Not under command, making way
Fishing (not trawling), making way
A pilot vessel under way
Trawling, making way
questions.why: Red over white: fishing other than trawling; the sidelight shows she is making way.

questions.q: This fishing boat off Sifnos is not making way. Where is her gear?
options: Under her: she is trawling
Nowhere: that is her anchor light
Out towards the lower white light
On the side away from the lower light
questions.why: Rule 26(c): gear out more than 150 m is shown by an all-round white light towards it.

questions.q: Coming up astern of a vessel at night, you see these lights. What is she doing?
options: Fishing
Lying at anchor
Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Towing
questions.why: A yellow towing light above the sternlight: a vessel towing.

questions.q: What do these lights tell you about the vessel and what is behind her?
options: She is towing, and the tow is over 200 m
She is towing, and the tow is under 200 m
She is constrained by her draught
She is a large ship of over 50 m
questions.why: Three masthead lights in a vertical line: towing, with a tow longer than 200 m.

questions.q: The tug on the left shows a tow of over 200 m. What must you assume the lone red light on the right is?

figure.note: Night · the right-hand light is about 400 m astern of the tug

options: A port-hand buoy: leave it to port
The tow: do not cross between them
A yacht: the gap is safe to cross
A second tug: pass astern of it
questions.why: A towed vessel shows only sidelights and sternlight; the tow line lies between it and the tug.

questions.q: A boat is heading for a ship waiting outside the port of Piraeus. These are its lights. What is it?
options: A vessel fishing, under way
A vessel not under command
A pilot vessel on duty, under way
A vessel towing
questions.why: White over red: pilot on duty ("white hat, red nose"); the sidelight shows she is under way.

questions.q: A loaded tanker is approaching Agioi Theodoroi at night with these lights. What is she showing?
options: Not under command
Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Aground
Constrained by her draught
questions.why: Three all-round reds in a vertical line, plus power-driven lights: constrained by draught.

questions.q: A naval vessel shows these lights. How close may you approach?
options: No closer than 1000 m
No closer than 100 m
No closer than 500 m
As close as you like astern of her
questions.why: Three all-round greens: mine clearance; it is dangerous to come within 1000 m.

questions.q: Far out at sea you first see the white light alone; about ten minutes later the red appears below it. What was the white light?
options: An anchor light, then a second vessel
The masthead light of a power vessel
A sternlight that became a sidelight
A lighthouse behind a yacht
questions.why: Masthead lights carry 5–6 M, sidelights only 2–3 M, so the masthead light shows first.

questions.q: A minute ago this vessel showed both sidelights. What has she just done?
options: Stopped in the water
Altered course to her starboard
Altered course to her port
Turned to come straight at you
questions.why: Bow on she showed red and green; now only green, so her bow has swung to her port (your right).

questions.q: Which navigation lights may you show?
options: Steaming light, sidelights and sternlight
One all-round white light only
Tricolour plus steaming light
Sidelights and sternlight, or a tricolour
questions.why: Rule 25: a sailing vessel under 20 m may combine sidelights and sternlight in a masthead tricolour.

questions.q: Which lights do you switch on?
options: Steaming light, sidelights and sternlight
Tricolour and sternlight
Tricolour only
Anchor light and sidelights
questions.why: Rule 23: under engine you are a power-driven vessel.

questions.q: Anchored here for the night, what light must you show?

figure.title: Overnight at anchor
lines: Bay on Kefalonia, other boats around

options: Your tricolour
One all-round white light where best seen
Sidelights and sternlight
Two all-round red lights
questions.why: Rule 30: at anchor, under 50 m, one all-round white light.

questions.q: Which lights should you have on?
options: None: it is daytime
Tricolour only
Steaming light, sidelights and sternlight
Tricolour and steaming light
questions.why: Rule 20: lights in restricted visibility too; with the engine in gear you show power-driven lights.

questions.q: What is the least light you must show?

figure.title: Back from the taverna
lines: Dark, boats moving in the bay

options: None: no light is needed in a bay
A torch, only if a boat comes near
Red and green sidelights only
An all-round white light
questions.why: Rule 23(d): power-driven, under 7 m and 7 kn max: an all-round white (sidelights if practicable).

questions.q: What light do you need?

figure.title: Rowing ashore at night
lines: Two yachts motoring in the anchorage

options: A white torch, ready to show in time
Red and green sidelights
None: rowing boats are exempt
An all-round red light
questions.why: Rule 25(d): under oars, a white torch or lantern shown in time to prevent collision.

questions.q: Is that allowed?

figure.title: Under sail at night
lines: Crew wants to add the all-round

options: Yes: it shows clearly you are sailing
No: red over green is not used with a tricolour
Yes, but only offshore
No: red over green is for fishing vessels
questions.why: Rule 25(c): the optional red-over-green goes only with separate sidelights and sternlight.

questions.q: Drifting like this in the dark, what lights do you display?

figure.title: Dismasted, engine fouled
lines: Not making way through the water

options: Your tricolour
An all-round white anchor light
Two all-round red lights, one above the other
Two all-round reds plus sidelights and sternlight
questions.why: Rule 27(a): NUC shows two all-round reds; sidelights and sternlight only when making way.

questions.q: Stuck on the sand until morning, what do you show at night?

figure.title: Aground at night
lines: Waiting for a tow at first light

options: Sidelights and sternlight
Tricolour and anchor light
Two all-round red lights only
Anchor light plus two all-round red lights
questions.why: Rule 30(d): aground = anchor light(s) plus two all-round reds (not required under 12 m).

questions.q: At night, which of your lights can this ship see?
options: Only your sternlight
Your green sidelight and sternlight
Your red and green sidelights
Only your green sidelight
questions.why: The sternlight covers 135° astern; sidelights stop 22.5° abaft the beam.

questions.q: Waiting like this until dawn, which lights must you show?
options: Two all-round red lights
Sail lights: tricolour, or sidelights and sternlight
No lights while you are stopped
An all-round white anchor light
questions.why: Hove-to you are still under way under sail, not anchored or disabled.

questions.q: Should your navigation lights be on?

figure.title: August, Saronic Gulf
lines: Now 20:30, still light enough to see

options: No: only once it is fully dark
No: only in poor visibility
Yes: they are required from sunset
Only if another vessel is near
questions.why: Rule 20: lights from sunset to sunrise, whatever the twilight.

questions.q: Your tricolour has gone out. What do you use instead?
options: The anchor light
The steaming light
Steaming light and sidelights
Deck-level sidelights and sternlight
questions.why: Rule 25: the tricolour and the deck-level sidelights and sternlight are alternatives under sail.

questions.q: You read the wind instruments before leaving the anchorage. What force is the mean wind?

figure.title: Wind instruments
lines: True wind 25 kn, steady for an hour

options: Force 6
Force 7
Force 5
Force 4
questions.why: F6 is 22–27 kn; the force is named from the mean wind, not the gusts.

questions.q: You look out from the harbour wall before deciding whether to go. Roughly what wind is blowing outside?

figure.title: Outside the breakwater
lines: is blown in streaks along the wind

options: F4, 11–16 knots
F7, 28–33 knots
F10, 48–55 knots
F5, 17–21 knots
questions.why: Sea heaping up with foam blown in streaks along the wind is the Beaufort picture of F7.

questions.q: You see this sea from the cockpit before leaving. How do you set the sails of your 40-ft charter yacht?
options: F2 — too light, motor instead
F8 — stay in harbour
F4 — full sail, a good breeze
F6 — two reefs before leaving
questions.why: Small waves with fairly frequent white horses is F4, 11–16 kn: full sail on a 40-footer.

questions.q: You are close-hauled under full main and genoa. The boat heels hard and fights the helm. What do you do?

figure.note: True wind rising 16 → 20 kn, weather helm

options: Wait for force 7, then reef
Sheet the main in harder to cut the heeling
Luff up and hold her there for an hour
Reef now, before the wind builds further
questions.why: Reef early — the first time you think of it, and well before F6 on a charter yacht.

questions.q: You have been running pleasantly under full sail for two hours. Now you must turn and beat back to harbour. What do you expect?

figure.note: Running · apparent wind 13 kn, sea easy

options: Much more wind and spray — reef first
Less wind, as you will be sailing slower
A lighter wind — shake out any reef
The same wind, just from ahead
questions.why: Downwind your boat speed is subtracted from the true wind; upwind it is added.

questions.q: You log the wind every hour. What is the true wind now, and what force do you write in the log?
options: About 7 kn — F3
About 21 kn — F5
About 28 kn — F7
About 14 kn — F4
questions.why: Dead downwind, true wind = apparent wind + boat speed: 14 + 7 = 21 kn, top of F5.

questions.q: You plan a day sail with a family crew. What do you set the boat up for?
options: The lulls — shake out reefs in them
The sea state only — the wind is fine
The gusts — reef to handle 30 kn
The mean wind — full sail for F5
questions.why: Gusts are what overpower the boat: reef for the gusts, not the mean wind.

questions.q: The mean wind is 20 knots in open water. Under the high island ahead, gusts typically run 50 % above the mean. What do you prepare for?
options: About 10 kn — the island shelters you
About 40 kn — double the mean wind
About 20 kn — the same as outside
Gusts of about 30 kn — F7 strength
questions.why: Gust factor: 20 kn × 1.5 = 30 kn, so reef for F7 gusts, not the F5 mean.

questions.q: You are in Paros, planning to cross to Naxos tomorrow. What wind does this warning forecast?
options: 34–40 kn, locally 41–47 kn
22–27 kn, locally 28–33 kn
28–33 kn, locally 34–40 kn
48–55 kn, locally 56–63 kn
questions.why: F8 is 34–40 kn and F9 41–47 kn — a gale: stay in harbour.

questions.q: You set full sail at 10 knots of wind this morning. By noon it blows 20 knots. How has the load on sails and rig changed?
options: About twice as much
About four times as much
About the same
About eight times as much
questions.why: Wind pressure rises with the square of the wind speed: double the wind, four times the force.

questions.q: Sailing close-hauled across the Gulf of Corinth, you see a dark ruffled patch on the water racing towards you from windward. What do you do?
options: Nothing — it is only a current line
Ease the sheets now — it is a calm patch ahead
Be ready to ease the main as the gust hits
Alter course away — it is a shoal patch
questions.why: Dark, ruffled water moving towards you from windward is a gust arriving.

questions.q: Your weather app shows the wind for this afternoon. Roughly how many knots is that?
options: About 5 knots
About 10 knots
About 36 knots
About 20 knots
questions.why: 1 m/s ≈ 2 kn, so 10 m/s ≈ 19–20 kn (F5); 36 is the km/h figure.

questions.q: This morning the wind blew from the south. Now it blows from the west. How do you describe the change?
options: It has veered — turned clockwise
It has backed — turned clockwise
It has veered — turned anticlockwise
It has backed — turned anticlockwise
questions.why: Veering = clockwise shift (S → W); backing = anticlockwise.

questions.q: You stand with your back to this wind. Where is the centre of low pressure?
options: To the north-east
To the south-east
To the south-west
To the north-west
questions.why: Buys Ballot, northern hemisphere: back to the wind, the low is on your left.

questions.q: From which direction does the wind blow where you are?

figure.note: You are east of the high

options: From the west
From the south
From the north
From the east
questions.why: Northern hemisphere: wind blows clockwise round a high, so on its east side it comes from the north.

questions.q: Which way is the wind blowing at your position on this chart?

figure.note: You are SW of the low

options: From the north-east
From the south-west
From the south-east
From the north-west
questions.why: Wind circulates anticlockwise round a low in the northern hemisphere, angled slightly inwards.

questions.q: You are south of the track of this depression. How will the wind change during the night?

figure.title: Forecast
lines: Depression moving east across the Ionian
Centre passing north of you tonight

options: Veer from south-west to north-west
Back from south-west to south-east
Stay south-west, only weaker
Back from north-west to south-west
questions.why: With a low passing to your north, the wind veers (clockwise) as it goes by.

questions.q: The depression centre will pass to the south of you, moving east. How will the wind shift as it goes by?

figure.title: Forecast
lines: Centre to pass 60 M south of you

options: Veer from south-east to south-west
Back from south-east through east to north-east
Stay south-east and die away
Veer from south-west through west to north-west
questions.why: Low passing south of you: the wind backs (anticlockwise) — the mirror of a low passing north.

questions.q: This high is forecast to sit over the Ionian for three days. What weather do you plan for?
options: A strong, steady northerly gale
Gales and heavy rain for most of the week
Light winds, sea breezes and sun
Fog that lasts all day long
questions.why: Widely spaced isobars round a high: light winds and settled weather with local breezes.

questions.q: You read this forecast before a passage. What does it tell you to expect?
options: An anticlockwise shift to west, F5, within 6 h
A shift to east, F5, in 6 to 12 h
Wind staying south, gusting F5, from noon
A clockwise shift to west, F5, after 12 h
questions.why: Veering = clockwise; "later" = more than 12 hours from the time of issue.

questions.q: You use this chart to estimate the wind at sea near the low. How does the surface wind blow relative to the isobars?
options: Nearly along them, angled in towards the low
Straight across them into the low
Straight out from the low centre
Nearly along them, angled outwards from the low
questions.why: Friction turns the surface wind 10–15° across the isobars towards low pressure at sea.

questions.q: You have watched the weather for six hours. What has just happened?
options: A high has moved over you — settled weather
A warm front has passed — warm sector now
A sea breeze has set in — it will die tonight
A cold front has passed — clearing is coming
questions.why: Warm front passing: wind veers, rain eases to drizzle, temperature rises, glass steadies.

questions.q: You are in the warm sector. What do you prepare for when this arrives?

figure.title: Looking west
lines: A line of towering dark cloud

options: Hours of light drizzle and thick fog
A steady rise in temperature and humidity
A sharp veer to NW, squalls, heavy rain
A slow back to the south, then calm
questions.why: A cold front brings a sharp veer, squalls and heavy but short rain.

questions.q: A front passed two hours ago. What do you expect for the rest of the day?
options: The wind backing south again soon
A calm, warm and humid afternoon
Rain and fog for many hours to come
Gusty NW wind, showers, clear air
questions.why: Behind a cold front the air is cooler, gusty and showery, with excellent visibility.

questions.q: This message is on the Navtex this evening. What sequence of weather do you expect overnight?
options: Thick cloud, rain, a veer, then clearing
Clear skies all night, wind steady
A sudden squall without any cloud warning
Two days of thick fog, then a gale
questions.why: An occluded front brings cloud and rain like a warm front, then a veer and clearing like a cold one.

questions.q: You see these clouds while sailing along the coast. What do they warn you of?

figure.title: Over the island's mountains
lines: They stay fixed over the peaks

options: Settled calm weather for the rest of the day
Strong wind aloft — hard gusts off the high land
A sea breeze is about to start along the coast
Fog will form by the evening
questions.why: Lens-shaped clouds parked over peaks show a strong airflow over the mountains: expect fall gusts in their lee.

questions.q: Morning in the Ionian: small white puffy clouds with flat bases form over the land and vanish in the evening. The barometer is steady. What does it mean?
options: Thunderstorms building by midday
A front arriving within the next few hours
Settled weather, sea breeze by day
A gale coming in tonight
questions.why: Small fair-weather cumulus over land with a steady glass means settled weather.

questions.q: A front passed at 14:00. What do you expect for the evening?
options: A gradual return of the rain
Fog forming in the harbour
A calm and settled night ahead
Strong gusty wind for a while
questions.why: A rapid rise brings strong wind just as a rapid fall does.

questions.q: This is the only reading you have. What does it tell you about the day ahead?

figure.title: Barometer
lines: No earlier readings in the log

options: Little on its own — trend matters
A gale is on its way tonight
Settled high pressure for the next few days
Fog is likely this morning
questions.why: The change over 3 hours matters far more than any single value.

questions.q: The forecast also says settled. What does your barometer log tell you?
options: A depression is close by
No change on the way
Strong wind by morning
A front is due tonight
questions.why: A steady glass over a day supports a settled forecast.

questions.q: You are in a sheltered harbour at 08:00 with 20 miles of open water to the next one. What do you do?

lines: Barometer −7 hPa in the last 3 h
Next harbour 20 M across open water

options: Leave with two reefs already tied in
Leave now to arrive before it hits
Stay in harbour and prepare the boat
Anchor off the beach outside the harbour
questions.why: A gale within 6 hours and a fast-falling glass: stay in shelter and secure the boat.

questions.q: By when should you expect the gale to arrive?
options: In 24 to 48 hours
After 12 hours
In 6 to 12 hours
Within 6 hours
questions.why: Imminent < 6 h, soon 6–12 h, later > 12 h from the time of issue.

questions.q: Between what times do you expect force 7?
options: Between 14:00 and 20:00
After 20:00
Not until tomorrow afternoon
Before 14:00
questions.why: "Soon" means 6 to 12 hours from the time of issue.

questions.q: You plan to leave at 06:00 tomorrow for a five-hour passage. How does this forecast affect you?
options: F6 is not due for two days
F6 may arrive at any time on passage
F6 will have passed before you leave
F6 comes this evening, then eases
questions.why: "Later" means more than 12 hours after issue — 06:00 tomorrow onward, right in your passage.

questions.q: The forecast says visibility moderate. Can you expect to see a headland 4 miles away?
options: No — moderate is under 1000 m
Yes — moderate is over 10 miles
Probably — moderate is 2 to 5 miles
No — moderate is 1000 m to 2 miles
questions.why: Visibility: good > 5 M, moderate 2–5 M, poor 1000 m–2 M, fog < 1000 m.

questions.q: The forecast for the northern Adriatic tomorrow morning gives visibility "fog". How far will you see?
options: 2 to 5 miles
1000 metres to 2 miles
More than 5 miles
Less than 1000 metres
questions.why: In a forecast, fog means visibility under 1000 m.

questions.q: What wave height should you expect?
options: About 2.5 to 4 metres
About 6 to 9 metres
About 1.25 to 2.5 metres
About 0.5 to 1.25 metres
questions.why: Sea state: slight 0.5–1.25 m, moderate 1.25–2.5 m, rough 2.5–4 m, very rough 4–6 m.

questions.q: You plan to pass through the Mykonos–Tinos channel this afternoon. What wind do you plan for there?

figure.title: Forecast, Cyclades
lines: N 4 to 5, locally 7 in the channels

options: F7 only after dark
F7 in the channel
F7 only far offshore
F4 to 5 everywhere
questions.why: "Locally" means in parts of the area — channels and capes are where it happens.

questions.q: You read this message at 13:00 Greek summer time (UTC+3). Until when could the gale arrive?
options: Not before 19:00 local
Not before 21:00 local
Any time before 18:00 local
Any time before 15:00 local
questions.why: Navtex times are UTC: 09:00 UTC = 12:00 local; imminent = within 6 h, so by 18:00 local.

questions.q: Your Navtex printout header reads "KB12". What kind of message is it?
options: A search and rescue notice
A routine weather forecast
A navigational warning
A meteorological warning
questions.why: The second letter is the type: A navigational warning, B met warning, D SAR, E forecast.

questions.q: You are chartering out of Split. Which service issues the official sea forecast for the Croatian coast?
options: DHMZ, the Croatian met service
The Turkish State Met Service
Poseidon, the Greek model service
Météo-France
questions.why: DHMZ issues the Adriatic forecast, also read in English by the Croatian coast radio stations.

questions.q: Sailing in the Cyclades, you want a detailed wind and wave forecast made for Greek waters. Which source do you use?
options: DHMZ
Poseidon (HCMR)
A 1° global GRIB file
Météo-France
questions.why: Poseidon runs high-resolution wind and wave models for the Greek seas.

questions.q: You are on passage from the Côte d'Azur to Corsica and hear a "BMS" announced for your area. What is it?
options: A navigational warning for a wreck
A marina berthing notice
A Météo-France strong-wind warning
A routine five-day outlook
questions.why: BMS (bulletin météorologique spécial) is Météo-France's warning of strong wind or gale.

questions.q: Why is the GRIB file so far from what you see?
options: Your wind instruments must be faulty
GRIB files show gusts, not mean wind
The GRIB shows wind at 1000 m altitude
The model smooths out the funnelling
questions.why: Coarse models miss local acceleration, gusts and thunderstorms — add a margin.

questions.q: You must decide tonight whether to cross to the next island tomorrow. Which forecast do you plan on?
options: The official gale warning
Whichever was issued more recently
The GRIB — it is more detailed
An average of the two, about F6
questions.why: Official warnings include forecaster judgement and local effects; a raw GRIB does not.

questions.q: You compare models for Thursday's passage. What does this tell you?
options: ICON is newest — expect exactly 30 kn
Low confidence — plan for the strong case
Average them — expect about 22 kn
ECMWF is always right — expect 15 kn
questions.why: When models disagree, confidence is low: plan for the worst plausible case and re-check.

questions.q: It is Monday. A GRIB file shows a perfect light-wind Saturday for your crossing back to base. How much do you rely on it?
options: Fully, as long as the file is high-resolution
Fully — models are good to 10 days
Little — check again each day as it nears
Not at all — GRIBs are never right
questions.why: Forecast skill falls off with time; five days out is a trend, not a plan.

questions.q: On channel 16 Olympia Radio announces a weather bulletin on a working channel. What do you do?
options: Ignore it — it is for ships only
Stay on 16 — it is read there
Call Olympia on 16 to ask for it
Switch to that channel and listen
questions.why: Coast radio announces on Ch 16, then reads the bulletin on a working channel.

questions.q: The Greek port police have issued a departure ban for yachts because of the wind. Your charter ends at base tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Stay in port and call the charter company
Leave at dawn, before the wind has built up
Leave — the ban is only advice
Leave if the crew all agree in writing
questions.why: A port-police departure ban is binding; the charter base deals with late returns.

questions.q: You want to leave tomorrow morning. Is this forecast enough?
options: Yes — if the sky looks the same
No — get a fresh one before leaving
Yes — forecasts hold for three days
No — only a TV forecast will do
questions.why: Always check the time of issue; use the latest forecast before you go.

questions.q: Cyclades, August. The Meltemi blows F6 most afternoons. When do you make a 15-mile upwind leg?
options: Mid-afternoon, when it is steadiest
Any time — its strength never varies
Early morning, before it builds
Late afternoon, as it peaks
questions.why: The Meltemi is usually lightest early in the day and strongest in the afternoon.

questions.q: You are sailing from Kos to Leros in July. From which direction does the Meltemi usually blow here?
options: From the south-east
From the south-west
From the north-east
From the north-west
questions.why: The Meltemi is NE in the north Aegean, N in the Cyclades and NW in the Dodecanese.

questions.q: Lavrion lies north-west of the islands you want to visit. How do you plan the week?

figure.title: Charter from Lavrion, 7 days
lines: Ideas: Kea, Syros, Tinos, Mykonos, Paros

options: Do the upwind legs first, finish with reaches
Sail every leg in the afternoon breeze
Stay in Lavrion until the Meltemi stops
Run south to Santorini, beat back at the end
questions.why: In Meltemi season, get your windward work done early so the last days are not a long beat home.

questions.q: You plan to pass through the strait at A. What do you expect?
options: Less wind — the islands shelter the strait
F7 or more and steep seas — consider waiting
Exactly the forecast wind and sea
Calmer water in the middle, away from the islands
questions.why: Wind funnels and accelerates between high islands; the Kafireas Strait is notorious.

questions.q: What kind of wind is this?

figure.title: Forecast, northern Adriatic
lines: Gusts up to 50 kn under Velebit

options: A gentle afternoon sea breeze
Warm, humid and steady from the sea
Cold and dry, with violent gusts
A long swell from a distant storm
questions.why: The Bora is a cold NE fall wind: the mean wind may be moderate, the gusts violent.

questions.q: Kvarner, clear sky. A white cloud cap sits on the Velebit mountains and the air turns cold. What is coming?
options: Jugo — slowly rising SE wind
A warm front with steady rain
Maestral — a pleasant NW breeze
Bora — sudden strong NE gusts
questions.why: A cloud cap on the coastal mountains is the classic warning of the Bora.

questions.q: Southern Croatia, October. Which wind is setting in?

figure.title: Southern Croatia, October
lines: Barometer falling slowly for a day
SE wind building, swell from the SE

options: Jugo — builds slowly, rain, big seas
Bora — sudden, and gone by tonight
Maestral — a pleasant fair-weather breeze
Land breeze — it eases by noon
questions.why: The Jugo (Adriatic sirocco) builds slowly with a falling glass, cloud, rain and a heavy SE sea.

questions.q: Which wind is this?

figure.title: Sicily, April
lines: Red dust on the deck and sails

options: Tramontana from the north
Sirocco from North Africa
Mistral from the Rhône valley
Bora from the Dinaric Alps
questions.why: Sirocco: hot SE–S wind off the Sahara, humid and hazy over the sea, often carrying red dust.

questions.q: You planned to leave Marseille today for Menorca. What do you do?
options: Go — it is a tailwind, so it is safe
Go, but keep close along the Gulf coast
Wait — clear sky or not, it is a gale
Go — a clear sky means fair weather
questions.why: The Mistral blows under clear skies and raises a short, steep sea in the Gulf of Lion.

questions.q: You are at the western end of the Strait of Bonifacio when a Mistral is forecast for the Gulf of Lion. What do you expect in the strait?
options: Nothing — the Mistral stays off the French coast
A warm southerly with heavy rain
A light easterly as the Mistral dies
Strong westerlies, funnelled by the strait
questions.why: The Mistral reaches Corsica and Sardinia as a westerly and funnels through the Bonifacio Strait.

questions.q: Menorca, July. Tramontana F6 is forecast for tonight. Where do you spend the night?
options: B, on the south coast
C, on the east coast
Any — it is only F6
A, on the north coast
questions.why: The Tramontana is a northerly: shelter on the south side of the island.

questions.q: You are in Gibraltar, bound west into the Atlantic. Levante for two days, then Poniente. When do you go?
options: During the Poniente — a fair wind west
During the Levante — a fair wind west
Either — both blow from the south
Neither — both are night winds only
questions.why: Levante is the easterly of the Strait, Poniente the westerly.

questions.q: You are wintering in Malta and a Gregale 8 is forecast. From which direction must your berth be sheltered?
options: South-east
South-west
North-east
North-west
questions.why: The Gregale is a strong NE wind of the central Mediterranean, notorious in Malta.

questions.q: You are anchored in a bay on Corsica's west coast, open to the south-west. Libeccio 7 is forecast for tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Stay — the Libeccio is a north-easterly
Stay — west-coast bays are sheltered from it
Wait until it arrives, then decide
Move today to shelter from the south-west
questions.why: The Libeccio is a SW wind that sends a heavy sea onto Corsica's west coast.

questions.q: Croatia, July. Calm morning; from about 11:00 a NW breeze builds to F4 and dies at sunset. The barometer is steady. What is it?
options: Maestral — a fair-weather breeze
A cold front — expect squalls
Jugo — expect rain tomorrow
Bora — expect violent gusts from the NE
questions.why: The maestral is the Adriatic's summer afternoon NW breeze, a sign of settled weather.

questions.q: You will leave the Dardanelles into the Aegean. Which wind gives the steepest sea at the entrance?

figure.title: Dardanelles
lines: Surface current sets SW, out to the Aegean

options: A moderate northerly
A strong south-westerly
A strong north-easterly
A light north-easterly
questions.why: Wind against current shortens and steepens the waves; a SW wind meets the outgoing current head-on.

questions.q: You must reach Mykonos, to the north, by Thursday. When do you sail?
options: Thursday afternoon, with the wind behind
Tuesday afternoon, to get it done
Wednesday, early in the morning
Thursday morning, as it builds
questions.why: Use the lull, and sail upwind legs early before the afternoon wind.

questions.q: You are anchored off a hot island in summer. Yesterday afternoon the wind blew onshore. What is this light breeze?

figure.note: 05:00 after a clear night, wind off the land

options: A sea breeze — it builds all morning
A front passing through
The Meltemi arriving early, ahead of the day
