A land breeze — it fades after sunrise
questions.why: At night the land cools below the sea and air drains offshore; it dies as the sun heats the land.

questions.q: What wind do you expect near the coast this afternoon?

figure.title: Forecast
lines: You are on a coast facing south-west

options: Stronger — sea breeze adds to it
Exactly F4, as forecast
Calm — the two winds cancel out
Weaker — the land slows the wind down
questions.why: An onshore gradient wind plus a sea breeze in the same direction gives a fresher afternoon wind.

questions.q: You are anchored at A. At 02:00 strong cold gusts pour down off the land. What is it, and what do you do next time?
options: Jugo — it builds for two more days
Katabatic — avoid the valley mouth
Warm front — rain follows by dawn
Sea breeze — it eases after midnight
questions.why: On clear nights cold air drains down valleys and bursts out of their mouths.

questions.q: Forecast W 5. You are about to round Cape Maleas. What do you expect?
options: A flat sea close under the cliffs
Exactly the forecast wind and sea
More wind and a confused sea there
Lighter wind in the lee of the cape
questions.why: Wind accelerates round high headlands; Maleas is notorious — reef before the cape.

questions.q: Meltemi F6. You sail in the lee of high Andros, close under the cliffs, and the wind has almost died. What do you do?
options: Shake out the reefs to keep moving
Motor in closer under the cliffs
Hoist the full genoa for the light air
Stay reefed — gusts fall off the hills
questions.why: Behind high islands calm patches alternate with fierce fall gusts; stay reefed.

questions.q: Same F6 wind across the whole gulf. Where is the sea smallest?
options: A — near the windward shore, short fetch
B — it is further from the land
Both the same — same wind, same sea
B — the waves lose energy crossing the gulf
questions.why: Waves grow with the distance the wind blows over open water (the fetch).

questions.q: You are on passage. What do you do now?

figure.title: 17:00, September, Ionian
lines: Towering cloud with an anvil top

options: Keep full sail and try to outrun it
Reef and prepare for a violent squall
Anchor close under the nearest high cliff
Wait for the first rain, then reef
questions.why: A cumulonimbus brings sudden gusts of 40 kn or more: reef, close hatches, lifejackets on.

questions.q: A thunderstorm cell is approaching against a light easterly. Just before it reaches you, what happens to the wind?

figure.note: Cb cell to the west, moving east

options: It swings gently round to blow towards the storm
The easterly strengthens steadily
It drops, then a hard gust hits from the storm
It stays light until the rain has passed
questions.why: The cold downdraft spreads out ahead of the storm as a sudden gust front.

questions.q: A thunderstorm is overhead and lightning is striking around you. Where do you keep the crew?
options: At the mast foot, ready to drop sail
On deck, holding on to the shrouds
At the stern, holding the backstay
Below, clear of the mast and rigging
questions.why: Lightning follows the mast and rigging to the water; keep people below and away from metal.

questions.q: Autumn, Ionian. A waterspout hangs under a dark cloud about two miles away. What do you do?
options: Watch its bearing and motor out of its path
Close up and sail nearer to watch it
Keep your course — they never cross boats
Heave to where you are and let it pass by you
questions.why: Waterspouts can be violent; check whether its bearing is steady and move clear of its track.

questions.q: You plan an afternoon passage. What wind do you allow for?
options: Calm — storms kill the wind
Squalls far above F3 near any storm
F3 all day — the GRIB shows no more
F3 with some rain, nothing more
questions.why: Thunderstorm gusts are local and short; forecasts and GRIBs give only the background wind.

questions.q: By 10:00 the cumulus over the mainland mountains is already towering high and darkening. What does it mean for your day?
options: Fog will form by the evening
A Meltemi will start tonight
Thunderstorms likely — be in port early
Fair weather — puffy cloud is a good sign
questions.why: Cumulus growing tall by mid-morning signals afternoon thunderstorms.

questions.q: A low, dark roll of cloud with a line of white water beneath it is racing towards you. What do you do?
options: Nothing — it is only rain
Slow down and sound fog signals
Shake out a reef for the breeze
Reduce sail now, before it hits
questions.why: A roll cloud with white water under it is a squall line — minutes away.

questions.q: What is forming, and will the breeze clear it?

figure.title: Northern Adriatic, May
lines: Sea still cold after the winter

options: Sea fog — it can persist despite the wind
Sea mist — it always clears by noon
Heat haze — it will lift by noon
Radiation fog — the breeze will clear it
questions.why: Advection fog: warm moist air cooled over a cold sea; wind does not disperse it.

questions.q: Your passage is 20 miles along the coast. What do you do?

figure.title: Marina, October, 06:30
lines: Thick fog in the harbour, blue sky above

options: Leave now — it is the same at sea all day
Wait — it should burn off by mid-morning
Leave now and steer by radar alone
Cancel — this fog will last all day
questions.why: Radiation fog forms over land on clear calm nights and clears as the sun warms it.

questions.q: What do you expect overnight?
options: A dry, clear night with good visibility
A strong land breeze
Fog or mist forming over the sea
Heavy thunderstorms with hail
questions.why: Moist air at its dew point flowing over colder sea will form advection fog.

questions.q: When are you most likely to meet sea fog in the northern Adriatic?
options: Every summer afternoon at 16:00
Only when the Bora is blowing
Mid-August, at the height of summer
Spring, while the sea is still cold
questions.why: Sea fog needs warm moist air over a sea still cold from winter.

questions.q: What does the swell tell you?

figure.title: Anchored, south coast
lines: Long, low swell from the SW, building

options: A distant system — swell runs ahead
A sea breeze will start up within the hour
It is the wake of a passing ship
Settled weather for days to come
questions.why: Swell travels faster than the weather that made it and is an early warning.

questions.q: Where will you spend a comfortable night?

figure.note: Wind N 2 · SW swell 1.5 m tonight

options: A — sheltered from the north wind
B — tucked away from the swell
C — open to the south
Any — the wind is light
questions.why: Swell can make an anchorage untenable even in light wind; hide from the swell direction.

questions.q: The Meltemi blew F7 for three days and stopped at dawn. You plan to leave Naxos northwards this morning. What do you expect?
options: The wind back within the hour
Flat calm water as soon as you leave
A big leftover sea for some hours
Fog from the cooled sea
questions.why: The sea takes hours to go down after a long blow.

questions.q: How do you plan the day's passage?
options: Ration water to make it last
Skip hats and shade — it is only a day
Sail in the midday heat, when it is calm
Sail early, shelter and rest at midday
questions.why: Avoid the midday sun, drink plenty and keep the crew in shade.

questions.q: What do you decide?
options: Stay and wait for the wind to ease
Go — it is a downwind run
Go with full sail to be quick
Go, but reef down if anyone feels ill
questions.why: Rough sea, strong gusts and a mostly new crew on an open crossing: wait for a better window.

questions.q: You must pick a night anchorage. Which one?

figure.note: Now NW 5 · backing SW 6 after midnight

options: A — handy for tomorrow's leg west
B — sheltered now and after the shift
C — calm now, behind the island
Any — the wind backs only after midnight
questions.why: Choose shelter for the wind you will have overnight, not only the wind you have now.

questions.q: Your Delta has skated across the bottom twice. The charter base offers a spare anchor. Which type do you take?

figure.title: Pilot notes for the bay
lines: Spare anchors held at the base

options: A Danforth-type flat anchor
A Bruce claw anchor
A fisherman (Admiralty) anchor
A mushroom anchor
questions.why: A fisherman's narrow fluke pierces weed and hooks rock where broad flukes skate.

questions.q: Your only anchor is well set in sand. What is the main concern tonight?
options: It needs at least 10:1 scope to hold at all
It holds well only in mud, not in sand
It will dig in too deep to raise in the morning
It may break out and not reset when the pull reverses
questions.why: Danforth types hold hard in sand and mud but often pull out and clog when the wind swings round.

questions.q: You plan to anchor on the shallow patch off Kalamos shown on the chart. What does the abbreviation tell you?
options: Weed — the anchor may skate; look for sand
Weak current — no stream to allow for
Wreck debris — an obstruction to avoid
Wide shelf — plenty of room to swing
questions.why: Wd = weed on the chart; anchors often fail to dig through it.

questions.q: You want a second anchor for kedging: light, stowing flat in a cockpit locker, holding well in sand and mud. Which type?
options: A Bruce claw
A Danforth type
A fisherman with a stock
A folding grapnel
questions.why: Danforth types give high holding for their weight in sand and mud and stow flat.

questions.q: You take the dinghy to snorkel off a rocky point near Paxos and want to anchor it. What do you use?
options: The yacht's spare Delta and its chain
A small Danforth that needs sand to bite
A small folding grapnel on a light line
The heavy fisherman from the yacht
questions.why: A light grapnel hooks into rock and is easy to handle from a dinghy.

questions.q: Looking down through clear water you see this bottom. Where do you drop the anchor?

figure.note: Seen from the bow, depth about 6 m

options: Between them, with the chain on the grass
A — the seagrass will grip the anchor
A — the meadow cushions anchor and chain
B — on the sand, clear of the seagrass
questions.why: Posidonia seagrass is protected and holds poorly; anchor and chain belong on sand.

questions.q: You are backing down on the anchor. What is happening and what do you do?
options: It is skating — lift it and try another spot
The chain is settling — wait ten minutes
It is setting well — add more revs
It has hooked a rock — ease off and stay
questions.why: A juddering chain and moving transits mean the anchor is not biting.

questions.q: You dragged in the night and have lifted the anchor. You see this. What do you do before trying again?

figure.title: Anchor at the bow roller
lines: A ball of weed jammed on the tip
Clean sand patches near the beach

options: Drop again in the same spot with more chain
Clear it and drop on a patch of clean sand
Fit the heavier spare and drop here again
Leave it on — it adds weight to the anchor
questions.why: A clump of weed on the tip stops any anchor digging in; change the spot too.

questions.q: The best sandy patch in the bay is crossed by the line shown on your chart. What do you do?

figure.title: Chart extract
lines: Magenta wavy line, beach to open sea
Sand, 5 m, either side of it
Rock along the rest of the shore

options: Anchor on it — it is a depth contour
Anchor on it — it marks a sand bar
Anchor well clear — it marks a submarine cable
Anchor beside it — it marks the swimming zone
questions.why: A magenta wavy line is a submarine cable; never anchor on or near it.

questions.q: You are about to anchor for a gusty night. How much chain do you pay out?
questions.why: (6 m depth + 1 m bow height) × 5 = 35 m; measure from the roller, not the surface.

questions.q: You are laying the kedge as your main anchor. How much rode do you pay out in total?
questions.why: (8 m + 1 m bow height) × 7 = 63 m; chain-and-rope needs about 6–8:1.

questions.q: You anchor at low water in a bay near Trieste. What length of chain do you let out?
questions.why: Use the depth at high water plus bow height: (5 + 1 + 1) × 4 = 28 m.

questions.q: You check the chain counter after anchoring. Is it enough for tonight, and what do you do?
options: About 3:1 — lift and re-anchor at once
About 5:1 — that is enough for F6
About 4:1 — let out more if there is room
About 7:1 — shorten so you swing less
questions.why: 30 m ÷ (6 + 1 m) ≈ 4.3:1; aim for 5–7:1 when strong wind is forecast.

questions.q: Your crew wants to leave the chain like this so the boat swings less. What is the risk?
options: None — a tight chain holds the boat better
None — the anchor's weight holds the boat
The anchor digs in too deep to raise
The chain lifts the shank and pulls the anchor out
questions.why: An anchor holds only when the pull along the bottom is near horizontal.

questions.q: What is the deepest water you can anchor in tonight?
options: 9 m
7 m
questions.why: 50 m ÷ 5 = 10 m from roller to seabed, less 1 m bow height = 9 m of water.

questions.q: You anchor in this spot. Will you stay afloat at low water?
options: Yes — about 1.1 m under the keel
Yes — about 0.4 m under the keel
Yes — about 0.7 m under the keel
No — you will touch at low water
questions.why: 3 − 0.7 = 2.3 m at low water; 2.3 − 1.9 m draught = 0.4 m clearance.

questions.q: Your crew wants to save weight by shackling the nylon kedge rope straight onto the anchor. What is wrong with that?
options: Rope stretches too little to absorb gusts
Nothing — rope alone holds just as well
The rope chafes on the bottom and lifts the shank
The rope sinks and fouls the flukes
questions.why: A few metres of chain at the anchor keeps the pull low and resists chafe.

questions.q: Which spot gives you the quietest night?

figure.note: Wind NW F3 · old swell rolling in from the SW

options: C — close under the beach at the head
B — in the middle, with the most room
Any of them — the wind is only light
A — tucked in behind the headland
questions.why: Swell, not just wind, decides comfort; anchor behind land that blocks it.

questions.q: You are anchored here for the night. What do you do?

figure.note: Forecast: wind W F6 after midnight

options: Leave before dark for a bay sheltered from the west
Move closer in, towards the beach
Stay, and let out more chain before midnight
Stay with the anchor alarm on and sleep
questions.why: A bay open to the forecast wind becomes a lee shore; move while it is light.

questions.q: Before dark, what do you prepare in case you must leave in the night?

figure.title: Unfamiliar bay, Ionian
lines: Rocks either side of the entrance
Wind may shift in the night

options: The dinghy in the water, ready to tow you out
An exit track on the plotter, hazards marked
A plan to wait for daylight, whatever happens
The anchor alarm set to its widest radius
questions.why: Plan the night exit in daylight, when you can still see the rocks.

questions.q: You arrive in this bay. Where do you let go your anchor?

labels: yacht at anchor, 40 m chain out

options: B — close astern, in its lee
Close alongside it, on short scope
C — well to one side, clear of its swing
A — ahead of it, in the open water
questions.why: Never drop over another boat's chain; keep both swinging circles apart.

questions.q: You want to anchor in the remaining gap for the night. How do you do it?

figure.title: Late arrival, cove near Göcek
lines: Every boat lies stern-to on a shore line
One free gap in the middle

options: Swing free in the gap on 5:1 scope
Swing free on short scope to stay small
Raft alongside the nearest boat unasked
Take a shore line too, like your neighbours
questions.why: Boats that cannot swing need neighbours that do not swing either.

questions.q: You anchor near a large motor yacht and a catamaran in a gusty, shifting wind. What do you allow for?
options: Extra room — they swing differently from you
Their anchors hold, so yours can be lighter
Less room — big boats barely move
Nothing — all boats swing the same way
questions.why: High-windage boats sheer about more than keel yachts; leave a margin.

questions.q: You are anchored as shown. What do you do before nightfall?

labels: shoal 35 m S of the anchor

options: Stay, and set the anchor alarm to warn you
Re-anchor further north, out of the shoal's reach
Stay — the south wind keeps you north of it
Stay, and let out more chain for holding
questions.why: When the wind goes north you lie south of the anchor: 35 m of chain reaches the shoal.

questions.q: You are motoring towards spot A to anchor. How do you make the final approach?
options: Fast, to keep steerage in the gusts
Across the wind at cruising speed
Slowly, head to wind, stopping over the spot
Downwind, so the wind carries you in
questions.why: Head to wind you can stop exactly where you want and fall back in line.

questions.q: You are head to wind over the spot. When does the bow crew let go?
options: After drifting back a full scope
As soon as the spot is in sight
While still moving ahead at two knots
As the boat stops and starts to drift astern
questions.why: Letting go as you gather sternway lays the chain out instead of on the anchor.

questions.q: The anchor is on the bottom, the boat is not moving, and the bow crew keeps running chain out fast. What happens?
options: The chain piles on the anchor and may foul it
The anchor digs in faster under the weight
The boat is pulled forward over the anchor
Nothing — the scope is the same in the end
questions.why: Pay out only as fast as the boat falls back, laying the chain along the bottom.

questions.q: You are reversing to set the anchor. What tells you it is holding?
options: The chain goes slack and hangs straight down
Transits abeam stay fixed and the chain is taut
The boat stops, then creeps slowly astern
The depth reading stays the same
questions.why: A fixed transit under load proves the anchor is dug in.

questions.q: To check the anchor is holding, which pair of objects do you line up?
options: Two yachts anchored near you, seen in line
A single headland straight ahead
Two fixed marks ashore, in line, abeam
A moored fishing boat and the beach behind
questions.why: Fixed objects abeam show the smallest movement along the boat's line.

questions.q: You set the GPS anchor alarm. Where do you centre it, and roughly what radius?

figure.title: Anchor alarm
lines: Boat length 12 m, GPS at the stern

options: Centred on the anchor, about 20 m
Centred on the boat now, about 100 m
Centred on the boat now, about 10 m
Centred on the anchor, about 50 m
questions.why: The antenna can be anywhere within chain plus boat length of the anchor: 34 + 12 ≈ 50 m.

questions.q: Your all-chain rode is set and the gusts are building. What do you rig to protect the gear?
options: A nylon snubber from a bow cleat to the chain
A tighter brake on the windlass gypsy
A lashing from the chain to the pulpit
A shorter chain so it stays taut
questions.why: A snubber absorbs shock loads and takes the strain off the windlass.

questions.q: You skipper a catamaran; the chain runs off a roller on the front beam. How do you take the load once anchored?
options: The chain lashed to the front beam
A bridle from both bow cleats to the chain
The chain led to one hull's bow cleat
The load left on the windlass gypsy
questions.why: A bridle shares the load between both hulls and keeps the cat head to wind.

questions.q: Night falls while you are at anchor in a bay. Which light do you switch on?
options: The masthead steaming light
The tricolour at the masthead
The all-round white anchor light
The red and green sidelights
questions.why: Rule 30: a vessel at anchor shows an all-round white light.

questions.q: You motor into a bay and see this yacht ahead. How do you pass it?

figure.note: Yacht ahead of you in the bay

options: Close across its bow — it cannot move
As if aground — keep to deeper water
Expect it to move off — the ball means leaving
Keep clear of its bow — its chain runs out ahead
questions.why: A black ball means at anchor; its chain runs forward from the bow.

questions.q: The water is clear and 5 m deep. What is the surest way to check the anchor has dug in?
options: Snorkel over it and look
Wait for the anchor alarm to stay quiet
Read the depth on the sounder
Ask the boat anchored next to you
questions.why: In clear Med water a look at the anchor beats any guess.

questions.q: Your plotter track looks like this. What is happening?

figure.note: Your GPS track over the last hour

options: The boat is swinging normally on its chain
The anchor is dragging downwind
The GPS position is jumping about
The wind has shifted and you swung round
questions.why: Swinging draws an arc; a straight line downwind means dragging.

questions.q: The alarm wakes you and you go on deck. What is your first action?
options: Call the charter base for advice
Let out all remaining chain and wait
Start the engine and motor up to take the strain
Launch the dinghy to lay a second anchor
questions.why: The engine buys time; then lift and re-anchor or leave.

questions.q: You decide to stay in an exposed anchorage with F7 forecast after midnight. What do you organise?
options: Lights off to save the batteries
The dinghy towed astern on a long line
Everyone to bed, the alarm as backup
An anchor watch rota, engine and crew ready
questions.why: In strong wind someone stays awake, checking position, chain and neighbours.

questions.q: You are on anchor watch when you see this. How do you respond?

figure.title: 0200, wind rising
lines: A yacht upwind is dragging towards you

options: Horn and torch to wake them; engine on, fenders out
Fend her off with the boathook when she arrives
Call a MAYDAY on channel 16
Raise your anchor and leave the bay at once
questions.why: Wake the other crew and get ready to manoeuvre or fend off safely.

questions.q: You anchored first. A yacht arrives, drops upwind and falls back to lie 5 m off your bow. What do you do?
options: Say nothing and hang fenders forward
Ask them politely to re-anchor further off
Lift your own anchor — newcomers have priority
Let out more chain to drop back from them
questions.why: The first boat to anchor has priority; a newcomer must leave it room to swing.

questions.q: Will you clear the rock when the wind goes round to the west?

labels: rock is 45 m from your anchor

options: Yes — the boat swings only on its 40 m of chain
Yes — the curved chain keeps you within 30 m
No — the stern could reach about 52 m from the anchor
Yes — the rock is beyond your 40 m of chain
questions.why: Swing radius ≈ horizontal chain (about 39.5 m) + boat length 13 m ≈ 52 m > 45 m.

questions.q: The anchor alarm goes off at 0300 in a steady F4. What do you do first?
options: Silence it and go back to sleep
Widen the alarm radius to stop it
Start lifting the anchor straight away
Check transits, plotter track and depth
questions.why: Confirm whether you are really dragging before you act.

questions.q: In a narrow anchorage you need a small swinging circle but want the bow still to turn to the wind. What do you lay?
options: A Bahamian moor: two bow anchors 180° apart
Bow and stern anchors, fore and aft
One anchor on short 2:1 scope
Two anchors in tandem on one chain
questions.why: Two opposed bow anchors keep you near one spot yet let you head to wind.

questions.q: How do you lay the two anchors?

figure.title: Forecast
lines: Two anchors and enough rode aboard

options: From the bow, 180° apart, Bahamian moor
Both from the bow, 30–45° apart, into the wind
Both on the same spot to double the weight
One from the bow, one from the stern
questions.why: A V of two bow anchors shares the load of a strong, steady wind.

questions.q: You want a quieter night without moving. What steadies the boat?

figure.title: Anchored off Kythnos
lines: Swell rolling in from the side

options: More chain on the bow anchor for a softer ride
A heavier nylon snubber on the bow chain
A stern kedge to hold her end-on to the swell
Moving in closer to the beach for shelter
questions.why: Holding the boat end-on to the swell stops the beam-on roll.

questions.q: Full astern does not move you off. What do you do next?
options: Wait for the tide to fall a little further
Rev hard ahead to push across the bar
Drop the kedge on the bar under the bow
Lay the kedge by dinghy towards deep water
questions.why: A kedge laid towards deep water gives a pull the engine alone cannot.

questions.q: You row the kedge out in the dinghy to lay it. How do you handle the rode?
options: Flake it in the dinghy and pay it out as you row
Coil it round the anchor and throw both together
Leave it aboard and tow it behind the dinghy
Drop the anchor first, then row the rode back
questions.why: Paying out from the dinghy avoids dragging heavy rode through the water.

questions.q: In a Turkish cove you take a shore line to a rock and want to leave later without going ashore. How do you rig it?
options: Made fast ashore with a bowline round the rock
Round the rock and back aboard, to slip from deck
Tied to your neighbour's shore line
Tied to the nearest bush beside the rock
questions.why: A doubled line can be slipped from the boat without anyone going ashore.

questions.q: The only shore point is a sharp-edged rock. How do you protect the line?
options: Tie it to a small bush beside the rock
Pull the line bar-tight so it cannot move
Pass a chain strop or chafe guard round the rock
Use a thinner line that slides over edges
questions.why: Sharp rock saws through rope as the boat moves; protect the contact point.

questions.q: Your stern-to berth in the cove has become uncomfortable. What do you add to fix it?

figure.title: Cove near Göcek, stern-to the rocks
lines: Anchor out ahead, one shore line
Afternoon gusts blow across the cove

options: More chain out on the anchor
A bridle rigged on the anchor chain
Extra fenders on the downwind side
A second shore line on the upwind side
questions.why: Two shore lines in a V stop the stern swinging in a cross wind.

questions.q: The anchor is down 50 m out and you have reversed to 10 m off the rocks in a light offshore breeze. What now?
options: Line ashore and back aboard, then tighten the chain
Tighten the chain fully, then take the line ashore
Switch off and wait for the breeze to die away
Swing on the anchor first, then take a line ashore
questions.why: Hold position with the engine until the shore line is on; then tension against the anchor.

questions.q: You are lifting 40 m of chain in F4. The windlass labours and the boat is not moving forward. What do you do?
options: Have the crew haul the chain in by hand
Motor slowly up so the windlass only takes in slack
Keep winching — the windlass will pull the boat
Winch in short, hard bursts until it moves
questions.why: The engine moves the boat; the windlass only lifts the chain and anchor.

questions.q: From the wheel you cannot hear the bow crew as you lift the anchor. How do they show you where the chain leads?
options: By calling on VHF channel 16
By banging on the deck
By pointing along the chain with an arm
By shouting louder over the wind
questions.why: Agree hand signals before you start: point to the chain, show up-and-down, show anchor off.

questions.q: You are lifting the anchor and reach this point. How do you break it out?

figure.title: Lifting the anchor
lines: Chain now straight up and down

options: Drift back and pull with the windlass again
Let out 20 m more and wait an hour
Keep the windlass running until it frees
Lock off the chain, then motor gently ahead
questions.why: Break an anchor out with the boat's momentum, not the windlass motor.

questions.q: The anchor is home in the bow roller and you are heading out into a lumpy sea. What do you do with it?
options: Set the chain stopper and lash the anchor down
Lower it a metre so it cannot bang the bow
Leave it held on the windlass brake alone
Leave the windlass breaker on, ready to drop
questions.why: A windlass is not a stopper; a loose anchor can run out or batter the bow.

questions.q: How do you free your anchor?

figure.title: Leaving a Med quay
lines: It hangs just below the surface

options: Ask the neighbour to cut and re-lay his chain
Hold their chain on a slip line, lower yours clear
Motor hard ahead to jerk the anchor free of it
Lift both and motor out dragging their chain
questions.why: Hold the other chain on a slip line while your anchor drops free.

questions.q: Which stern line do you let go last?
options: The leeward one, rigged as a slip line
Both at the same moment
The windward one, rigged as a slip line
Whichever one is easier to reach
questions.why: The windward line stops the stern blowing onto the leeward boat until you have way on.

questions.q: Your anchor will not break out with the chain up and down and the engine gently ahead. You have no trip line. What do you try?
options: Winch hard until the windlass frees it
Let all the chain go and leave the anchor
Rev ahead harder on the short chain
Motor past it and pull from the other side
questions.why: A fouled anchor often comes out the way it went in — backwards.

questions.q: You arrive at this town quay with a free berth. How do you moor?

figure.title: Pilot notes
lines: Rubble ledge just under the water
along the foot of the quay

options: Bow-to, so the rudder stays in deep water
Stern-to, but closer, so the passerelle reaches
Stern-to, with fenders over the stern
Stern-to, pushing off with a boathook
questions.why: Bow-to keeps the rudder away from shallows at the foot of the quay.

questions.q: You reverse into a gap on the quay. How do you keep the boat straight?

figure.title: Your boat astern
lines: when you first go astern from rest
No wind; gap between two yachts

options: Stop and restart astern each time it swings
Get sternway early, then steer with the rudder
Keep the wheel hard over the whole way in
Use short bursts of full astern to stay straight
questions.why: Prop walk is strongest from rest; once moving astern the rudder bites.

questions.q: You will moor stern-to in the marked berth. Where do you drop the anchor?

figure.note: Wind on the beam of the berth, F4

options: Any of them — the chain straightens out
C — downwind, so you drift in
B — upwind of the line of the berth
A — straight out from the berth
questions.why: Dropped upwind, the chain holds the bow up to windward as you reverse.

questions.q: You are reversing stern-to in a cross wind and the stern nears the quay. Which line goes ashore first?
options: The leeward stern line
A midships spring to the quay
A bow line to the next boat
The windward stern line
questions.why: The windward line stops the stern blowing down onto the leeward neighbour.

questions.q: You are stern-to on a town quay and conditions change as shown. How do you adjust the mooring?

figure.title: Town quay, swell working in
lines: Boat surging on the stern lines

options: Ease stern lines, haul in chain to sit further off
Let out chain so the boat can move freely
Tighten the stern lines to pull the boat in close
Rest the passerelle firmly down on the quay
questions.why: In surge sit 1–2 m off the quay on a tight chain, with the passerelle raised.

questions.q: You rig two stern lines to the bollards on the quay. How do you lead them?
options: Both to a single bollard in the middle
Crossed, each quarter to the opposite bollard
Straight to its own bollard, left slack
One line only, to the windward bollard
questions.why: Crossed stern lines keep the stern centred and give longer, springier lines.

questions.q: Reversing in, the crew is lifting the lazy line from the water at the stern. The helm wants a burst ahead to stop. What do you say?
options: Go ahead — the line is well behind the boat
Steer away from the line with full rudder
Stay in neutral until the line is clear of the prop
Go astern instead — that is safer for the line
questions.why: A sinking lazy line near the stern winds easily round a turning propeller.

questions.q: You moor bow-to on a marina pontoon with lazy lines. Where does the lazy line go?
options: Left in the water; bow lines hold you
On the bow cleat beside the pontoon line
Led to a midships cleat
Walked aft and made fast on a stern cleat
questions.why: The lazy line holds the end away from the pontoon — here, the stern.

questions.q: On a crowded town quay in Poros the harbour master tells you to reverse in straight. Why does it matter?
options: Your chain then lies clear of the neighbours' anchors
Prop walk then cancels itself out
You then need less chain to hold
The passerelle then lines up with the bollards
questions.why: A chain laid at an angle crosses others and causes fouled anchors on departure.

questions.q: What do you have ready to show?

figure.title: Town quay, Greece
lines: Port police office on the quay
An officer walks over to your boat

options: The insurance certificate and nothing else
Boat papers, crew list, licence, cruising tax receipt
Nothing — papers are checked only in marinas
Passports only — the boat is a charter boat
questions.why: Greek port police check boat and crew papers and the cruising tax (TEPAI).

questions.q: You prepare to moor stern-to between two yachts. Where do you hang the fenders?
options: On the bow, in case you hit the quay
Only across the stern, facing the quay
Both sides, amidships and at the quarters
Only on the windward side of the boat
questions.why: Neighbours lie close on both sides; protect where the hulls will touch.

questions.q: On a Greek island town quay, a long empty stretch is signed for the ferry. Can you moor there?
options: Yes — but for one night only
Yes — an empty quay is free for all
Yes — if you leave before 0800
No — keep it clear for the ferry
questions.why: Ferry and tripper berths must stay clear whatever the time.

questions.q: You pick up a buoy in a Croatian bay. It has a thin pick-up line with a loop on the end. How do you use it?
options: Only to lift the ring, then run your own line through
Tie your line to the pick-up line
Leave it and anchor next to the buoy
Drop its loop over a bow cleat and stay on it
questions.why: Pick-up lines are not made for the load; never lie on one alone.

questions.q: You are staying on a buoy for the night. How do you rig your lines to the ring?
options: A single line knotted to the ring
From each bow cleat, through the ring, back to the same cleat
The buoy's pick-up line on one cleat
One line from port cleat through the ring to starboard
questions.why: Same-side loops cannot saw across the ring and can be slipped from aboard.

questions.q: From which spot do you start your final approach to the buoy?
options: B — so the wind carries you down onto it
C — across the wind, for a clear view
A — so you motor slowly up into the wind
Any — at the speed the wind allows
questions.why: Approach a buoy into the wind so you can stop beside it.

questions.q: You lie to a buoy in a buoy field near Hvar. A boat comes by to collect a fee. What do you do?
options: Pay only if you stay on it after dark
Refuse — buoys are free of charge in Croatia
Move off and anchor among the buoys
Pay and keep the receipt — it is a concession
questions.why: Croatian buoy fields are concessions; anchoring inside them is not allowed.

questions.q: The only free buoy is a small private one with a thin chain, used by a local fishing boat. Your yacht is 14 m. Do you use it?
options: No — its ground tackle may be too light for you
Yes — with two lines for double strength
Yes — with longer lines to reduce snatching
Yes — any buoy holds a yacht in calm weather
questions.why: A buoy holds only what its sinker and chain were sized for.

questions.q: You pick up a buoy in a catamaran. How do you lie to it?
options: The buoy pulled up tight under the front beam
A line from each bow cleat to the ring, as a bridle
One line from the windlass roller to the ring
One line from the windward bow cleat only
questions.why: A bridle from both hulls keeps the cat straight and stops the buoy hitting the hulls.

questions.q: You are alongside and an offshore breeze holds the bow away from the pontoon. Which line pulls it in close?
options: A stern spring, led forward to the pontoon
A midships spring, led aft to the pontoon
A bow breast line, square to the pontoon
A longer bow line, led well forward
questions.why: Breast lines run at right angles and pull the boat in; springs stop surge.

questions.q: You are coming alongside a low floating pontoon. Where do you set the fenders?
options: Across the stern, under the passerelle
High, at the rail, to protect the deck
Only at the bow, where you touch first
Low, near the waterline, at the widest part
questions.why: Fenders must sit where the hull meets the pontoon edge.

questions.q: You come alongside this pontoon. How do you approach?
options: At a steeper angle, getting a line on fast
Fast and parallel, then full astern
Stern first, letting the wind hold the bow
Parallel, stopped a metre off, let it blow you in
questions.why: Wind off the berth blows you away; aim in more and get a line ashore quickly.

questions.q: This time the wind blows onto the berth. How do you come alongside?
options: At right angles, then turn at the last moment
Stop parallel, a metre off; let the wind push you in
At a steep angle, bow first and fairly quick
Parallel at speed, then full astern to stop
questions.why: An onshore wind does the work; arrive stopped and parallel, well fendered.

questions.q: Short-handed, you have one line on: a midships spring, led aft to a pontoon cleat. Engine gently ahead — where do you put the wheel?
options: Amidships, so the boat stays straight
Turned towards the pontoon, at full ahead
Turned away from the pontoon, pushing the stern in
Turned towards the pontoon, pulling the bow in
questions.why: Against a midships spring, gentle ahead with helm away holds the boat alongside.

questions.q: You are alongside and the wind is blowing you off the pontoon. How do you leave?
options: Spring off on a bow line with full power
Motor ahead with the wheel hard towards it
Push off hard from the pontoon with your feet
Let the lines go and let the wind blow you clear
questions.why: With the wind off the berth there is no need for springs.

questions.q: You will swing the stern out and leave astern. What do you rig, and which gear?
options: Bow spring led aft, bow fendered, gently ahead
Bow spring led aft, gently astern
Stern line only, hard astern
Stern spring led forward, gently ahead
questions.why: Ahead against a bow spring pivots on the bow and swings the stern out.

questions.q: You raft up outside a yacht of the same size on a busy town quay. What do you do?
options: Borrow her shore lines to save your own
Stagger the masts and run your own lines ashore
Tie breast lines only, to her cleats
Line up the masts and tie only to her
questions.why: Staggered spreaders cannot clash; own bow and stern lines carry your load.

questions.q: You need to cross a neighbour's yacht in a raft to get ashore late at night. How do you go?
options: Through their cockpit — it is shortest
Knock and walk through the saloon
Quietly across their foredeck
Along the outside of their guardrail
questions.why: Etiquette: cross by the foredeck, keep clear of the cockpit.

questions.q: How do you set your lines?
options: Tight now, adjusted in the morning
Short lines, all bar-tight to hold you close
Breast lines only, made up tight
Long springs, slack left in bow and stern lines
questions.why: Long lines tolerate a change of level; tight short ones hang the boat.

questions.q: How do you protect the hull?

figure.title: Alongside an old quay
lines: Vertical wooden piles along the wall

options: A fender board outside the fenders
Fenders hung flat between the piles
Fenders tied to the piles themselves
Fewer fenders, so they cannot roll off
questions.why: A plank outside the fenders spans the piles so the fenders cannot slip between.

questions.q: You are coming alongside a pontoon with room on either side. Which side do you put to it, and why?

figure.title: Your boat
lines: Stern kicks to port going astern
You stop with a burst astern

options: Port side-to — astern pushes the stern clear
Port side-to — the stop astern pulls the stern in
Either — prop walk acts only in ahead
Starboard side-to — astern pulls the stern in
questions.why: Use prop walk: the burst astern to stop walks the stern towards the berth.

questions.q: You check the anchor locker before the season. How should the bitter end of the chain be secured?
options: Shackled tight so it can never be lost
Wound twice round the windlass drum
With a strong lashing that can be cut
Loose in the locker, ready to run
questions.why: If the anchor must be abandoned, the chain can be cut free in seconds.

questions.q: You have lifted the anchor and are motoring out of the bay. What do you do with this?
options: Leave it up until you hoist sail
Keep it up while motoring
Keep it up until clear of the bay
Lower it — it says you are at anchor
questions.why: The ball means at anchor; take it down as soon as you are under way.

questions.q: Your diesel cranks at normal speed but will not fire. Which three things must it have to run?
options: Fuel, air and compression
Spark, air and oil pressure
Fuel, spark and a full battery
Fuel, spark and compression
questions.why: A diesel has no spark: compression heats the air enough to ignite the injected fuel.

questions.q: You trace the fuel line from the tank to the engine to find a leak. In what order do you meet the parts?
options: Lift pump, injectors, fine filter, water separator
Water separator, lift pump, fine filter, injectors
Injectors, water separator, lift pump, fine filter
Fine filter, lift pump, water separator, injectors
questions.why: Fuel is cleaned twice on its way: coarse primary filter first, fine filter just before the injection pump.

questions.q: During the morning check you look at the primary fuel filter bowl. What do you do?

figure.title: Primary filter / water separator
lines: Bottom 2 cm: a clear, separate layer
Fuel sits above it with a sharp line between

options: Top up the coolant — it is leaking into the bowl
Bleed the injectors — it is air in the fuel
Drain the water from the bowl until clean fuel runs
Leave it — it settles out by the next service
questions.why: Water is heavier than diesel and collects at the bottom of the separator; drain it before it reaches the engine.

questions.q: The engine has stopped twice in a week with a blocked filter. This is what you find. What is it?

figure.title: Fuel filter bowl
lines: Black-brown slimy sludge in the bowl
Boat little used, tank kept half empty

options: Soot from the exhaust blown back in
Engine oil leaking into the fuel tank
Wax from the fuel in cold weather
Diesel bug growing where fuel meets water
questions.why: Microbes live at the fuel–water layer and make sludge that blocks filters; keep tanks dry and treated.

questions.q: You ran the tank dry yesterday and have just put 60 litres in. The engine cranks strongly but will not start. Why?

figure.title: After running out of fuel
lines: No firing, no smoke at the exhaust

options: Air in the fuel lines — bleed the system
Cold engine — hold the preheat longer
Blocked air filter — take it off and retry
Flat battery — switch to the house bank
questions.why: Running dry pulls air into the fuel system; the injectors cannot spray air, so it must be bled.

questions.q: Bleeding the engine, you have opened the bleed screw on the fine filter. The lift pump has a hand lever. What next?
options: Leave it open and start the engine to clear it
Pump the lever until fuel comes out bubble-free, then close
Crank the starter until diesel sprays out, then close
Close it at the first drop of diesel you see
questions.why: Bleed in the direction of the fuel flow and close each screw only when solid, bubble-free fuel runs.

questions.q: You plan to motor through a calm day to the next fuel quay. How far can you go without touching your reserve?

lines: Calm sea, same revs all the way

options: 60 miles
120 miles
90 miles
15 miles

questions.q: Your next leg is 54 miles at 6 knots, at the same revs as before. How much fuel will you use?

figure.title: Fuel log
lines: Since then: 12 engine hours, cruising revs
Today the tank took 36 litres to brim

options: 18 litres
54 litres
36 litres
27 litres

questions.q: Fuel is getting low and the next fuel quay is 20 miles away into a short headsea. How do you stretch your range?
options: Ease back the revs a little
Switch off the alternator to save power
Run at full revs to get there sooner
Shift into neutral every half hour
questions.why: Fuel use rises steeply near full throttle while speed barely does; a few hundred rpm less saves the most.

questions.q: Motor-sailing hard on the wind, the engine stutters and stops. What is the most likely cause?

lines: Oil alarm only after it stopped

options: The raw-water impeller has broken
Low fuel sloshing away from the pickup
The engine overheated and cut out
The gearbox has seized under load
questions.why: With a low tank and a big heel the pickup sucks air; level the boat, refuel and bleed.

questions.q: You are about to start the engine at the berth. What is the right sequence?
options: Preheat, start, then open the raw-water seacock
Start, preheat, select neutral, then check the oil
Neutral, battery on, preheat, start, check exhaust water
Battery on, start in gear, then preheat if needed
questions.why: Start in neutral so the boat cannot move, preheat a cold diesel, and confirm cooling water at once.

questions.q: Early April in Croatia, you turn the key straight to start. What do you do differently?

figure.title: Cold start
lines: Engine cranks well but does not catch
Puffs of white smoke at the exhaust

options: Crank for a full minute without a break
Open the throttle fully and keep cranking
Spray easy-start into the air intake
Hold the preheat 10–15 seconds, then crank
questions.why: Glow plugs heat the chambers so a cold diesel fires; ether with glow plugs can wreck the engine.

questions.q: After three hours at cruising revs you reach the anchorage. How do you stop the engine?
options: Idle in neutral a few minutes, then stop
Turn the battery isolator off to stop it
Rev it hard, then stop to clear soot
Stop it at once to save fuel
questions.why: A short idle lets heat even out before shutdown; never stop an engine with the isolator.

questions.q: With the engine running, a crew member reaches for the battery isolator to turn it off and save power. What do you say?
options: Fine — but only at high revs
Stop — it can blow the alternator diodes
Fine — the engine runs without the battery
Fine — the alternator then charges faster
questions.why: Opening the circuit while the alternator charges causes a voltage spike that destroys it.

questions.q: You turn the key and hear one click, but the engine does not turn. What do you do?

lines: Key turned: a click, no cranking

options: Disconnect the house bank and keep trying
Wait a day for the solar to charge it
Parallel the banks, then start the engine
Turn the key to preheat for a full minute
questions.why: The emergency parallel switch lets the house bank start the engine; separate the banks once it runs.

questions.q: Motoring along the coast, you see this. What do you do?
options: Top up the coolant and carry on
Ignore it — oil alarms are often false
Reduce revs and carry on to port
Stop the engine at once and check the oil
questions.why: Without oil pressure the bearings are destroyed within minutes; stop first, then investigate.

questions.q: You turn the key to ON before starting. This is what you see and hear. What does it mean?

lines: Key at ON, engine not yet started

options: Normal — they go out once the engine runs
Broken alternator — call the base
Flat battery — switch to the house bank
Low oil — top up before starting
questions.why: With the engine stopped there is no oil pressure and no charge, so both lights and the buzzer come on.

questions.q: Ten minutes after leaving the marina you see this. What do you check first?
options: The glow-plug relay
The alternator drive belt
The raw-water strainer
The engine oil level
questions.why: A charge light on with the engine running means the alternator is not charging; a slipping or broken belt is the usual cause.

questions.q: Motoring out of Kos, you hear a squeal, then quiet. Soon after the panel looks like this. Most likely cause?

lines: Plenty of water at the exhaust

options: The engine oil is low
The raw-water strainer is blocked
The belt has broken
The propeller is fouled
questions.why: One belt drives both the alternator and the coolant pump, so no charge plus rising heat points to it.

questions.q: You follow the raw-water cooling circuit through the boat. In what order does the seawater go?
options: Heat exchanger, seacock, strainer, exhaust, impeller pump
Seacock, impeller pump, exhaust, strainer, heat exchanger
Strainer, seacock, heat exchanger, impeller pump, exhaust
Seacock, strainer, impeller pump, heat exchanger, exhaust
questions.why: Seawater is filtered, pumped through the heat exchanger and then injected into the exhaust to cool it.

questions.q: You have stopped the engine and let it cool. Where do you look first?

figure.title: Overheat
lines: Motored through a bay full of floating weed
Temperature alarm, little water at exhaust

options: The raw-water strainer
The battery terminals
The fuel filter
The engine oil level
questions.why: Floating weed or plastic is the commonest cause of lost cooling water; the strainer catches it.

questions.q: You take out the raw-water impeller. This is what you find. What do you do?

figure.title: Old impeller
lines: Two vanes broken off and missing

options: Fit the new one; the pieces wash out the exhaust
Find the missing pieces before fitting the new one
Fit the new one and run at high revs to clear it
Refit the old one; four vanes are still enough
questions.why: Broken vanes travel on and block the heat exchanger inlet; recover every piece.

questions.q: The coolant level is low on a freshwater-cooled engine. Where and how do you top it up?
options: Header tank, engine hot, with seawater
Raw-water strainer, engine running, with seawater
Header tank, engine cold, with coolant mix
Oil filler, engine cold, with fresh water
questions.why: The closed circuit holds antifreeze coolant under pressure; open the cap only when cold.

questions.q: The engine will not fire. Before you crank again, what do you do?
options: Open the strainer lid to let air out
Keep cranking — it will catch once warm
Give it full throttle and crank a minute
Close the raw-water seacock until it fires
questions.why: Cranking without firing keeps pumping water into the waterlock until it floods the engine; reopen once it runs.

questions.q: The temperature keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
options: Low coolant on the freshwater side
An impeller with missing vanes
A raw-water seacock half closed
Weed blocking the raw-water strainer
questions.why: Raw-water faults show as weak exhaust water; a strong flow points to the freshwater circuit.

questions.q: Motoring into a headsea at cruising revs, what does this tell you?

figure.title: Exhaust
lines: Revs drop when you open the throttle
Water flow at the exhaust normal

options: The engine is burning its own oil
The engine is overloaded or short of air
Water has got into the fuel
Coolant is leaking into the cylinders
questions.why: Black smoke is unburnt fuel: too much load (fouled hull or prop, headsea) or a blocked air intake.

questions.q: After an hour at cruising revs you see this. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Exhaust
lines: Oil on the dipstick lower than this morning

options: Warming up — it will clear soon
Water in the fuel — drain the bowl
Burning oil — report it to the base
Overloaded — ease back the throttle
questions.why: Blue smoke is oil burning in the cylinders: worn rings or valve seals, or an overfilled sump.

questions.q: On a cool morning the engine starts with white smoke that clears within a minute. What do you do?

figure.title: Start-up
lines: Air 10 °C, first start of the day
Good water flow at the exhaust

options: Stop — there is water in the fuel
Rev it hard to burn the smoke off
Stop — the head gasket has failed
Nothing — normal for a cold diesel
questions.why: Some unburnt fuel and vapour are normal until the cylinders warm up.

questions.q: During the daily check, the oil on the dipstick looks like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Dipstick
lines: Level slightly above the max mark
Oil light brown and milky, like latte

options: Do not start it — call the base
Drain the fuel filter bowl
Run it to dry the oil out
Top up with fresh oil and go
questions.why: Milky oil means water in the engine (head gasket, cooler or siphoning exhaust); running it wrecks the bearings.

questions.q: You want an accurate reading of the engine oil level. When do you check it?
options: Engine running at idle, boat level
Engine stopped a while, boat level
Straight after stopping a long motor
Any time, even heeled under sail
questions.why: Oil must drain back to the sump and lie level for the dipstick to read true.

questions.q: During the daily check you press the alternator belt. What does this tell you?

figure.title: Alternator belt
lines: Deflects about 3 cm under your thumb
Shiny sides, black dust around the pulleys

options: Normal — the dust is from the exhaust
Too tight — slacken it off a little
Slack and wearing — get it tensioned
Normal — belts loosen when warm
questions.why: A belt should deflect about 1 cm under thumb pressure; black dust is rubber worn off a slipping belt.

questions.q: Coming into the berth you need to go from ahead to astern. How do you shift?
options: Shift at any revs once the boat is slow
Straight from ahead to astern at cruising revs
Stop the engine, then select astern
Throttle to idle, pause in neutral, then astern
questions.why: Shifting at idle through neutral protects the gearbox and the clutch.

questions.q: Motoring along the coast off Paros, you notice this. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Under power
lines: Speed 3 kn at your usual cruising revs
You crossed a line of fishing floats

options: A line or net round the propeller
The gearbox oil level is too low
The raw-water strainer is blocked
The fuel filter is partly blocked
questions.why: Vibration with lost speed at normal revs is a fouled prop; stop and check before it damages the shaft.

questions.q: In astern your stern walks to port. You must turn round in a narrow marina fairway. Which way do you turn?

figure.note: Narrow fairway · stern walks to port in astern

options: To port — astern bursts kick the bow to port
To starboard — astern kicks the stern to port
To port — the bow follows the prop walk
Either way — prop walk only matters at speed
questions.why: Short bursts ahead with full starboard helm and astern in between both rotate the boat clockwise.

questions.q: Reversing towards the quay with sternway on, you want the stern to go to port. Which way do you turn the wheel?
options: To starboard — astern, the bow follows the wheel
Amidships — steer with prop walk only
To port — astern, the stern follows the wheel
To starboard — astern, steering is reversed
questions.why: With sternway on, the stern moves the way you turn the wheel.

questions.q: Stopped in a tight marina, you want to swing the stern sideways without gaining much speed. What do you do?
options: Rudder hard over, a long gentle push astern
Rudder hard over, coast in neutral
Rudder amidships, a short burst astern
Rudder hard over, a short burst ahead
questions.why: Prop wash over the rudder turns the boat before she gathers way.

questions.q: Motoring slowly ahead, you turn to port. Which part of your boat swings towards the moored yacht?

figure.note: Turning to port, moored yacht close to starboard

options: The stern — it swings out opposite the turn
The bow — the boat pivots round the stern
The bow — it always swings towards the wind
Neither — the boat pivots round its middle
questions.why: Going ahead a yacht pivots about a third from the bow, so the stern swings wide.

questions.q: You approach the fuel quay at 4 knots, planning a hard burst astern at the last moment. What is the problem?
options: None — astern stops a yacht in her own length
She carries way and the stern kicks sideways
The engine always stalls when shifted astern
The rudder locks hard over when you go astern
questions.why: A heavy yacht needs several lengths to stop, and prop walk swings the stern; come in slowly.

questions.q: Your charter catamaran is stopped in the marina. You want to spin her to starboard on the spot. What do you do?

figure.note: Catamaran, twin engines · turn to starboard

options: Port engine astern, starboard in neutral
Both engines ahead, wheel hard to starboard
Port engine ahead, starboard engine astern
Starboard engine ahead, port engine astern
questions.why: Twin screws far apart give a turning couple: push one side forward and pull the other back.

questions.q: You check the stern gland of a traditional packed shaft. What do you do?

figure.title: Stern gland, engine in gear
lines: Packed gland on a turning shaft
Two or three drops a minute
No drips with the shaft stopped

options: Stop the engine and call the base
Tighten it until it is fully dry
Close the cockpit drain seacock
Nothing — a slow drip keeps it cool
questions.why: Packing needs a few drops a minute with the shaft turning to lubricate and cool it.

questions.q: This is your morning check on a saildrive boat. What do you do?

figure.title: Saildrive check
lines: Engine oil: clean, at the mark

options: Seawater is in the leg — report it now
Diesel bug — drain the fuel filter bowl
Normal condensation — top it up later
Coolant leak — top up the header tank
questions.why: Milky saildrive oil means the lower seals let seawater in; the leg can fail and must be inspected.

questions.q: At check-in you lift the floor over the saildrive. What do you do?

figure.title: Saildrive well
lines: Seawater pooled on top of it

options: Normal — the seal is meant to weep
Report it — the hull seal may be leaking
Sponge it dry and check again next week
Normal — it is rain from the cockpit
questions.why: The rubber diaphragm is the only seal round a big hole in the hull; any seawater there is serious.

questions.q: Holding the bow off the berth against a crosswind, you have run the bow thruster without a break. It now stops. Why?
options: The thruster fuse is meant to blow each time
The engine is off — the thruster needs it in gear
It overheated and cut out — use short bursts
The thruster's shear pin has broken
questions.why: Thrusters are built for short bursts; a thermal cut-out stops them when they overheat.

questions.q: Motor-sailing off Lefkada, this happens. What do you do?

figure.title: Steering
lines: Boat rounds up, no response to the wheel
No bang, no water coming in

options: Press Standby — the autopilot is slipping
Call Mayday — the rudder has fallen off
Turn the wheel harder to free the jam
Fit the emergency tiller and steer with it
questions.why: A slack wheel means the cable or linkage has failed; the emergency tiller goes straight on the rudder stock.

questions.q: You are on autopilot when a fishing boat appears ahead. You need to steer by hand at once. What do you do?
options: Press Standby, then take the wheel
Press Auto again to cancel the course
Switch off the main battery isolator
Turn the wheel hard; the pilot gives way
questions.why: Standby releases the autopilot drive so the wheel answers you.

questions.q: At check-in the base points out the emergency tiller in the lazarette. What do you do?
options: Put it ashore — the wheel has a spare cable
Try it on the rudder stock and stow it handy
Leave it there — it is for the surveyor
Nothing — the autopilot steers if needed
questions.why: The emergency tiller is useless if nobody knows where it fits or where it lives.

questions.q: Raising the anchor, the windlass stops and its breaker has tripped. What do you do?
options: Switch off the engine and try again
Fit a bigger breaker from the spares
Let it cool, find the cause, reset it once
Hold the breaker on and keep winding
questions.why: The breaker protects the motor and wiring; something is overloading it.

questions.q: You are about to raise the anchor with the electric windlass. What do you do first?
options: Switch on the bow thruster too
Turn the battery isolator off
Stop the engine to save the battery
Start the engine to support the battery
questions.why: A windlass draws over 100 A; the running alternator keeps the voltage up.

questions.q: The chain has jumped off the gypsy. A crew member reaches in to free it while another stands on the foot switch. What do you say?
options: Switch the windlass off at the breaker
Let him wear gloves and carry on
Keep winding slowly while he frees it
Use the up switch in short bursts only
questions.why: A windlass can take a finger in an instant; switch it off at the breaker before hands go near the gypsy.

questions.q: The boat has rested all afternoon with nothing switched on. What does the house bank reading tell you?
options: About 90 % — no need to charge
About half charged — time to charge
Fully charged — 12 V is the target
About 10 % — the bank is ruined
questions.why: Resting 12.7 V ≈ full, 12.2 V ≈ 50 %, below 12.0 V deeply discharged.

questions.q: The engine is running. A crew member says the batteries are being overcharged. Are they right?
options: Yes — 12.7 V is the safe maximum
Yes — turn the isolator off now
No — it is normal while charging
Yes — stop the engine at once
questions.why: While charging a 12 V bank reads 13.8–14.4 V.

questions.q: At anchor, how many amp-hours does the house bank supply in a day?
options: About 240 Ah
About 12 Ah
About 96 Ah
About 120 Ah
questions.why: Amps × hours for each: 96 + 10 + 10 + 5 = 121 Ah.

questions.q: Starting full, how many days can you stay at anchor before you must charge?

lines: Daily use per 24 h, no solar

options: 2 days
1 day
4 days
3 days
questions.why: Half of 400 Ah = 200 Ah usable; 200 ÷ 100 = 2 days.

questions.q: The house bank is 100 Ah down. Roughly how long must you run the engine to put it back?

lines: Alternator current into the house bank

options: About 10 minutes at high revs
At least 2½ hours, more as it tapers
About 40 minutes at cruising revs
About 1 hour if you rev it up
questions.why: 100 Ah ÷ 40 A = 2.5 h, and the current falls as the bank fills.

questions.q: It is a sunny midday at anchor. Why is the solar giving so little?

lines: 200 W panel on the stern arch
Boom swinging across it at anchor

options: Med heat stops panels working
The controller stops above 50 %
The boom shades part of the panel
Solar only charges the engine bank
questions.why: Even a small shadow across one cell cuts a panel's output sharply.

questions.q: You arrive at a marina in Croatia and connect shore power. In what order?
options: Either order with the RCD on
Pedestal first, boat breakers on
Pedestal end first, then the boat
Boat end first, then the pedestal
questions.why: The live end goes in last and comes out first, so you never handle a live plug.

questions.q: On shore power, the RCD trips every time you switch on the water heater. What do you do?

figure.title: Shore power
lines: RCD trips when heater switched on

options: Leave the heater off — it leaks to earth
Hold the RCD in until the heater warms
Bypass the RCD for the heater circuit
Run a second shore cable for the heater
questions.why: An RCD trips on current leaking to earth, a shock risk; find the fault, never bypass it.

questions.q: The base tells you this at the end of the week. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Anodes
lines: Week on shore power in a busy marina
Shaft anode half gone in one week

options: Stray current from the bow thruster
Galvanic current through the shore earth
The batteries overcharging the hull
Normal wear in warm Med water
questions.why: The shore earth links your underwater metals to other boats; a galvanic isolator blocks that current.

questions.q: At anchor a crew member wants to use a 2000 W hair dryer. Can they?
options: Yes — in bursts under a minute
Yes — with the engine idling
No — it overloads the inverter
Yes — once the bank shows 12.7 V
questions.why: An inverter cannot supply more than its rating; it trips or fails.

questions.q: Roughly what current does this draw from the 12 V house bank?
options: About 900 A
About 9 A
About 4 A
About 90 A
questions.why: 1000 W ÷ 12 V ≈ 83 A, plus inverter losses.

questions.q: Before a night passage the navigation lights do not work. You reset the breaker and it trips again at once. What do you do?
options: Leave it off and look for a short
Fit a higher-rated breaker
Switch to the other battery bank
Hold the breaker on until it stays
questions.why: A breaker that trips straight away is protecting the wiring from a short; find it first.

questions.q: The fridge fuse has blown. Which do you fit from the spares box?
options: A strip of foil
The 10 A fuse
The 20 A fuse
The 5 A fuse
questions.why: Replace like with like; a bigger fuse lets the wiring overheat.

questions.q: Anchored overnight with the fridge on, where do you set the battery selector?
options: Both banks together
Engine bank only
House bank only
Off for the night
questions.why: Keep the engine battery out of the house loads so you can always start in the morning.

questions.q: This is the house bank first thing in the morning. What do you do?
options: Top up the cells with seawater
Run the fridge off the engine bank
Nothing — a normal reading
Cut loads and charge now
questions.why: Below 12.0 V the bank is deeply discharged and damaged if left there.

questions.q: Motoring for two hours, you smell rotten eggs near the battery locker. What is happening?

lines: Battery cases warm to the touch

options: Overcharging — stop charging, ventilate
Holding tank smell — pump out soon
Diesel leak — check the fuel filter
Normal fast charge — open the locker
questions.why: Above about 14.8 V a faulty regulator boils the batteries and they give off gas.

questions.q: The water pump keeps running but the tap only spits air. What do you do?

figure.title: Galley tap
lines: Air and spluttering from the tap

options: Leave the pump on to clear the air
Switch off the pump and change tanks
Fit a bigger fuse to the pump
Prime it with the galley tap open
questions.why: The tank is empty; a pump running dry burns out.

questions.q: At night, with every tap closed, you hear the water pump run for a few seconds every few minutes. Why?

figure.title: Water pump
lines: All taps closed, no one using water

options: The water heater is warming up
The tanks are full and overflowing
A leak or a dripping tap somewhere
Normal — it keeps the pressure up
questions.why: A pressure pump only runs when water leaves the system; look in the bilge too.

questions.q: How many days can you go before refilling the tanks?

figure.title: Water
lines: Careful use: 20 litres each a day

options: 5 days
2 days
6 days
3 days

questions.q: Two days from the next water quay, the tanks are a quarter full. Which habit saves the most?
options: Washing up in seawater first
Pumping the heads less often
Drinking bottled water instead
Switching off the water heater
questions.why: Washing up and showers use the most fresh water; the heads already flush with seawater.

questions.q: Your charter boat has a watermaker. Where do you avoid running it?
options: At anchor over clean sand
In the marina, where oily water fouls it
Offshore, where the water is saltier
Under sail, while the boat heels
questions.why: Oil and dirt in harbour water ruin the membrane; make water in clean sea.

questions.q: At anchor with no shore power, the crew want hot showers. When will the water be hot?
options: Only after the gas boiler is lit
Only once the solar has charged
After motoring — the engine heats it
Any time — the heater runs off the batteries
questions.why: The calorifier is heated by engine coolant, or by its 230 V element on shore power.

questions.q: You arrive in a Croatian marina for the night. Where do you set the heads Y-valve?
options: Overboard — the marina is flushed
Either — rules apply at anchor only
Overboard, with plenty of flushing
Holding tank — nothing overboard
questions.why: No sewage goes overboard in marinas and harbours; use the holding tank and a pump-out.

questions.q: Your holding tank is full and you are anchored in a small crowded bay. What do you do?
options: Empty it at a pump-out or far offshore
Empty it here if you add a cleaner
Empty it now — the tide carries it away
Empty it at night when nobody swims
questions.why: Only discharge at a pump-out station or well out to sea where local rules allow.

questions.q: In Göcek a Turkish coastguard officer asks to see your blue card. What is it?
options: Your VHF radio operator's licence
A log of your holding-tank pump-outs
Your cruising permit for Turkey
Proof of the boat's third-party cover
questions.why: Turkey's blue card logs each pump-out; boats without a record risk a heavy fine.

questions.q: Sailing heeled, you find the heads bowl slowly filling with seawater. What is happening?

figure.title: Heads
lines: Bowl slowly filling with clean seawater
Y-valve set to the holding tank

options: The holding tank is overflowing back
Rain from the deck is draining in
Seawater siphons in through the inlet
The bilge pump is pushing water back
questions.why: Heeled, the inlet can siphon if its seacock is open; close heads seacocks after use.

questions.q: You check the engine-intake seacock. Is it open or closed?
options: Half open
Open
It depends on the maker
Closed
questions.why: A ball-valve seacock is open when the handle lies along the pipe, closed when across it.

questions.q: At check-in, the galley sink seacock will not turn. What do you do?
options: Report it to the base before you sail
Leave it — seacocks are meant to stay fixed
Hammer the handle until it moves
Grease the handle and sail anyway
questions.why: Every seacock must close in an emergency; exercise them and get a seized one fixed.

questions.q: This is what you find under the aft cabin. What do you do first?

figure.title: Leak
lines: Through-hull snapped off below its seacock
Water pouring in through the hole
Tapered wooden bung tied beside it

options: Run the bilge pump and wait
Hammer in the softwood bung
Close the seacock above the break
Stuff a towel in and keep sailing
questions.why: A tapered softwood bung, tied beside each through-hull, plugs a broken fitting.

questions.q: Sailing on a beam reach, the electric bilge pump runs every ten minutes. What do you do?
options: Nothing — pumps cycle when boats heel
Close all seacocks and keep sailing
Find the source — start by tasting it
Switch the pump off to save the battery
questions.why: Fresh means a tank or pipe; salt means a through-hull, stern gland or rudder seal.

questions.q: The bilge is full, but the manual pump moves almost no water. What do you check first?

figure.title: Manual bilge pump
lines: Bilge water over the floor boards
Handle pumps easily, little water out

options: The electric pump's float switch
The cockpit drain seacock
The pump handle's locking pin
The strum box at the end of the hose
questions.why: The strum box keeps debris out of the pump; when it clogs, the pump sucks nothing.

questions.q: At the berth, the electric bilge pump runs non-stop, but the bilge is dry. What is wrong?
options: The float switch is stuck up
Normal — it keeps the bilge dry
The pump is blocked by debris
The hull is leaking into the keel
questions.why: A jammed float switch runs the pump dry until it burns out or flattens the battery.

questions.q: You light the cooker but no gas comes through. What do you do?
options: Bleed the gas line at the cooker
Switch on the gas solenoid
Open the burner knob wider
Change the bottle for a new one
questions.why: The solenoid valve at the bottle shuts the gas off until switched on at its panel.

questions.q: You have finished cooking. How do you turn the gas off?
options: Burner knob only; leave the solenoid on
Burner knob off, then the solenoid
Solenoid off first, then the burner knob
Bottle valve only; leave the knob open
questions.why: Shutting the supply first burns off the gas left in the pipe.

questions.q: At check-in you find the gas locker's drain hole blocked with rubbish. Why does it matter?
options: The solenoid cannot vent heat
The regulator will freeze up
Rainwater will rust the bottle
Leaked gas cannot drain overboard
questions.why: Bottled gas is heavier than air; the locker drain lets any leak run out over the side.

questions.q: You are filling the tender's outboard. Which do you use?
options: Plain unleaded petrol
Any of the three
Diesel from the yacht
Petrol mixed with 2T oil
questions.why: A four-stroke has its own oil sump; only two-strokes take oil mixed in the fuel.

questions.q: You have just started the tender's outboard alongside the yacht. What do you do?

figure.title: Outboard
lines: No water from the tell-tale hole

options: Carry on and check it at the beach
Stop it — no cooling water flowing
Normal — it only flows at full throttle
Normal — the jet is for the exhaust
questions.why: The tell-tale stream shows the water pump is working; without it the engine overheats.

questions.q: On the beach, the outboard refuses to start. What is the fix?

figure.title: Outboard
lines: Fuel tap open, tank half full
Choke out, ten pulls, no firing

options: Tip the engine up
Take out the spark plug
Clip on the kill cord
Pull with more choke
questions.why: With the kill cord off, the stop switch keeps the engine from running.

questions.q: Heading back from the beach, the outboard does this. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Outboard
lines: Restarts after a rest, then dies again
Fuel in the tank, choke off

options: The kill cord is too long
The fuel mix is too rich
The spark plug is fouled
The fuel tank vent is closed
questions.why: A closed vent builds a vacuum in the tank until fuel stops; a pause lets air in again.

questions.q: First start of the day, the outboard is cold. How do you use the choke?
options: Pull it out, push it in as it warms
Pull it out and leave it all day
Use it only after the engine stalls
Leave it in — choke is for hot engines
questions.why: Choke richens the mixture for a cold start; left out, it floods and stalls the engine.

questions.q: At the fuel berth, how do you stop diesel spraying out of the tank breather?
options: Fill fast so the nozzle cuts out
Fill slowly and hold a rag at the vent
Fill to the brim so no air is left
Tape over the breather before filling
questions.why: The breather lets air out; when fuel comes up it, the tank is full. Spills are fined.

questions.q: You are leaving the marina, talking to the fuel dock on its working channel, but you must not miss a call on 16. Which radio function do you use?
options: Low power
Full squelch
Dual watch
DSC call log
questions.why: Dual watch listens to 16 and one working channel at the same time.

questions.q: Your VHF hisses loudly on 16 although nobody is talking. How do you set it?
options: Turn the squelch right up to maximum
Turn the volume right down to zero
Switch the set to low power, 1 W
Turn the squelch up until the hiss just stops
questions.why: Squelch set just past the hiss; any higher and weak stations are cut out.

questions.q: You are about to call the marina office. Which transmit power do you use?

figure.title: Calling the marina
lines: Ten yachts waiting to berth nearby

options: Low power, 1 W
Either — power changes nothing
High power to call, low to reply
High power, 25 W
questions.why: Use 1 W for short range so you do not block the channel for everyone nearby.

questions.q: The coast station answers your fixed set but not the handheld. Why?

figure.title: Two radios
lines: Fixed VHF: 25 W, antenna at the masthead
Handheld: 5 W, held in the cockpit

options: Handhelds only work on intership channels
Lower antenna and less power: VHF is line of sight
Coast stations do not answer handhelds
Handhelds cannot transmit on channel 16
questions.why: VHF range depends mostly on antenna height; a handheld reaches a few miles.

questions.q: You need to call the coastguard. How do you get the best range now?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Emergency antenna in the chart table

options: Fixed set with no antenna, on high power
Fixed set on low power to save the battery
Emergency antenna on the fixed set, rigged up high
Handheld on high power, from inside the cabin
questions.why: With the masthead antenna gone, range depends on getting a new antenna up high.

questions.q: A friend suggests chatting on channel 70 because it is always quiet. What do you tell them?
options: Fine, as long as you use low power
Only after asking the coastguard
Fine, but only inside the marina
No — 70 is for DSC data, never for voice
questions.why: Channel 70 carries only DSC alerts and calls; voice would block distress alerts.

questions.q: You call a friend's yacht on 16 and they answer. What do you do next?
options: Agree an intership channel such as 72 and move to it
Move to the marina's port channel for the chat
Stay on 16 but keep the chat under a minute
Move both radios to channel 70 for the chat
questions.why: Channel 16 is for calling and distress; conversations move to an intership channel.

questions.q: You want to call the yacht Thalassa from your yacht Kalliope. Which call is correct?
options: Hello Thalassa, Kalliope here, over and out
Thalassa ×3, this is Kalliope ×3, over
This is Thalassa ×3, Kalliope ×3, out
Kalliope ×3, calling Thalassa, over
questions.why: Name the station called, then "this is" and your own name, end with OVER.

questions.q: The marina has given you your berth. You have nothing more to say and expect no reply. Which proword ends the call?
options: OVER
OVER AND OUT
OUT
ROGER
questions.why: OVER asks for a reply, OUT ends the call; never both together.

questions.q: The marina asks you to wait outside the fuel dock until called. You understand and will do as asked. Which single proword says both?
options: AFFIRMATIVE
SAY AGAIN
ROGER
WILCO
questions.why: WILCO = received, understood and will comply; ROGER only means received.

questions.q: The marina's reply was broken up and you missed the berth number. What do you say?
options: SAY AGAIN
WAIT
REPEAT
CORRECTION
questions.why: SAY AGAIN asks for the message again; REPEAT is not a VHF proword.

questions.q: You have fitted a new VHF antenna and want to check that the radio transmits. What do you do?
options: Make a voice test call on channel 70
Ask the marina or a nearby yacht on a working channel
Call the coastguard on 16 for a radio check
Press the DSC distress button briefly to test
questions.why: Radio checks go on a working channel; 16 and 70 must stay clear for distress.

questions.q: You must spell your yacht's name, Hydra, over the radio. Which is correct?
options: Hotel Yellow Delta Romeo Alpha
Hotel Yankee Delta Roger Alpha
Hotel Yankee Delta Romeo Alpha
Harbour Yankee Delta Romeo Alpha
questions.why: Use the international phonetic alphabet so names survive a bad signal.

questions.q: Reading out your MMSI, how do you say the digits 3, 5 and 9?
options: Trey, fife, nine
Tree, five, nein
Three, five, nine
Tree, fife, niner
questions.why: Radio numbers: tree, fower, fife, niner — they cannot be confused.

questions.q: You give your position by radio from this landmark. What do you say?
options: 180° from Cape Sounion light, 2 miles
180° to Cape Sounion light, 2 miles
Cape Sounion light 2 miles, heading 180°
000° from Cape Sounion light, 2 miles
