questions.why: A position by landmark is the true bearing FROM the landmark, then the distance.

questions.q: Can you use the yacht's VHF for routine calls this week?

figure.title: Charter check-in
lines: Fixed DSC VHF and a handheld aboard
Ship radio licence in the papers

options: Yes — if the charter base gives permission
No — routine use needs an operator's certificate (SRC)
Yes — no licence is needed within 12 miles
Yes — the ship's licence covers anyone aboard
questions.why: The ship licence covers the set; the operator needs a certificate such as the SRC.

questions.q: Your DSC radio shows this incoming call. Who is calling you?
options: A group of ships
An EPIRB
A coast station
Another yacht
questions.why: An MMSI starting 00 is a coast station; a single 0 is a group; ships start with the country code.

questions.q: You have a few seconds to spare before you send the DSC alert. How do you send it?

figure.title: Flooding
lines: Crew in lifejackets, DSC radio on

options: Send it undesignated — DSC cannot carry the nature
Send an individual call to the nearest yacht
Send an all-ships routine call on channel 70
Select "flooding" as the nature, then hold the red button
questions.why: With time in hand, give the nature of distress so rescuers know what to bring.

questions.q: What is the quickest correct way to raise the alarm now?

figure.title: Knocked down
lines: Yacht on her side, water pouring in
She will sink within a minute
DSC radio at the chart table

options: Hold the red button: an undesignated alert
Speak the MAYDAY on 70 first, then on 16
Make an individual DSC call to the coastguard
Select the nature of distress first, then send it
questions.why: An undesignated alert still sends your MMSI and position; seconds count.

questions.q: Your DSC distress alert has gone out. What do you do next?
options: Wait silently until the coastguard calls back
Send the voice MAYDAY on channel 16
Send the alert again by hand every minute
Give the voice MAYDAY on channel 70
questions.why: DSC raises the alarm; the details follow by voice on 16. The radio repeats the alert itself.

questions.q: Your DSC radio sounds this alarm. What do you do first?

figure.title: DSC alarm
lines: Position: about 20 miles south of you

options: Silence the alarm and carry on
Relay the alert to all ships by DSC
Listen on 16 for the voice MAYDAY that follows
Acknowledge the alert with your own DSC
questions.why: Coast stations acknowledge DSC alerts; yachts listen on 16 and help by voice.

questions.q: Your crew tells you what just happened at the chart table. How do you put it right?

figure.title: False alert
lines: A child pressed the red DSC button

options: Wait for the coastguard to call you back on 16
Switch the radio off and say nothing more
Send a second DSC alert to cancel the first
Cancel it on the set, then tell all stations on 16
questions.why: Cancel at once: "All stations, this is…, cancel my distress alert of [time] UTC".

questions.q: What will a distress alert from this radio tell the rescue centre?
options: Your MMSI, but not your position
Your position, but not your MMSI
Nothing — the alert will not send
Your MMSI and your satellite position
questions.why: DSC takes the position from the GPS; without it, enter it by hand or give it by voice.

questions.q: You want to talk to a friend's yacht whose MMSI you know, without calling on 16. How?
options: A voice call on channel 70
An individual DSC call to their MMSI
An all-ships DSC call
A DSC distress call with their MMSI
questions.why: An individual call rings only their set and proposes a working channel.

questions.q: Which radio call do you make now?

figure.title: Man overboard
lines: The crew have lost sight of the casualty

options: A routine call to the coastguard
SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY
PAN-PAN
questions.why: A person in the water and out of sight is in grave and imminent danger.

questions.q: What call do you make in this situation?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Rig cut away, no injuries, hull sound
Engine unusable: lines round the prop
Drifting 1 kn towards a coast 6 miles off

options: SÉCURITÉ
No call — wait for the wind
MAYDAY
PAN-PAN
questions.why: Urgent help needed but no immediate danger to life: urgency, not distress.

questions.q: What call do you make about this?

figure.title: Container adrift
lines: In the ferry route off Mykonos
Your own yacht is not at risk

options: SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY
MAYDAY RELAY
PAN-PAN
questions.why: A danger to navigation is a safety message: SÉCURITÉ.

questions.q: Which call gets this crew member medical advice and help?

figure.title: Injury aboard
lines: Crew fell in the cabin: arm likely broken
15 miles from port, wants a doctor

options: SÉCURITÉ to all stations
PAN-PAN medico to the coastguard
An undesignated DSC alert
MAYDAY to all stations
questions.why: Serious but not life-threatening: an urgency (PAN-PAN) call for medical help.

questions.q: Which call do you make for this crew member?

figure.title: Collapse in the cockpit
lines: Barely breathing, CPR may be needed

options: A routine call to a doctor in Kos
PAN-PAN medico
MAYDAY
SÉCURITÉ
questions.why: A life in immediate danger is distress, even when the yacht itself is fine.

questions.q: You want to warn other boats about a large log drifting in the channel. How do you transmit it?
options: Read the warning out by voice on channel 70
Send an undesignated DSC distress alert about it
Give the whole warning on 16 every 10 minutes
Announce SÉCURITÉ on 16, details on a working channel
questions.why: Safety messages are announced on 16 and passed on a working channel.

questions.q: What is missing from this message?

figure.title: Your MAYDAY draft
lines: Holed and sinking, need immediate help

options: The position
The yacht's home port
The weather
The skipper's name
questions.why: MIPDANIO: MMSI, identity, position, distress, assistance, number, information, over.

questions.q: Your MAYDAY has given position, nature, help needed and number aboard. What goes in the last part before OVER?
options: The skipper's full name and licence number
Other useful facts: liferaft, EPIRB, hull colour
Your home port, last port and destination
The charter company's name and phone number
questions.why: The "I" in MIPDANIO: anything that helps rescuers find and help you.

questions.q: Nobody has answered. What is your next step to raise help?

figure.title: No reply
lines: No answer, the radio seems to work

options: Switch to channel 70 and call by voice
Wait an hour, then try the radio again
Activate the EPIRB and keep repeating the MAYDAY
Abandon ship into the liferaft at once
questions.why: Use every means of alerting: EPIRB by satellite, VHF, then visual signals.

questions.q: You hear this on channel 16. What is your part?

figure.title: MAYDAY heard
lines: Yacht on fire 30 miles north of you

options: Send a MAYDAY RELAY to all stations at once
Acknowledge the MAYDAY yourself, then stand by
Call the burning yacht on 16 to offer advice
Stay off 16, keep listening, note the details
questions.why: The coast station is in control; keep the channel clear and be ready to help.

questions.q: No one has answered this MAYDAY. What do you do?

figure.title: MAYDAY, no answer
lines: No coast station answers after 3 minutes
You can be there in 30 minutes

options: Acknowledge, head there, inform the coast station
Send your own DSC distress alert for them
Stay silent — only coast stations may reply to it
Switch to channel 70 and call them by voice
questions.why: If no coast station answers and you can help, acknowledge: "RECEIVED MAYDAY".

questions.q: How do you help from here?

figure.title: Faint MAYDAY
lines: Weak MAYDAY from a yacht 40 miles away
No station has answered for 5 minutes
You cannot reach them in time

options: Acknowledge it and say you are coming
Send a MAYDAY RELAY to the coast station
Stay silent — you are too far to help
Call the yacht on 16 for more details
questions.why: If you cannot help yourself, pass the distress on to someone who can.

questions.q: You see this and hear nothing on the radio. What do you do?

figure.note: Red hand flare from this yacht

options: Assume someone is testing old flares
Sound five short blasts to reply
MAYDAY RELAY on 16, then go to help
Wait to see if they send a MAYDAY
questions.why: A vessel that cannot call for itself needs you to relay and assist.

questions.q: You must pass on a distress message for a yacht that cannot transmit. How does your call begin?
options: SÉCURITÉ ×3, all stations ×3, [their yacht] in distress
MAYDAY ×3, this is [their yacht] ×3
PAN-PAN ×3, all stations ×3, this is [your yacht] ×3
MAYDAY RELAY ×3, all stations ×3, this is [your yacht] ×3
questions.why: MAYDAY RELAY, then your own identity; the distressed vessel's details follow.

questions.q: You are about to call the marina on 16 when you hear "SEELONCE MAYDAY". What do you do?
options: Stay off 16 until you hear SEELONCE FEENEE
Reply ROGER, then make your call
Make your call quickly — it is short
Wait five minutes, then call
questions.why: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes silence on the channel for all but the distress traffic.

questions.q: After a long rescue you hear "SEELONCE FEENEE" on 16. What does it mean?
options: Restricted working may resume with care
The distress is over; normal use of 16 resumes
Silence: distress traffic still in progress
The casualty is found but not yet rescued
questions.why: SEELONCE FEENEE ends the distress traffic and the radio silence.

questions.q: During a long search you hear "PRUDONCE", and you need to arrange a berth. What may you do?
options: Calls by voice on channel 70 only, not on 16
Nothing at all until you hear SEELONCE FEENEE
Short, essential calls only — the distress is not over
Any call you like — the distress is over now
questions.why: PRUDONCE: restricted working allowed while the distress continues.

questions.q: Mid-crossing, which equipment can still alert a rescue centre on its own?

figure.title: Passage plan
lines: Middle 40 miles beyond VHF coast range
Aboard: DSC VHF, EPIRB, handheld VHF

options: The handheld VHF on high power
The DSC VHF, through a coast station
The DSC VHF, on channel 70
The EPIRB, by satellite
questions.why: Beyond VHF coast range (GMDSS area A1), satellite alerting is what reaches a rescue centre.

questions.q: Before a night passage you want the latest navigational warnings for the area — lights out, drifting objects, firing exercises. Where do you look?
options: Navtex
Channel 70
The DSC call log
The AIS display
questions.why: Navtex prints navigational, weather and SAR warnings automatically.

questions.q: You are sailing near Paros when your Navtex shows this. What does it ask of you?

figure.title: Navtex message
lines: SAR: yacht overdue, 12 m, white hull
Vessels in the area keep a lookout

options: Nothing — it is for coastguard vessels
Keep a sharp lookout and report any sighting
Return to port until the search ends
Send a MAYDAY RELAY at once
questions.why: SAR messages ask all vessels in the area to watch and report.

questions.q: Which signal shows the lifeboat where you are?

figure.title: Daylight search
lines: Lifeboat in sight 1 mile away, searching

options: A torch flashed at it
Red parachute rocket
Orange smoke
White hand flare
questions.why: Orange smoke is the daylight signal when help is close.

questions.q: Which flare do you light to guide the lifeboat in?

figure.title: Night search
lines: It has not seen you yet

options: Orange smoke
White hand flare
Red parachute rocket
Red hand flare
questions.why: At night with help close, a red hand flare pinpoints you.

questions.q: Which signal must you not use now?

figure.title: Helicopter overhead
lines: Pilot asks you to show your position

options: Red parachute rocket
A torch shone on the sails
Orange smoke
Red hand flare
questions.why: A rocket can hit the helicopter; use hand flares or smoke.

questions.q: You must light a red hand flare on a yacht in 15 knots of wind. How do you hold it?
options: Above your head, pointing upwind
At arm's length over the leeward side
Upright in the middle of the cockpit
At arm's length over the windward side
questions.why: Leeward, so hot drips and smoke blow away from you and the boat.

questions.q: You find these flares aboard during the charter check-out. What do you do?
options: Keep them — dry, sealed flares never expire
Fire a couple off at sea to test the rest
Ask for new flares; hand the old ones in for disposal
Throw them overboard well outside the marina
questions.why: Out-of-date flares may fail; never fire or dump them except in distress.

questions.q: What is the person in the dinghy telling you?

figure.note: Person slowly raising and lowering both arms

options: They are waving hello
They want you to slow down
Keep clear — divers below
They are in distress and need help
questions.why: Slowly raising and lowering outstretched arms is a distress signal.

questions.q: At night your radio is dead and you have only a torch. Which signal asks for help?
options: SOS: three short, three long, three short
Five short flashes, repeated every minute
One long flash, repeated every minute
Three long flashes, repeated every minute
questions.why: SOS by light or sound is a recognised distress signal.

questions.q: What is this yacht asking for?

figure.note: Yacht flying code flag V (white, red X)

options: Keep clear — manoeuvring with difficulty
Assistance — but it is not in distress
Immediate help — grave and imminent danger
Help — I have a man overboard
questions.why: Flag V: "I require assistance". Distress is NC, flares, MAYDAY.

questions.q: What do you do with the EPIRB?

figure.title: Abandoning ship
lines: EPIRB in its bracket, not activated
Handheld VHF in the grab bag

options: Leave it — it will float free by itself
Throw it clear of the raft to float
Take it, switch it on, tie it to the raft
Keep it off to save the battery
questions.why: An activated EPIRB with you is how rescuers find the raft.

questions.q: Clearing the cockpit locker, you accidentally set off the EPIRB. What do you do?
options: Wait for the coastguard to call you
Leave it on until the battery runs out
Switch it off and say nothing
Switch it off and tell the coastguard at once
questions.why: Report a false alert at once so a rescue is not launched.

questions.q: You buy a PLB to wear on your lifejacket. What must you do before you go sailing?
options: Register it with your details
Test it by setting it off once
Nothing — it works straight from the box
Have the charter base program it
questions.why: Registration tells the rescue centre who you are and whom to call.

questions.q: Which device does what you want?

figure.title: Choosing a beacon
lines: Must alarm on your own chartplotter
And on nearby boats if someone falls in

options: A radar reflector
An AIS MOB beacon
A PLB
A 406 MHz EPIRB
questions.why: An AIS MOB beacon alarms on AIS sets nearby, including your own plotter.

questions.q: Which beacon on your lifejacket is most likely to bring rescue?

figure.title: Delivery trip
lines: 20 miles offshore, no ships in sight

options: A whistle — it carries over the water
An AIS MOB beacon — it alarms on nearby AIS
A PLB — it alerts a rescue centre by satellite
A strobe light — it is easy to see at night
questions.why: With nobody nearby, only a satellite alert reaches a rescue centre.

questions.q: What does this target on your plotter mean, and what do you do?
options: A wreck buoy: alter course to pass well clear
A fishing-net marker: keep well clear of it
A test transmission: note it and carry on
Survivors in distress: tell the coastguard and go
questions.why: An AIS-SART marks survivors; report it and assist.

questions.q: Why is the EPIRB mounted like this?

figure.title: Check-out
lines: In a bracket with a hydrostatic release

options: It floats free and switches on if she sinks
So it stays dry in the cockpit locker
So the crew can test it every morning
So it transmits all the time at sea
questions.why: A float-free EPIRB alerts even if the crew had no time to grab it.

questions.q: You activated the EPIRB an hour ago. A ship is now coming towards you, 2 miles away. What about the EPIRB?
options: Switch it off to save the battery
Leave it on until you are rescued
Switch it off — help has arrived
Switch it off and on for a new fix
questions.why: Its 121.5 MHz signal homes the rescuers in until you are safe.

questions.q: Which alert do you send first?

figure.title: Sinking near the coast
lines: Holed, sinking slowly, 5 miles off Naxos
Two yachts and a ferry in sight

options: The EPIRB only — it is the most reliable
A red parachute rocket only
DSC alert and voice MAYDAY on the VHF
A phone call to the charter base
questions.why: Near the coast VHF reaches the coastguard and nearby boats at once; add the EPIRB too.

questions.q: Which chartplotter button do you press at once?

figure.title: Man overboard at night
lines: Crew member falls over the side

options: Route
AIS targets
Track log
MOB
questions.why: The MOB button marks the spot where the casualty went in.

questions.q: You want to stay close to the casualty. What do you do at once?

figure.note: Close reach, crew has just gone over

options: Tack at once, leaving the headsail backed
Bear away onto a run to gain sea room
Hold course and drop all the sails first
Start the engine and go hard astern
questions.why: The quick-stop keeps the boat near the casualty.

questions.q: You are sailing back to the casualty. On which point of sail do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Returning to the casualty under sail

options: Run, dropping the sails at the last moment
Close reach, easing the sheets to slow down
Head to wind from 200 m away
Beam reach at speed, then luff up hard
questions.why: On a close reach you can spill wind to stop and fill the sails to go.

questions.q: How do you get the casualty aboard?

figure.title: Getting him back aboard
lines: Choppy sea, the stern is pitching

options: Tow him slowly alongside to calmer water
Two crew haul him in by the arms at the side
Halyard to the lifting loop, winched up at the side
Up the stern bathing ladder, as it is lowest
questions.why: A pitching stern can injure; a winched halyard does the lifting.

questions.q: This casualty must come out of the water. Which way do you lift him?

figure.title: Long immersion
lines: Very cold, confused, cannot help himself
Halyard and a spare sail ready

options: Lift him upright on the halyard, fast
Have him climb the stern ladder
Let him rest in the water first
Lift him horizontally, e.g. in a sail parbuckle
questions.why: A cold casualty lifted upright can collapse as blood pressure drops.

questions.q: The casualty is alongside at the shrouds. What is your first job?
options: Get a line on them so they stay attached
Lower the stern bathing ladder
Start lifting them by the arms
Put the engine astern to stop
questions.why: Once attached, the boat cannot drift away from the casualty.

questions.q: What is the quickest fix?

figure.title: Water in the heads
lines: Water spraying from a split hose
Hose runs to the heads inlet seacock

options: Run the bilge pump and wait
Close the seacock
Wrap the hose with tape
Send a MAYDAY first
questions.why: Close the valve and the leak stops; then repair.

questions.q: Which action stops most of the water fastest?

figure.title: Broken through-hull
lines: Seacock snapped off at the hull
Water gushing in through the hole

options: Pump and head for port as it is
Try to screw the seacock back on
Hammer a softwood bung into the hole
Stuff a towel in and keep sailing
questions.why: Tapered softwood bungs tied at each seacock are for exactly this.

questions.q: How can the engine help here?

figure.title: Losing the battle
lines: Water rising faster than all pumps

options: Run it flat out to reach port before she sinks
Stop it at once so it does not flood
Open its cooling seacock wider for more flow
Make it pump the bilge: intake hose into the bilge
questions.why: Close the raw-water seacock, lead the intake hose into the bilge: the engine pump bails.

questions.q: Where is the water most likely coming from?

figure.title: Bilge check
lines: Water in the bilge tastes fresh

options: A leak in the fresh-water tank or pipes
A split hose on a cockpit drain seacock
A crack in the hull below the waterline
A leaking stern gland on the shaft
questions.why: Taste it: fresh water comes from the tanks, salt water from the sea.

questions.q: How do you stop the water while you plug the hole?

figure.title: Hole in the bow
lines: Hole just above the waterline, starboard bow
On port tack, heeled to starboard
Water pours in with each wave

options: Bear away and sail faster
Tack onto starboard so the hole lifts clear
Motor straight into the waves
Ease the sheets but stay on port tack
questions.why: On starboard tack she heels to port, lifting the starboard bow out of the water.

questions.q: How do you reduce the draft to get off?

figure.title: Aground on sand
lines: Engine astern alone will not free her

options: Move all the crew and weight to the bow
Drop the mainsail and wait for help
Heel her: crew to one side, boom swung out
Fill the water tanks to settle her
questions.why: Heeling lifts the keel and reduces the draft.

questions.q: What is your next step?

figure.title: Still aground
lines: Bow on sand, deep water astern

options: Wait aboard for the tide to float her off
Go full ahead to push her over the bank
Lay the kedge ahead, on the sand bank
Take the kedge out astern by dinghy and winch off
questions.why: Kedge towards deep water; in the Med the tide will not float you off.

questions.q: You have just come off a rock you touched at slow speed. What do you check first?
options: Bilges, keel bolts and steering
The fuel and water levels
The sails and halyards
The anchor and windlass
questions.why: A grounding can loosen keel bolts and damage the rudder.

questions.q: Before you try to reverse off, what do you do?

figure.title: Hard on the rocks
lines: Hit rocks at 6 knots, stuck fast
Calm sea, 1 mile from a harbour

options: Full astern at once before it gets worse
Find the damage — off the rock she may sink
Heel her over and motor ahead
Abandon ship into the liferaft
questions.why: The rock may be plugging the hole; check before deep water.

questions.q: The mast may hole the hull. What do you do?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Mast broken, over the side to port
Rough sea, it is hammering the hull
Bolt cutters and tools at hand

options: Start the engine and motor clear of it
Lash it alongside and keep it with you
Cut it away: pull the pins, cut the shrouds
Haul it back aboard by hand with the crew
questions.why: In a sea a mast in the water acts as a battering ram.

questions.q: The broken rig has been cut away. Before you start the engine, what do you check?
options: The batteries are fully charged
The fuel tank is full
The engine oil level is correct
No lines or wires are left in the water
questions.why: A rope round the propeller leaves you without an engine.

questions.q: How do you get steering back?

figure.title: Steering failure
lines: Emergency tiller in the cockpit locker

options: Fit the emergency tiller to the rudder stock
Call for a tow at once and wait for it
Lock the wheel amidships with a line
Drop the sails and wait for help to come
questions.why: The emergency tiller bypasses the wheel steering.

questions.q: How do you steer the yacht home?

figure.title: Rudder lost
lines: Spare warps, a bucket, two winches

options: Lash the wheel amidships and motor
Tow a drogue on a bridle, steering with the winches
Motor at full speed and steer with the throttle
Stream the anchor from the bow
questions.why: A drogue pulled to one side or the other steers the stern.

questions.q: Before you take their line, what do you do?

figure.title: Tow offered
lines: Fishing boat offers to tow you in

options: Take the line at once, talk later
Refuse — only the coastguard may tow
Agree the terms: a tow, not salvage
Pay in cash once you are towed
questions.why: Without an agreement the helper may claim salvage on the yacht.

questions.q: Where do you make the towline fast on your yacht?

figure.note: Being towed by the boat ahead

options: To the pulpit rail at the bow
To a single bow cleat, well secured
Round the anchor windlass drum
To a bridle between both bow cleats
questions.why: A bridle spreads the load over two strong points.

questions.q: When may you touch the wire?

figure.title: Helicopter lift
lines: Winchman being lowered on the wire

options: After it has touched the water or deck
Never — the winchman grabs you
Only once it stops swinging
As soon as you can reach it
questions.why: The wire carries a static charge until it earths.

questions.q: The helicopter lowers a weighted hi-line to your yacht. What do you do with it?
options: Make it fast to a strong cleat to steady it
Pull it in by hand, keep it loose — never tie it
Let it trail in the water until the lift
Tie it to the casualty's harness at once
questions.why: The helicopter must be able to break away at any moment.

questions.q: How do you prepare the deck?

figure.title: Helicopter coming
lines: Cushions and sail bags on deck

options: Hoist full sail so the yacht rolls less
Send all the crew below out of the way
Drop the main, secure the boom and loose gear
Hoist the ensign so the helicopter can see you
questions.why: The downdraught catches anything loose; the winchman needs a clear area.

questions.q: In what order do you act?

figure.title: Sinking
lines: Deck nearly awash, she is going down
Liferaft in its cradle, grab bag ready

options: Launch the raft, then MAYDAY from it
Launch the raft and stay off the radio
Stay aboard until the deck is under
MAYDAY first, then launch the raft
questions.why: The MAYDAY goes from the yacht's fixed VHF while it still works.

questions.q: You have one minute before stepping into the liferaft. What do you take?
options: The grab bag and the EPIRB
The ship's papers
Spare fuel
Passports and phones
questions.why: The grab bag and EPIRB are what get you found and kept alive.

questions.q: How do you place the yacht to the wind?

figure.title: Fire aft
lines: Fire under the cockpit, out of control

options: It makes no difference once sails are down
Bow to the wind, so the smoke blows aft
Stern to the wind, to stop her rolling
Beam on to the wind, to keep her steady
questions.why: Keep the fire downwind of the crew.

questions.q: You are anchored off Hvar with no VHF and need sea rescue. Which phone number goes straight to MRCC Rijeka?
questions.why: In Croatia 195 is the sea search-and-rescue number; 112 also works.

questions.q: How do you call for help first?

figure.title: Medical emergency
lines: 4 miles off Bodrum, phone has signal

options: Wait a few minutes to see if he recovers
Phone the hospital in Bodrum for an ambulance
Phone the charter base and ask for advice
MAYDAY on VHF: coastguard and boats nearby hear it
questions.why: A VHF MAYDAY reaches every station in range at once; a phone call reaches one.
